uni-bsc-chem-physical-chemistry-2.title: Physical Chemistry II — Equilibrium, Kinetics & Electrochemistry
uni-bsc-chem-physical-chemistry-2.description: Chemical and ionic equilibria, the phase rule, chemical kinetics and catalysis, conductance and electrochemical cells with the Nernst equation, plus the standard physical chemistry practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Chemical equilibrium and the phase rule
courses.summary: Law of mass action, Kp, Kc and Kx, degree of dissociation, the thermodynamic basis of equilibrium (ΔG° = −RT ln K), Le Chatelier's principle and the van 't Hoff equation, and the Gibbs phase rule applied to the water and sulphur systems.
outcomes: Write K expressions and convert between Kp and Kc
Calculate degree of dissociation from Kp
Relate ΔG°, Q and K and predict the direction of reaction
Use the van 't Hoff equation to find K at another temperature
Apply F = C − P + 2 to one-component phase diagrams

lessons.title: Law of mass action, Kp and Kc

story.title: The brown gas in a sealed tube

scenes.text: A sealed tube of NO₂ is brown at room temperature and nearly colourless in ice.
2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ never stops reacting, but the forward and reverse rates become equal — dynamic equilibrium.

steps.title: Equilibrium constants
steps.body:
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD:

- **Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b** (concentrations in mol L⁻¹)
- **Kp = p_C^c p_D^d / p_A^a p_B^b** (partial pressures)
- **Kp = Kc (RT)^Δn**, Δn = (c + d) − (a + b) for gases only; Kp = Kx P^Δn
- Pure solids and liquids are omitted (activity = 1).
- Reversing a reaction gives 1/K; multiplying the equation by n gives Kⁿ.

steps.title: Solved: degree of dissociation of PCl₅
steps.body:
PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂. Start 1 mol PCl₅; α dissociates. Moles at equilibrium: (1 − α), α, α; total (1 + α).

- Kp = [α/(1+α) P]² / [(1−α)/(1+α) P] = **α²P/(1 − α²)**
- If α = 0.50 at P = 1.0 bar: Kp = 0.25/0.75 = **0.333 bar**
- At P = 4 bar: α²/(1 − α²) = 0.0833 → α² = 0.0769 → **α = 0.277** (pressure suppresses dissociation)

steps.title: Vapour density method
steps.body: For a dissociating gas, α = (D − d)/[d(n − 1)], where D = vapour density of undissociated gas, d = observed vapour density and n = moles of products per mole. E.g. PCl₅: D = 104.25; if d = 62.0, α = 42.25/62.0 = 0.68.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including solids or pure liquids in K.
- Counting non-gaseous species in Δn.
- Using R = 8.314 when concentrations are in mol L⁻¹ and pressures in bar; use 0.08314 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction to its Kp–Kc relation.

quiz.q: For C(s) + CO₂(g) ⇌ 2CO(g), Δn used in Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn is:
quiz.why: Only gases count: 2 mol CO minus 1 mol CO₂ gives Δn = 1; solid carbon is ignored.

quiz.q: If K for A ⇌ B is 10, K for 2B ⇌ 2A is:
quiz.why: Reversing gives 1/10, and doubling the equation squares it: (1/10)² = 0.01.

quiz.q: Increasing total pressure on PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ makes α:
quiz.why: From Kp = α²P/(1 − α²) at constant Kp, a larger P requires a smaller α; the equilibrium shifts to fewer gas moles.

quiz.q: Kc for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI with [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.10 M and [HI] = 0.70 M:

scenes.text: A plant chemist mixes reactants and products in odd ratios and asks which direction the reaction will move.
Comparing the reaction quotient Q with K, through ΔG, answers it every time.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
For an ideal gas μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln pᵢ. Summing over the reaction:

**ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q**

At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K, so **ΔG° = −RT ln K**.

- Q < K → ΔG < 0 → forward reaction
- Q > K → ΔG > 0 → reverse reaction
- Q = K → equilibrium

ΔG° < 0 means K > 1 (products favoured).

steps.title: Solved: direction from Q
steps.body:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Kp = 6.0 × 10⁵ at 298 K (bar⁻²). A mixture has p(N₂) = 1, p(H₂) = 1, p(NH₃) = 10 bar.

- Q = 10²/(1 × 1³) = 100
- Q < K, so ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) = 2477.6 × ln(1.667 × 10⁻⁴) = 2477.6 × (−8.70) = **−21.6 kJ**
- More NH₃ forms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ΔG° to decide direction for non-standard mixtures — use ΔG (i.e. compare Q with K).
- Forgetting to convert kJ to J in ln K = −ΔG°/RT.
- Saying K = 0 means no reaction; K is never exactly zero.

activity.prompt: Match each condition to the result.

quiz.q: ΔG° = 0 corresponds to K equal to:
quiz.why: From ΔG° = −RT ln K, ΔG° = 0 gives ln K = 0, so K = 1.

quiz.q: At 298 K, K = 1.0 × 10⁻³. ΔG° is about:
If Q > K, the reaction:
quiz.why: Q > K means too much product, so ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) > 0 for the forward direction and the reverse reaction occurs.

quiz.q: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q applies:
quiz.why: This equation gives ΔG for any mixture composition; at equilibrium it reduces to ΔG° = −RT ln K.

lessons.title: Le Chatelier's principle and the van 't Hoff equation

scenes.text: A fertiliser plant runs ammonia synthesis at about 200 bar and 700 K with an iron catalyst.
Low temperature would give more ammonia at equilibrium, but far too slowly. Engineers balance yield and rate.

steps.title: Le Chatelier's principle
steps.body:
A system at equilibrium responds to a change by shifting so as to partly oppose it.

- Add reactant → shifts forward
- Increase pressure → shifts to fewer gas moles
- Add inert gas at constant volume → no shift; at constant pressure → shifts to more gas moles
- Raise temperature → shifts in the endothermic direction (K changes)
- Catalyst → no shift; equilibrium reached faster

steps.title: van 't Hoff equation
steps.body:
From ΔG° = −RT ln K and Gibbs–Helmholtz: d ln K/dT = ΔH°/RT².

Integrated (ΔH° constant): **ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)**

A plot of ln K vs 1/T is a straight line of slope −ΔH°/R.

steps.title: Solved: K at a higher temperature
Solved: ΔH° from two K values
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a catalyst increases yield.
- Saying pressure changes K — it shifts composition; K depends only on T.
- Sign errors in the van 't Hoff equation; check that K rises with T for endothermic reactions.

activity.prompt: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH < 0), match the change to the effect on NH₃ at equilibrium.

quiz.q: For an exothermic reaction, raising temperature:
quiz.why: By van 't Hoff, d ln K/dT = ΔH°/RT²; with ΔH° < 0, K falls as T rises.

quiz.q: Slope of ln K vs 1/T is:
quiz.why: ln K = −ΔH°/RT + ΔS°/R, so the slope against 1/T is −ΔH°/R.

quiz.q: Adding an inert gas at constant pressure to PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂:
quiz.why: At constant pressure the volume grows, lowering partial pressures, so the equilibrium shifts to the side with more gas moles (forward).

quiz.q: A catalyst affects:
quiz.why: A catalyst lowers activation energy equally for forward and reverse steps, speeding attainment of equilibrium without changing K.

lessons.title: Phase equilibria: the Gibbs phase rule

scenes.text: Calibration labs keep a triple-point cell where ice, water and vapour coexist.
It can exist at only one temperature and pressure. The phase rule explains why.

steps.title: The phase rule
steps.body:
**F = C − P + 2**

- P = number of phases (physically distinct, separable parts)
- C = number of components (minimum independent species needed to describe all phases) = species − independent reactions − restrictions
- F = degrees of freedom (intensive variables that can be changed independently)

For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g): 3 species − 1 reaction = C = 2; P = 3 → F = 1.

steps.title: Water system
steps.body:
Phase diagram (P vs T) with three areas (ice, liquid, vapour; F = 2), three curves (F = 1) and one triple point (F = 0).

- OA: vaporisation curve, ends at the critical point (647 K, 221 bar)
- OB: sublimation curve
- OC: fusion curve, slopes **backwards** (negative slope) because ice is less dense than water
- O: triple point, 273.16 K and 611 Pa
- Dotted OA′: metastable supercooled water

steps.title: Sulphur system
steps.body: Four phases: rhombic (Sᵣ), monoclinic (Sₘ), liquid, vapour. Sᵣ ⇌ Sₘ transition at 368.5 K (95.5 °C). Three triple points are stable (Sᵣ/Sₘ/vapour, Sₘ/liquid/vapour, Sᵣ/Sₘ/liquid) plus a metastable one. All four phases can never coexist because F = 1 − 4 + 2 = −1 is impossible.

steps.title: Solved: counting C, P and F
steps.body:
- NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g) with no excess gas: species 3, reaction 1, restriction p(NH₃) = p(HCl) → C = 1; P = 2 → F = 1.
- Same with extra NH₃ added: restriction lost → C = 2, F = 2.
- Water at its normal boiling point (liquid + vapour): C = 1, P = 2 → F = 1 (fix P and T is fixed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting each solid compound in a mixture as one phase only if it is distinct; two solids = two phases, but a gas mixture is always one phase.
- Forgetting restrictions when counting components.
- Drawing the ice–water line with a positive slope.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to apply the phase rule to a system.
items: List all chemical species present
Subtract independent equilibria and concentration restrictions to get C
Count distinct phases P
Calculate F = C − P + 2
Interpret: invariant, univariant or bivariant

quiz.q: Degrees of freedom at the triple point of water:
quiz.why: C = 1 and P = 3, so F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0; the triple point is invariant.

quiz.q: The ice–water equilibrium line has a negative slope because:
quiz.why: Melting decreases volume (ΔV < 0), so by Clapeyron dP/dT = ΔH/TΔV is negative.

quiz.q: Number of components for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g):
quiz.why: Three species linked by one equilibrium give C = 3 − 1 = 2.

quiz.q: Why can four phases of sulphur never coexist?
options: The phase rule does not apply
quiz.why: For C = 1 and P = 4, F = 1 − 4 + 2 = −1, which is impossible, so at most three phases coexist.

questions.why: Gas moles change from 3 to 2, so Δn = −1.

questions.why: The equilibrium constant changes only with temperature, as shown by the van 't Hoff equation.

questions.q: Endothermic reaction: K at 300 K = 1.0, ΔH° = 20 kJ. K at 400 K is about:
Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium:
questions.why: Catalysts speed forward and reverse reactions equally and leave the equilibrium composition unchanged.

questions.q: In the water phase diagram, the area labelled 'liquid' has F =
questions.why: One phase of a one-component system: F = 1 − 1 + 2 = 2, so P and T can both vary.

questions.q: Triple point of water:
questions.why: Ice, water and vapour coexist only at 273.16 K and about 611 Pa.

questions.q: Kc for 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂ if Kc for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI is 50:
questions.why: Reversing the reaction inverts K: 1/50 = 0.02.

questions.q: Q = 5, K = 50. The reaction:
questions.why: Q < K means products are below their equilibrium level, so ΔG < 0 for the forward reaction.

questions.q: Rhombic ⇌ monoclinic sulphur transition temperature:
questions.why: Rhombic sulphur changes reversibly to monoclinic at about 95.5 °C (368.5 K).

questions.q: Components in a system of NH₄Cl(s) heated alone in a closed vessel:
questions.why: Three species, one reaction and the restriction p(NH₃) = p(HCl) give C = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.

questions.q: Kx for a reaction with Δn ≠ 0 depends on:
questions.why: Kx = Kp P^(−Δn), so at fixed T it still changes with total pressure when Δn ≠ 0.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Ionic equilibria
courses.summary: Ostwald's dilution law and pH of weak acids and bases, buffer solutions and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, salt hydrolysis, acid–base indicators, solubility product and the common-ion effect.
outcomes: Calculate pH and degree of ionisation of weak electrolytes
Design a buffer of required pH and predict its response to added acid
Find the pH of salt solutions from hydrolysis constants
Choose an indicator for a titration
Compute solubility from Ksp, with and without a common ion

lessons.title: Weak electrolytes, Ostwald's law and pH

scenes.text: 0.1 M HCl has pH 1, yet 0.1 M acetic acid in vinegar is only around pH 2.9.
Acetic acid ionises only slightly. Ostwald's dilution law tells us exactly how much.

steps.title: Ostwald's dilution law
steps.body:
HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, concentration C, degree of ionisation α:

- Ka = Cα²/(1 − α) ≈ Cα² (α ≪ 1)
- **α = √(Ka/C)**, **[H⁺] = √(Ka C)**, pH = ½(pKa − log C)
- Dilution increases α but decreases [H⁺].
- Water: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K; pH + pOH = 14; for a conjugate pair Ka × Kb = Kw.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using α ≈ √(Ka/C) when α > 5%: solve the quadratic instead.
- Applying the weak-acid formula to very dilute strong acids (10⁻⁸ M HCl is not pH 8; water's own H⁺ matters and pH ≈ 6.98).
- Forgetting that Kw changes with temperature (neutral pH at 37 °C ≈ 6.8).

activity.prompt: Match each solution to its approximate pH.

quiz.q: Diluting a weak acid solution 100-fold makes α:
quiz.why: α = √(Ka/C), so cutting C by 100 increases α by √100 = 10.

quiz.q: pH of 0.01 M HCOOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴):
Kb of CH₃COO⁻ if Ka of CH₃COOH is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵:
quiz.why: For a conjugate pair Kb = Kw/Ka = 10⁻¹⁴/1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.

quiz.q: pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl is approximately:
quiz.why: Water supplies about 10⁻⁷ M H⁺, which dominates; solving the full balance gives [H⁺] ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M, pH ≈ 6.98.

scenes.text: After a sprint, lactic acid floods Kavya's muscles, yet her blood pH barely moves from 7.4.
The carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer soaks up the extra H⁺.

steps.title: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
steps.body:
A buffer is a weak acid plus its conjugate base (or weak base plus conjugate acid).

- **pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid])**
- Basic buffer: pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base])
- Best buffering when [salt] = [acid] (pH = pKa); useful range pKa ± 1.
- **Buffer capacity** β = dn/dpH — moles of strong acid/base per litre needed to change pH by one unit.

steps.title: Solved: acetate buffer
steps.body:
0.10 M CH₃COOH + 0.20 M CH₃COONa, pKa = 4.74.

- pH = 4.74 + log(0.20/0.10) = 4.74 + 0.30 = **5.04**

Add 0.010 mol HCl to 1 L: acetate reacts → acid = 0.11, salt = 0.19.
- pH = 4.74 + log(0.19/0.11) = 4.74 + 0.237 = **4.98** (change of only 0.06)
- The same HCl in 1 L pure water would give pH 2.

steps.title: Solved: preparing a buffer
steps.body:
Make an NH₃/NH₄Cl buffer of pH 9.50 (pKb = 4.74).

- pOH = 4.50 = 4.74 + log([NH₄⁺]/[NH₃])
- log ratio = −0.24 → [NH₄⁺]/[NH₃] = **0.575**
- With 0.20 M NH₃, use 0.115 M NH₄Cl.

steps.title: Buffers in practice
steps.body:
- Blood: H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ (pKa ≈ 6.1 at 37 °C); ratio HCO₃⁻:H₂CO₃ ≈ 20:1 gives pH 7.4.
- Phosphate buffers (pKa₂ ≈ 7.2) in biochemistry labs.
- NH₃/NH₄Cl buffer (pH ≈ 10) for EDTA titration of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing [acid]/[salt] inside the log.
- Forgetting to update both concentrations after adding acid or base.
- Using pKb directly to give pH for a basic buffer (convert pOH → pH).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find pH after adding HCl to a buffer.
items: Find initial moles of weak acid and conjugate base
Subtract added H⁺ from the base and add it to the acid
Check the buffer is not exhausted
Apply pH = pKa + log(base/acid)
Compare with the initial pH

quiz.q: An acetate buffer with equal acid and salt concentrations has pH:
quiz.why: When [salt] = [acid] the log term is zero, so pH = pKa = 4.74.

quiz.q: Ratio [salt]/[acid] needed for pH 5.74 with acetic acid:
quiz.why: 5.74 = 4.74 + log ratio, so log ratio = 1 and ratio = 10.

quiz.q: Blood with pKa 6.1 and [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃] = 20 has pH:
Buffer capacity is greatest when:
quiz.why: Equal amounts of acid and conjugate base let the buffer neutralise added acid or base equally well, maximising β.

scenes.text: A solution of sodium acetate turns phenolphthalein pink, even though no base was added.
The acetate ion reacts with water to produce OH⁻. That is salt hydrolysis.

steps.title: Hydrolysis of salts
steps.body:
- **Weak acid + strong base salt** (CH₃COONa): A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻; Kh = Kw/Ka; **pH = 7 + ½pKa + ½log C** (basic)
- **Strong acid + weak base salt** (NH₄Cl): pH = 7 − ½pKb − ½log C (acidic)
- **Weak acid + weak base salt** (CH₃COONH₄): pH = 7 + ½pKa − ½pKb, independent of C
- Strong acid + strong base salt (NaCl): no hydrolysis, pH 7
- Degree of hydrolysis h = √(Kh/C)

steps.title: Acid–base indicators
steps.body:
An indicator HIn is a weak acid whose two forms differ in colour: pH = pK_In + log([In⁻]/[HIn]). The eye sees a colour change roughly over pK_In ± 1.

- Methyl orange: 3.1–4.4 (red → yellow)
- Methyl red: 4.4–6.2
- Phenolphthalein: 8.3–10.0 (colourless → pink)

Choose an indicator whose range lies on the steep part of the titration curve:
- Strong acid–strong base: either
- Weak acid–strong base (equivalence pH > 7): phenolphthalein
- Strong acid–weak base (equivalence pH < 7): methyl orange
- Weak acid–weak base: no sharp end point; use conductometry or potentiometry

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using phenolphthalein for NH₃ vs HCl — it changes colour before the equivalence point.
- Writing −½log C in the basic salt formula with the wrong sign (for C = 0.1, ½ log C = −0.5).
- Assuming every salt solution is neutral.

activity.prompt: Match each titration to the suitable indicator.

quiz.q: An aqueous solution of NH₄Cl is:
quiz.why: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of a weak base and donates H⁺ to water, making the solution acidic.

quiz.q: pH of 0.01 M CH₃COONa (pKa 4.74):
Phenolphthalein is unsuitable for titrating NH₃ with HCl because:
options: The equivalence point is acidic, below its range
quiz.why: The NH₄Cl formed makes the equivalence pH about 5, well below phenolphthalein's 8.3–10 range.

quiz.q: pH of ammonium acetate solution is nearly independent of:
quiz.why: For a weak-acid–weak-base salt pH = 7 + ½pKa − ½pKb, which contains no concentration term.

scenes.text: Calcium oxalate stones form when the ion product in urine exceeds its Ksp.
In the qualitative analysis lab, the same idea decides which group a cation precipitates in.

steps.title: Ksp and solubility
steps.body:
For AₓBᵧ(s) ⇌ xAʸ⁺ + yBˣ⁻: **Ksp = [A]ˣ[B]ʸ**.

- AB (AgCl): Ksp = s²
- AB₂ or A₂B (PbI₂, Ag₂CrO₄): Ksp = 4s³
- AB₃ (Fe(OH)₃): Ksp = 27s⁴
- Precipitation occurs when ionic product Q > Ksp.
- **Common-ion effect**: adding a common ion lowers solubility.

steps.title: Solved: AgCl in water and in NaCl
Solved: Ag₂CrO₄ and precipitation check
steps.body:
Ksp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹².
- 4s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹² → s³ = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³ → s = **6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M**
- Although Ksp is smaller than AgCl's, Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble in molar terms — compare s, not Ksp, for different formula types.

Will PbI₂ (Ksp = 7.1 × 10⁻⁹) precipitate when [Pb²⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M and [I⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M? Q = 10⁻³ × (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁹ < Ksp → **no precipitate**.

steps.title: Group separation in salt analysis
steps.body:
- Group II: H₂S in dilute HCl. The common ion H⁺ suppresses S²⁻ so only very insoluble sulphides (CuS, PbS, CdS) precipitate.
- Group IV: H₂S in ammoniacal solution raises [S²⁻], precipitating ZnS, MnS, NiS, CoS.
- Group III: NH₄Cl suppresses OH⁻ from NH₄OH, so only Fe(OH)₃, Al(OH)₃ and Cr(OH)₃ precipitate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Ksp = s² for every salt.
- Comparing solubilities of salts of different types by Ksp alone.
- Forgetting to account for dilution when two solutions are mixed before computing Q.

activity.prompt: Match each salt to the relation between Ksp and molar solubility s.

NH₄Cl is added before NH₄OH in group III to:
options: Suppress OH⁻ by the common-ion effect
quiz.why: NH₄⁺ suppresses ionisation of NH₄OH, keeping [OH⁻] low so that only hydroxides with very small Ksp precipitate.

quiz.q: Precipitation occurs when:
quiz.why: When the ionic product exceeds Ksp the solution is supersaturated and solid separates until Q = Ksp.

quiz.why: With [Ag⁺] fixed at 0.10 M, s = Ksp/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M.

Methyl orange colour range:
questions.why: Methyl orange changes from red to yellow between pH about 3.1 and 4.4.

questions.why: The common ion acetate shifts CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left, suppressing ionisation.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Chemical kinetics and catalysis
courses.summary: Rate, rate laws, order and molecularity, integrated rate equations for zero, first and second order, methods of finding order, the Arrhenius equation, collision and transition-state theories, complex reactions with the steady-state approximation, and homogeneous and enzyme catalysis.
outcomes: Derive and apply integrated rate laws and half-lives
Determine reaction order by initial-rate, half-life and graphical methods
Calculate activation energy from rate constants at two temperatures
Explain collision theory and transition-state theory
Apply the steady-state approximation and Michaelis–Menten kinetics

scenes.text: Archaeologists at a dig in Gujarat find charcoal from an ancient hearth.
Carbon-14 decays by first-order kinetics with a fixed half-life, so the fraction left tells them its age.

steps.title: Rate, order and molecularity
steps.body:
- Rate = −(1/a) d[A]/dt = (1/c) d[C]/dt for aA → cC
- **Rate law** rate = k[A]^m[B]^n is found experimentally; order = m + n (can be zero, fractional or negative).
- **Molecularity** = number of species colliding in an elementary step (1, 2, rarely 3); always a whole number.
- Units of k: mol^(1−n) L^(n−1) s⁻¹ — first order s⁻¹, second order L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- **Pseudo-first-order**: hydrolysis of an ester in excess water, inversion of cane sugar.

steps.title: First-order integrated law
steps.body:
−d[A]/dt = k[A] → ∫d[A]/[A] = −k∫dt → **ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt**

- k = (2.303/t) log(a/(a − x))
- **t½ = 0.693/k**, independent of initial concentration
- Plot of ln[A] vs t: straight line, slope −k
- Radioactive decay, N₂O₅ decomposition and H₂O₂ decomposition are first order.

steps.title: Solved: radiocarbon dating
steps.body:
t½(¹⁴C) = 5730 years. A sample has 25% of the ¹⁴C of living wood.

- 25% = (½)² → **2 half-lives = 11 460 years**

If 40% remains: t = (5730/0.693) ln(1/0.40) = 8268 × 0.916 = **7575 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking order from the balanced equation's coefficients — only for elementary steps.
- Using log instead of ln (or forgetting the factor 2.303).
- Thinking first-order t½ depends on starting amount.

activity.prompt: Match each rate-constant unit to its reaction order.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction is 50% complete in 20 min. Time for 75% completion:
quiz.why: 75% complete means 25% left = two half-lives = 2 × 20 = 40 min.

quiz.q: Hydrolysis of ethyl acetate in large excess of water is:
quiz.why: Water is in such excess that its concentration is effectively constant, so the rate depends only on the ester: pseudo-first order.

quiz.q: For a first-order reaction, the plot that gives a straight line is:
quiz.why: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt is linear in t with slope −k.

quiz.q: k = 6.93 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. t½ is:

lessons.title: Zero and second order; determining order

story.title: The drug that clears at a fixed rate

scenes.text: The liver removes ethanol at a roughly constant rate, whatever the blood concentration (once the enzyme is saturated).
That is zero-order behaviour. Other reactions slow down sharply as reactants are used up.

steps.title: Integrated rate laws
steps.body:
- **Zero order**: [A] = [A]₀ − kt; t½ = [A]₀/2k; plot [A] vs t linear. Examples: decomposition of NH₃ on hot Pt, enzyme at saturation.
- **Second order (one reactant or equal concentrations)**: 1/[A] − 1/[A]₀ = kt; t½ = 1/(k[A]₀); plot 1/[A] vs t linear. Example: saponification of ethyl acetate with NaOH.
- **Second order, unequal a and b**: k = [2.303/t(a − b)] log[b(a − x)/a(b − x)]
- General: t½ ∝ [A]₀^(1−n)

steps.title: Methods for finding order
steps.body:
1. **Integration (trial) method** — check which equation gives a constant k.
2. **Graphical** — which plot ([A], ln[A] or 1/[A] vs t) is linear.
3. **Half-life method** — n = 1 + log(t₁/t₂)/log(a₂/a₁).
4. **Initial rates (van 't Hoff differential)** — vary one concentration at a time.
5. **Ostwald isolation** — keep all but one reactant in large excess.

steps.title: Solved: initial rates
steps.body:
2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂.

| [NO] | [O₂] | rate |
| 0.01 | 0.01 | 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ |
| 0.02 | 0.01 | 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ |
| 0.01 | 0.02 | 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ |

- Doubling [NO] → rate × 4 → order 2 in NO
- Doubling [O₂] → rate × 2 → order 1 in O₂
- Rate = k[NO]²[O₂], overall third order; k = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵/(10⁻⁴ × 10⁻²) = **25 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹**

steps.title: Solved: second-order half-life and order from half-lives
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using t½ = 0.693/k for a second-order reaction.
- Computing order from a single experiment.
- Mixing up which concentration was changed in an initial-rate table.

quiz.q: For a zero-order reaction, doubling [A]₀ makes t½:
quiz.why: t½ = [A]₀/2k for zero order, so it is directly proportional to the initial concentration.

quiz.q: Rate increases 9 times when [A] is tripled. Order in A:
quiz.why: 3ⁿ = 9 gives n = 2.

quiz.q: Saponification of ethyl acetate by NaOH is:
quiz.why: The rate depends on both ester and hydroxide concentrations to the first power, making it second order overall.

quiz.q: For a second-order reaction with [A]₀ = 0.10 M and k = 2.0 L mol⁻¹ min⁻¹, t½ is:

story.title: Why milk keeps in the fridge

scenes.text: Milk sours in a day on the kitchen shelf in summer but lasts several days in the fridge.
Rates of chemical and microbial reactions fall steeply as temperature drops — the Arrhenius equation quantifies it.

steps.title: Arrhenius equation
steps.body:
**k = A e^(−Ea/RT)**; ln k = ln A − Ea/RT.

- Plot ln k vs 1/T: slope = −Ea/R
- Two temperatures: **ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)**
- Rough rule: many reactions near room temperature double or triple their rate for a 10 K rise (temperature coefficient 2–3).
- Only molecules with energy ≥ Ea (fraction e^(−Ea/RT)) react.

steps.title: Collision theory and transition-state theory
steps.body:
**Collision theory**: rate = P Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT), where Z_AB is collision frequency and P (steric factor) accounts for orientation. P is often ≪ 1 for complex molecules.

**Transition-state (activated complex) theory**: reactants form an activated complex in quasi-equilibrium; k = (k_B T/h) e^(−ΔG‡/RT) = (k_B T/h) e^(ΔS‡/R) e^(−ΔH‡/RT) (Eyring equation). A negative ΔS‡ corresponds to a small steric factor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in the Arrhenius equation.
- Getting a negative Ea from swapping T₁ and T₂.
- Thinking a catalyst changes ΔH of the reaction — it changes only the pathway (Ea).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find Ea graphically from rate constants.
items: Measure k at several temperatures
Convert temperatures to kelvin and compute 1/T
Compute ln k for each
Plot ln k against 1/T
Find the slope and calculate Ea = −slope × R

quiz.q: Slope of ln k vs 1/T is −6000 K. Ea is:
In collision theory the steric factor P accounts for:
quiz.why: Not every energetic collision has the right geometry; P is the fraction of collisions correctly oriented to react.

quiz.q: A catalyst increases rate by:
quiz.why: It provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a larger fraction of molecules can react.

quiz.q: With Ea = 50 kJ/mol, rate at 310 K relative to 300 K is about:

scenes.text: Protease enzymes in detergent break down protein stains at 40 °C in minutes.
At high stain concentration the enzymes are all busy and the rate levels off — Michaelis–Menten kinetics.

steps.title: Complex reactions
steps.body:
- **Opposing**: A ⇌ B; ln[(xₑ)/(xₑ − x)] = (k₁ + k₋₁)t
- **Parallel**: A → B (k₁), A → C (k₂); [B]/[C] = k₁/k₂; overall k = k₁ + k₂
- **Consecutive**: A → B → C; [B] passes through a maximum at t_max = ln(k₁/k₂)/(k₁ − k₂)
- **Steady-state approximation**: for a reactive intermediate I, d[I]/dt ≈ 0.
- **Chain reactions** (H₂ + Br₂): initiation, propagation, termination.
- **Lindemann mechanism**: unimolecular gas reactions are first order at high P and second order at low P.

steps.title: Enzyme catalysis
steps.body:
E + S ⇌ ES → E + P. Steady state on ES gives the **Michaelis–Menten equation**:

**v = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S])**

- [S] ≪ K_m: v ≈ (V_max/K_m)[S] — first order
- [S] ≫ K_m: v ≈ V_max — zero order
- [S] = K_m: v = V_max/2
- Lineweaver–Burk: 1/v = (K_m/V_max)(1/[S]) + 1/V_max

steps.title: Solved: Michaelis–Menten
steps.body:
K_m = 2.0 mM, V_max = 10 µM s⁻¹.

- [S] = 6.0 mM: v = 10 × 6.0/(2.0 + 6.0) = **7.5 µM s⁻¹**
- [S] = 2.0 mM: v = **5.0 µM s⁻¹** (half of V_max)
- Lineweaver–Burk intercept = 1/V_max = 0.10 s µM⁻¹; slope = K_m/V_max = 0.20 mM s µM⁻¹.

steps.title: Solved: parallel reactions
steps.body:
A decomposes by two first-order paths: k₁ = 0.030 min⁻¹ (to B), k₂ = 0.010 min⁻¹ (to C).

- Overall k = 0.040 min⁻¹; t½ = 0.693/0.040 = **17.3 min**
- Product ratio B : C = 3 : 1, so B = **75%** of products at all times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the steady-state approximation to stable reactants or products.
- Saying enzymes shift equilibrium.
- Confusing K_m with the equilibrium constant of binding; it also includes k₂.

activity.prompt: Match each case to the behaviour.

quiz.q: Michaelis constant K_m equals the substrate concentration at which v is:
quiz.why: Substituting [S] = K_m into v = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]) gives v = V_max/2.

quiz.q: The steady-state approximation assumes:
options: Concentration of a reactive intermediate stays nearly constant
quiz.why: Reactive intermediates form and are used up at nearly equal rates, so d[I]/dt ≈ 0.

quiz.q: In H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr, the step Br· + H₂ → HBr + H· is:
quiz.why: It consumes one radical and produces another, carrying the chain forward, so it is a propagation step.

quiz.q: For A → B → C, intermediate B:
options: Rises to a maximum then falls
quiz.why: B is formed from A and consumed to C; it builds up first and then declines as A runs out.

questions.why: For zero order rate = k, so k has the units of rate, mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

questions.why: Each half-life halves the amount: (½)⁵ = 1/32.

questions.why: t = (2.303/k) log 1000 = 6.909/k and t½ = 0.693/k, so the ratio is about 10.

questions.q: Rate = k[A]^½[B]². Overall order:
questions.why: Order is the sum of exponents: ½ + 2 = 2.5.

questions.q: k at 300 K = 0.010 s⁻¹, Ea = 60 kJ/mol. k at 320 K about:
Molecularity can be:
questions.why: Molecularity counts the species in one elementary collision, so it must be a small positive integer.

questions.q: Half-lives 100 s at 0.1 M and 50 s at 0.2 M imply order:
In the Eyring equation, the pre-factor k_BT/h has units:
questions.why: Boltzmann constant × temperature is energy, divided by Planck's constant (J s) gives s⁻¹.

questions.q: Lineweaver–Burk plot has y-intercept equal to:
questions.why: When 1/[S] = 0 the double reciprocal equation gives 1/v = 1/V_max.

questions.q: Inversion of cane sugar in acid is:
questions.why: Water is in large excess and H⁺ is a catalyst, so the rate depends only on sucrose: pseudo-first order.

questions.q: For a 10 K rise the rate becomes 3 times. This is called the:
questions.why: The ratio k(T + 10)/k(T) is the temperature coefficient, typically 2–3 near room temperature.

questions.q: For parallel first-order paths with k₁ = 2k₂, percentage of product from path 1:
questions.why: Products form in ratio k₁ : k₂ = 2 : 1, so path 1 gives 2/3 ≈ 67%.

courses.summary: Conductance, cell constant and molar conductivity, Kohlrausch's law and its applications, transport numbers and conductometric titrations, galvanic cells, electrode potentials and the Nernst equation, thermodynamics of cells, concentration cells and pH measurement.
outcomes: Calculate cell constant, conductivity and molar conductivity
Use Kohlrausch's law to find Λ° and Ka of weak electrolytes
Write cell notation and compute EMF with the Nernst equation
Relate E° to ΔG°, K, ΔS and ΔH

scenes.text: An RO water plant checks its output with a conductivity meter: lower reading, purer water.
Dissolved ions carry current. Measuring conductance tells us how many and how mobile they are.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Resistance R = ρ(l/A); conductance G = 1/R (siemens, S).
- **Conductivity κ = G × (l/A)**; l/A = **cell constant** (cm⁻¹), found using standard KCl.
- **Molar conductivity Λm = κ × 1000/C** (S cm² mol⁻¹, C in mol L⁻¹).
- Measured with a Wheatstone bridge using AC (to avoid electrolysis/polarisation) and platinised Pt electrodes.
- On dilution κ decreases (fewer ions per cm³) but Λm increases.

steps.title: Variation with concentration
steps.body:
- **Strong electrolytes**: Λm = Λ°m − A√C (Debye–Hückel–Onsager); a plot of Λm vs √C is linear and extrapolates to Λ°m.
- **Weak electrolytes**: Λm rises steeply at low C because α increases; Λ° cannot be found by extrapolation — use Kohlrausch's law.
- Relaxation (asymmetry) and electrophoretic effects lower Λm at higher C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the factor 1000 when C is in mol L⁻¹ and κ in S cm⁻¹.
- Using DC for conductance measurement.
- Saying conductivity increases on dilution — molar conductivity does, κ does not.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the molar conductivity of an unknown solution.
items: Measure R of standard 0.01 M KCl in the cell
Calculate the cell constant = κ(KCl) × R
Rinse and fill the cell with the unknown solution; measure R
Calculate κ = cell constant/R
Calculate Λm = 1000κ/C

quiz.q: Units of molar conductivity:
quiz.why: Λm = κ × 1000/C has units S cm⁻¹ × cm³ mol⁻¹ = S cm² mol⁻¹.

quiz.q: Cell constant 1.0 cm⁻¹, R = 200 Ω. κ is:
quiz.why: κ = cell constant/R = 1.0/200 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹.

quiz.q: AC is used in conductance measurement to:
options: Avoid electrolysis and polarisation at electrodes
quiz.why: Alternating current reverses rapidly, so no net electrolysis or polarisation builds up at the electrodes.

quiz.q: Λ°m of a strong electrolyte is found by:
quiz.why: For strong electrolytes Λm varies linearly with √C, so extrapolation to C = 0 gives Λ°m.

lessons.title: Kohlrausch's law, transport numbers and conductometric titrations

scenes.text: A dark coloured fruit juice hides any indicator colour change.
Following conductance as base is added gives a sharp V-shaped graph with the end point at the corner.

steps.title: Kohlrausch's law
steps.body:
At infinite dilution each ion contributes independently: **Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋**.

Applications:
- Λ° of weak electrolytes: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(CH₃COONa) + Λ°(HCl) − Λ°(NaCl)
- Degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λ°m and Ka = Cα²/(1 − α)
- Solubility of sparingly soluble salts: s = 1000κ/Λ°m

**Transport number** t₊ = λ₊/(λ₊ + λ₋), t₊ + t₋ = 1 (Hittorf and moving-boundary methods). H⁺ and OH⁻ have very high λ° (≈ 350 and 199 S cm² mol⁻¹) due to the Grotthuss proton-hopping mechanism.

steps.title: Solved: solubility of AgCl
steps.body:
κ(saturated AgCl) − κ(water) = 1.86 × 10⁻⁶ S cm⁻¹; Λ°(AgCl) = 138.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.

- s = 1000 × 1.86 × 10⁻⁶/138.3 = **1.34 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹**
- Ksp = s² = **1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰**

steps.title: Conductometric titration curves
steps.body:
- **Strong acid vs strong base** (HCl + NaOH): conductance falls (fast H⁺ replaced by slow Na⁺), then rises after the end point (excess OH⁻) — V shape.
- **Weak acid vs strong base** (CH₃COOH + NaOH): small initial dip, slow rise (salt formation), then steeper rise after end point.
- **Weak acid vs weak base** (CH₃COOH + NH₄OH): rises, then flat after end point.
- **Precipitation** (AgNO₃ + KCl): nearly flat, then rises after end point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding all three Λ° values instead of subtracting NaCl.
- Forgetting to subtract the conductivity of water for sparingly soluble salts.
- Using a dilute titrant — volume change bends the lines; use a titrant about 10 times more concentrated.

activity.prompt: Match each titration with the shape of its conductance curve.
pairs: Slight rise, then steeper rise after end point

quiz.q: Λ°(NH₄OH) from Λ°(NH₄Cl) = 129.8, Λ°(NaOH) = 248.1, Λ°(NaCl) = 126.5:
quiz.why: Λ°(NH₄OH) = Λ°(NH₄Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) − Λ°(NaCl) = 129.8 + 248.1 − 126.5 = 251.4 S cm² mol⁻¹.

quiz.q: H⁺ has unusually high ionic conductivity because of:
options: Grotthuss proton hopping through hydrogen bonds
quiz.why: Protons pass along hydrogen-bonded water chains by bond rearrangement rather than moving as whole ions, giving very high mobility.

quiz.q: In HCl vs NaOH conductometric titration, conductance initially:
quiz.why: Highly mobile H⁺ ions are replaced by much slower Na⁺ ions, so the conductance falls until the end point.

quiz.q: If t₊ for an electrolyte is 0.40, t₋ is:
quiz.why: Transport numbers of cation and anion add up to 1, so t₋ = 1 − 0.40 = 0.60.

story.title: The Daniell cell on the bench

scenes.text: A zinc rod in ZnSO₄ and a copper rod in CuSO₄, joined by a salt bridge, light a small LED.
The voltmeter shows about 1.1 V. Change the concentrations and the reading shifts, as Nernst predicted.

steps.title: Cells and electrode potentials
steps.body:
- Cell notation: Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s) — anode (oxidation) on the left, cathode (reduction) on the right, || = salt bridge.
- Standard hydrogen electrode (SHE): Pt | H₂(1 bar) | H⁺(a = 1), E° = 0 by definition.
- **E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode)**, using standard reduction potentials.
- Common values: Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V.
- Reference electrodes: saturated calomel electrode (SCE) +0.2415 V; Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) about +0.197 V.

steps.title: Nernst equation and thermodynamics
steps.body:
From ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q and ΔG = −nFE:

**E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q** at 298 K.

- ΔG° = −nFE°; **log K = nE°/0.0592**
- ΔS = nF(∂E/∂T)_P; ΔH = −nFE + TnF(∂E/∂T)_P (Gibbs–Helmholtz)
- F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹

steps.title: Solved: ΔS and ΔH from temperature coefficient
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying E° by stoichiometric coefficients — E° is intensive.
- Writing Q from half-reactions instead of from the overall cell reaction.
- Getting a negative E for a cell written the 'wrong' way round and not realising the reaction runs in reverse.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to calculate the EMF of a cell at non-standard concentrations.
items: Identify anode and cathode half-reactions
Calculate E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode
Write the overall balanced reaction and find n
Write Q from the overall reaction
Apply E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q

quiz.q: E° for Zn | Zn²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag:
quiz.why: E° = E°(Ag⁺/Ag) − E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V; it is not doubled because E° is intensive.

quiz.q: ΔG° for a cell with n = 1 and E° = 0.50 V:
If Q increases, the cell EMF:
quiz.why: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q, so a larger Q lowers E as the reaction approaches equilibrium.

quiz.q: A cell with a positive temperature coefficient has ΔS that is:
quiz.why: ΔS = nF(∂E/∂T)_P, so a positive dE/dT means ΔS > 0.

story.title: The pH meter in every lab

scenes.text: A microbiology student dips a glass electrode into a culture medium and reads pH 6.8.
Behind the display is a tiny cell whose EMF changes by 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C.

steps.title: Concentration cells
steps.body:
Same electrodes, different concentrations: E° = 0.

- Electrode concentration cell: Ag | Ag⁺(c₁) || Ag⁺(c₂) | Ag, **E = (0.0592/n) log(c₂/c₁)** with c₂ > c₁.
- Example: c₁ = 0.010 M, c₂ = 0.10 M → E = 0.0592 × log 10 = **0.0592 V**.
- Used to find Ksp, e.g. Ag | AgCl(s), KCl || AgNO₃ | Ag.

steps.title: Electrodes for pH
steps.body:
- **Hydrogen electrode**: E = −0.0592 pH (accurate, inconvenient).
- **Quinhydrone electrode**: E = 0.6996 − 0.0592 pH; usable below pH 8.5.
- **Glass electrode**: thin glass membrane; potential varies linearly with pH; calibrated with standard buffers (pH 4.00, 7.00, 9.20). Works in coloured and oxidising solutions.

Cell with SCE: Pt, H₂ | H⁺ || SCE → E_cell = 0.2415 + 0.0592 pH.

steps.title: Solved: pH from EMF and Ksp from a cell
Potentiometric titrations
steps.body:
EMF is recorded against volume of titrant. The end point is the steepest point, found more precisely from a first-derivative (ΔE/ΔV vs V) peak or a second-derivative zero crossing.

- Acid–base: glass electrode vs SCE
- Redox (Fe²⁺ vs K₂Cr₂O₇ or Ce⁴⁺): Pt electrode vs SCE
- Precipitation (Cl⁻ vs AgNO₃): Ag electrode

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the quinhydrone electrode in alkaline solutions (hydroquinone ionises/oxidises above pH ~8.5).
- Forgetting to recalibrate a glass electrode at the measurement temperature.
- Choosing the end point at the highest EMF instead of the steepest rise.

Plot pH vs V and ΔpH/ΔV vs V to locate the end point

Every numerical in the paper uses something on that sheet. Here it is.

steps.title: Equilibrium and ions
steps.body:
- Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn; ΔG° = −RT ln K; ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q
- ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁); F = C − P + 2
- α = √(Ka/C); pH = ½(pKa − log C)
- pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid])
- Salt of WA + SB: pH = 7 + ½pKa + ½log C; SA + WB: pH = 7 − ½pKb − ½log C
- Ksp: AB = s², AB₂ = 4s³, AB₃ = 27s⁴

steps.title: Kinetics and electrochemistry
steps.body:
- First order: k = (2.303/t) log(a/(a − x)); t½ = 0.693/k
- Second order: 1/[A] − 1/[A]₀ = kt; t½ = 1/(k a)
- Zero order: t½ = a/2k; n = 1 + log(t₁/t₂)/log(a₂/a₁)
- ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂); v = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S])
- κ = cell constant/R; Λm = 1000κ/C; α = Λm/Λ°
- E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q; ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.0592; ΔS = nF(dE/dT)

Q2. Derive the Michaelis–Menten equation using the steady-state approximation and explain the significance of K_m.

Q3. Derive the Nernst equation from ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and show how it is used to determine pH with a hydrogen electrode.

Q4. State the phase rule and discuss the water system with a labelled diagram.

lessons.title: Lab: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of methyl acetate

scenes.text: Ishaan pipettes 5 mL from a flask every 10 minutes and titrates it against NaOH.
The titre creeps up as acetic acid forms. From the titres he extracts a rate constant.

steps.title: Aim and principle
steps.body:
CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + CH₃OH, catalysed by HCl. Water is in large excess, so the reaction is **pseudo-first order**.

The titre against NaOH measures HCl (constant) + acetic acid formed. With V₀ (t = 0), Vt (time t) and V∞ (complete):

**k = (2.303/t) log[(V∞ − V₀)/(V∞ − Vt)]**

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Take 100 mL of 0.5 M HCl in a flask in a thermostat at 25 °C.
2. Add 5 mL methyl acetate, mix, start the stopwatch.
3. Immediately pipette 5 mL into ice-cold water (to arrest the reaction) and titrate with 0.1 M NaOH using phenolphthalein → V₀.
4. Repeat at 10, 20, 30, 40, 60 min → Vt.
5. Heat a sealed portion at about 60 °C for 1 h (to complete hydrolysis), cool and titrate → V∞.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why is ice-cold water used? — Cooling and dilution practically stop the reaction at the moment of sampling.
- Why is V₀ not zero? — The HCl catalyst is titrated too.
- Why pseudo-first order? — Water is in large excess, so its concentration stays constant.
- Why heat for V∞? — To drive hydrolysis to completion quickly.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body:
- Delay between pipetting and quenching.
- Loss of volatile methyl acetate when heating for V∞ (use a stoppered flask or reflux).
- Temperature drift in the thermostat.

quiz.q: In this experiment V₀ corresponds to:
options: HCl catalyst present at the start
quiz.why: At t = 0 no ester has hydrolysed, so the NaOH titre measures only the HCl catalyst.

quiz.q: If V₀ = 20, V∞ = 45 and Vt = 32.5 mL at 30 min, k is:
A constant k from several readings confirms:
quiz.why: Only if the reaction is first order will the first-order equation give the same k at every time.

lessons.title: Lab: Conductometric titration of HCl with NaOH

scenes.text: Sneha's conductance readings fall steadily, then start climbing again.
She draws two straight lines through the points; where they cross is the end point.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Pipette 20 mL of the HCl solution into a beaker; add water to cover the conductivity cell.
2. Fill a burette with about 0.2 M NaOH (≈ 10 times stronger than the acid, to keep volume change small).
3. Record conductance after each 0.5 mL addition, stirring well.
4. Continue about 5 mL beyond the minimum.
5. Plot conductance vs volume of NaOH; draw best-fit lines through both arms; the intersection gives V_eq.

steps.title: Solved: calculation
steps.body:
Intersection at 10.4 mL of 0.200 M NaOH for 20.0 mL HCl.

- Moles NaOH = 0.200 × 10.4/1000 = 2.08 × 10⁻³
- [HCl] = 2.08 × 10⁻³/0.0200 = **0.104 M**
- Mass of HCl per litre = 0.104 × 36.46 = **3.79 g L⁻¹**

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why does conductance fall at first? — Mobile H⁺ (λ° ≈ 350) is replaced by slower Na⁺ (≈ 50).
- Why does it rise after the end point? — Excess OH⁻ (λ° ≈ 199) and Na⁺ are added.
- Advantage over indicator titration? — Works with coloured/turbid solutions and very dilute or weak acids.
- Why should the titrant be concentrated? — To avoid dilution curving the lines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the minimum reading as the end point instead of the intersection of the fitted lines.
- Not stirring before each reading.
- Letting the electrodes touch the beaker or stirrer.

Why does conductance rise after the end point?
options: Excess Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions increase conductance
quiz.why: Beyond equivalence the added NaOH is unreacted, and the highly mobile OH⁻ ions raise the conductance.

quiz.q: The end point is taken at:
options: The intersection of two straight lines
quiz.why: Near the end point readings are rounded by hydrolysis and dilution, so the intersection of extrapolated lines is more accurate.

lessons.title: Lab: Potentiometric titration of Fe²⁺ with K₂Cr₂O₇

story.title: A jump of a few hundred millivolts

scenes.text: A platinum wire and a calomel electrode dip into Mohr's salt solution.
As dichromate is added the EMF creeps up, then leaps at the end point.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O.

Before equivalence, E is set by Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺: E = E° − 0.0592 log([Fe²⁺]/[Fe³⁺]). At half-equivalence [Fe²⁺] = [Fe³⁺] and E = E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) ≈ 0.77 V vs SHE. After equivalence the Cr₂O₇²⁻/Cr³⁺ couple controls E, so the potential jumps sharply.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Pipette 25 mL Mohr's salt solution; add 10 mL dilute H₂SO₄.
2. Dip a Pt electrode and an SCE (via salt bridge); connect to a potentiometer.
3. Add 0.0167 M K₂Cr₂O₇ in 1 mL portions, then 0.1 mL portions near the jump; record EMF.
4. Plot E vs V and ΔE/ΔV vs V; the peak gives V_eq.

steps.title: Solved: calculation
steps.body:
End point = 12.5 mL of 0.0167 M K₂Cr₂O₇.

- Moles Cr₂O₇²⁻ = 0.0167 × 12.5/1000 = 2.09 × 10⁻⁴
- Moles Fe²⁺ = 6 × 2.09 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.25 × 10⁻³
- [Fe²⁺] = 1.25 × 10⁻³/0.025 = **0.0501 M**
- E° (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) can be read as the EMF at 6.25 mL (half-equivalence), corrected for SCE.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why platinum? — It is inert and only transfers electrons between the redox couple and the circuit.
- Why add H₂SO₄? — Dichromate needs H⁺ for reduction.
- Why is no indicator needed? — The EMF jump itself marks the end point.
- What is the formal potential? — The potential at half-equivalence under the actual conditions (acid concentration).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1 : 6 stoichiometry between dichromate and Fe²⁺.
- Adding large portions near the end point and missing the jump.
- Using HCl instead of H₂SO₄ in some redox titrations (Cl⁻ can be oxidised, e.g. with KMnO₄).

quiz.q: At half-equivalence the EMF equals:

quiz.q: The indicator electrode in this titration is:

uni-bsc-chemistry.title: B.Sc Chemistry — core papers, unit by unit
uni-bsc-chemistry.description: Inorganic, organic and physical chemistry core units of a typical B.Sc Chemistry programme: atomic structure and bonding, organic fundamentals and stereochemistry, thermodynamics and kinetics, electrochemistry and equilibria, and coordination chemistry.

courses.title: Inorganic I · Atomic structure and chemical bonding
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Quantum numbers, orbitals and electron configuration, ionic bonding with lattice energy and Fajans' rules, VSEPR shapes and hybridisation, and molecular orbital theory of diatomics.
outcomes: Learners can write configurations and count radial and angular nodes
Learners can compute lattice energy with a Born–Haber cycle
Learners can predict shapes using VSEPR
Learners can find bond order and magnetism from MO diagrams

scenes.text: Simran writes copper's configuration as [Ar]3d⁹4s² and loses marks. Her teacher writes [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.
A completely filled d subshell is extra stable. Exceptions make sense once you know why the rules exist.

steps.title: Quantum numbers and nodes
steps.body:
- n (principal: 1, 2, 3…) — size and energy
- l (azimuthal: 0 to n − 1) — shape: s, p, d, f
- mₗ (−l to +l) — orientation
- mₛ (±½) — spin

Nodes: **radial = n − l − 1**, **angular = l**, total = n − 1.

Filling rules: **Aufbau** (lower n + l first; equal n + l → lower n first), **Pauli** (no two electrons share all four numbers), **Hund** (singly fill degenerate orbitals with parallel spins first).

steps.title: Solved: nodes and configurations
steps.body:
- 3p: radial = 3 − 1 − 1 = **1**, angular = **1**
- 4d: radial = 4 − 2 − 1 = **1**, angular = **2**
- Fe (Z = 26): [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Fe³⁺: remove 4s first → **[Ar] 3d⁵** (5 unpaired electrons)
- Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (half-filled/filled d stability)

steps.title: Solved: Slater's rules
steps.body:
Zeff for the 4s electron of K (Z = 19). Groups: (1s²)(2s²2p⁶)(3s²3p⁶)(4s¹).

- Same group (4s): none
- n − 1 shell (8 electrons) × 0.85 = 6.80
- n − 2 and lower (10 electrons) × 1.00 = 10.00
- S = 16.80; Zeff = 19 − 16.8 = **2.2**

This low Zeff explains why K loses its 4s electron so easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming transition-metal ions.
- Mixing radial and angular nodes (a 2p orbital has 0 radial, 1 angular node).
- Writing l = n (l runs only up to n − 1).
- Pairing electrons in a p subshell before each orbital has one.

activity.prompt: Match the orbital to its number of radial nodes.

quiz.q: Number of angular nodes in a 3d orbital:
quiz.why: The number of angular nodes equals l. For a d orbital, l = 2, so there are 2 angular nodes.

quiz.q: Configuration of Cr (Z = 24):
quiz.why: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, not 3d⁴4s². Moving one 4s electron gives a half-filled d subshell, which is extra stable due to exchange energy and symmetry.

quiz.q: Which rule says degenerate orbitals fill singly first?
quiz.why: Hund's rule says degenerate orbitals are filled singly with parallel spins before pairing begins. Pauli limits two electrons per orbital, and Aufbau gives the filling order.

quiz.q: Unpaired electrons in Mn²⁺ (Z = 25):
quiz.why: Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s². Losing the two 4s electrons gives Mn²⁺ = 3d⁵, with five d orbitals each holding one unpaired electron.

quiz.q: For n = 3, allowed l values are:
quiz.why: For a given n, l runs from 0 to n − 1. For n = 3, l = 0, 1, 2 (s, p, d).

lessons.title: Ionic solids: lattice energy and Fajans' rules

scenes.text: Kiran heats table salt on a gas burner; it does not melt (NaCl melts near 801 °C).
A Born–Haber cycle reveals the huge lattice energy holding the ions together.

steps.title: Lattice energy
steps.body:
Lattice energy U is the energy change when one mole of an ionic solid forms from gaseous ions (negative, by this convention).

- **Born–Landé**: U ∝ z⁺z⁻/r₀ — higher charges and smaller ions give larger |U|
- **Born–Haber cycle** (Hess's law): ΔH_f = ΔH_sub + IE + ½D + EA + U

Radius-ratio guide (r⁺/r⁻): 0.414–0.732 → octahedral, coordination 6 (NaCl, ≈ 0.52); > 0.732 → cubic, coordination 8 (CsCl, ≈ 0.93); 0.225–0.414 → tetrahedral (ZnS).

steps.title: Solved: Fajans' rules
steps.body:
Covalent character increases with: small, highly charged cation; large, easily polarised anion; cation with pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron) shell.

- LiI more covalent than LiF (I⁻ is larger, more polarisable)
- AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl (Al³⁺ small and highly charged)
- CuCl more covalent than NaCl (18-electron Cu⁺)
- Hence AlCl₃ sublimes and dissolves in organic solvents.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½ for dissociating Cl₂ per mole of NaCl.
- Writing EA as positive when energy is released.
- Treating radius-ratio rules as exact — they are guides; many solids deviate.
- Saying polarisation depends only on the cation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl starting from elements.
items: Sublime Na(s) → Na(g)
Ionise Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
Dissociate ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g)
Add electron: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)
Combine gaseous ions into the lattice (U)

quiz.q: Lattice energy magnitude is larger for:
quiz.why: Lattice energy rises with ionic charge and falls with ionic size. MgO has 2+ and 2− charges and small ions, so it has the largest value.

quiz.q: Radius ratio 0.52 suggests coordination number:
quiz.why: A radius ratio of 0.414–0.732 corresponds to octahedral holes, i.e. coordination number 6. 0.52 lies in this range.

quiz.q: Most covalent among these:
quiz.why: By Fajans' rules a larger anion is more polarisable, so covalent character increases. I⁻ is the largest, so LiI is the most covalent.

quiz.q: The Born–Haber cycle is an application of:
quiz.why: The Born–Haber cycle applies Hess's law: enthalpy is a state function, so the formation enthalpy equals the sum of the steps of any route.

quiz.q: CsCl structure has coordination number:
quiz.why: In CsCl each ion is surrounded by 8 of the opposite ion at the corners of a cube, so the coordination number is 8 (6 is for NaCl).

scenes.text: Arjun's model kit lets him build a straight H–O–H. His professor bends it to about 104.5°.
Lone pairs push harder than bond pairs, like balloons tied together. That is VSEPR.

steps.title: Steric number decides the geometry
steps.body:
Steric number (SN) = bonded atoms + lone pairs on the central atom. Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

- SN 2: linear (sp) — BeCl₂, CO₂
- SN 3: trigonal planar (sp²) — BF₃
- SN 4: tetrahedral (sp³) — CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ pyramidal ≈ 107°, H₂O bent ≈ 104.5°
- SN 5: trigonal bipyramidal (sp³d) — PCl₅; SF₄ see-saw; ClF₃ T-shaped; XeF₂ linear (lone pairs go equatorial)
- SN 6: octahedral (sp³d²) — SF₆; BrF₅ square pyramidal; XeF₄ square planar

steps.title: Solved: XeF₄ and ClF₃
steps.body:
- **XeF₄**: Xe has 8 valence electrons; 4 used in bonds, 4 left = 2 lone pairs. SN = 6 → lone pairs opposite → **square planar**.
- **ClF₃**: Cl has 7; 3 bonds, 4 left = 2 lone pairs. SN = 5; both lone pairs equatorial → **T-shaped**, angles slightly under 90°.

steps.title: Solved: ions
steps.body:
- NH₄⁺: SN 4, no lone pair → tetrahedral
- I₃⁻: central I has 3 lone pairs + 2 bonds, SN 5 → **linear**
- NO₂⁺: SN 2 → linear; NO₂⁻: SN 3 (one lone pair) → bent ≈ 115°

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing electron geometry with molecular shape (NH₃ electron geometry tetrahedral, shape pyramidal).
- Putting lone pairs axial in trigonal bipyramids (they go equatorial).
- Forgetting to add/subtract electrons for ionic charge.
- Counting a double bond as two electron domains (it counts once).

activity.prompt: Sort the molecules by shape.

quiz.q: Hybridisation of S in SF₆:
quiz.why: SF₆ has six bond pairs and no lone pairs on S, so steric number 6, which means sp³d² hybridisation and octahedral geometry.

quiz.q: Shape of SF₄:
quiz.why: SF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, steric number 5. The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, giving a see-saw shape.

quiz.q: Bond angle order:
quiz.why: Lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, compressing the angle. CH₄ (no lone pairs) 109.5° > NH₃ (one, ~107°) > H₂O (two, ~104.5°).

quiz.q: Shape of BrF₅:
quiz.why: BrF₅ has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, steric number 6. Octahedral arrangement with one position lone gives a square pyramidal shape.

quiz.q: Lone pairs on Xe in XeF₂:
quiz.why: Xe has 8 valence electrons; 2 are used to bond with the two F atoms, leaving 6 electrons = 3 lone pairs.

story.title: Liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet

scenes.text: In a famous demonstration, liquid oxygen poured between magnet poles clings there.
A Lewis structure predicts all electrons paired. MO theory predicts two unpaired electrons — and wins.

steps.title: Building MO diagrams
steps.body:
Atomic orbitals of similar energy and symmetry combine into bonding (lower) and antibonding (higher, *) MOs.

**Bond order = (N_bonding − N_antibonding)/2**. Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond; zero → no stable molecule.

- For O₂, F₂: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p_z < π2p_x = π2p_y < π*2p < σ*2p_z
- For B₂, C₂, N₂ (s–p mixing): π2p lies **below** σ2p_z

steps.title: Solved: oxygen family
steps.body:
O₂ has 16 electrons; valence MO filling ends π*2p².

- O₂: BO = (10 − 6)/2 = **2**, two unpaired → paramagnetic
- O₂⁺: BO **2.5** (shortest bond)
- O₂⁻ (superoxide): **1.5**; O₂²⁻ (peroxide): **1**, diamagnetic

steps.title: Solved: N₂, B₂ and He₂
steps.body:
- N₂: BO = **3**, diamagnetic, very strong bond (≈ 945 kJ/mol)
- B₂: with s–p mixing the last two electrons occupy degenerate π2p singly → **paramagnetic**, BO = 1
- He₂: (σ1s)²(σ*1s)² → BO = **0**, not stable

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the O₂ ordering for N₂ (s–p mixing changes it for Z ≤ 7).
- Forgetting to count core electrons consistently (count both bonding and antibonding or neither).
- Pairing electrons in degenerate π* orbitals before Hund's rule allows.
- Thinking bond order must be an integer.

activity.prompt: Complete the MO facts.
activity.text: The bond order of N₂ is ___, of O₂ is ___, and O₂ is ___ because of two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals.

quiz.q: Bond order of O₂⁻:
quiz.why: O₂⁻ has 17 electrons: 10 in bonding MOs and 7 in antibonding MOs. Bond order = (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5.

quiz.q: Which is paramagnetic?
quiz.why: B₂ has its last two electrons in separate degenerate π orbitals with parallel spins, so it is paramagnetic. N₂, C₂ and F₂ have all electrons paired.

quiz.q: Shortest bond among O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻, O₂²⁻:
quiz.why: Bond length falls as bond order rises. O₂⁺ has bond order 2.5, higher than O₂ (2), O₂⁻ (1.5) and O₂²⁻ (1), so it has the shortest bond.

quiz.q: He₂ is not stable because bond order is:
quiz.why: He₂ would have 2 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons, so bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0. With no net bonding it is not stable.

quiz.q: s–p mixing is significant in:
quiz.why: s–p mixing occurs when the 2s–2p energy gap is small, as in lighter diatomics like B₂, C₂ and N₂. For N₂ it places σ2p above π2p; O₂ and F₂ lack this.

questions.q: Quantum number deciding orbital shape:
questions.why: The azimuthal quantum number l determines the shape of an orbital (0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d). n gives size and energy; mₗ gives orientation.

questions.q: Hybridisation of C in CH₄:
questions.why: Carbon in CH₄ has four bond pairs, i.e. four electron domains, so it is sp³ hybridised with tetrahedral geometry.

questions.q: Bond order of N₂:
questions.why: N₂ has 10 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons: bond order = (10 − 4)/2 = 3, matching the triple bond.

questions.q: Total nodes in a 4f orbital:
questions.why: Total nodes = n − 1 = 3 for n = 4. Of these, l = 3 are angular and n − l − 1 = 0 are radial.

questions.q: Shape of XeF₄:
questions.why: XeF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (steric number 6). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving a square planar shape.

questions.q: Cu⁺ salts are more covalent than Na⁺ salts mainly because Cu⁺:
questions.why: Cu⁺ has a pseudo-noble-gas 18-electron shell. The d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so Cu⁺ polarises anions strongly and its salts are more covalent than Na⁺ salts.

questions.q: Unpaired electrons in Fe³⁺:
questions.why: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. Five d electrons occupy five orbitals singly, giving 5 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Assertion: NH₃ has a smaller bond angle than CH₄. Reason: Lone pair–bond pair repulsion exceeds bond pair–bond pair repulsion.
questions.why: Both statements are true: NH₃ has one lone pair, and lone pair–bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair–bond pair, so its angle is smaller than CH₄'s. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Shape of I₃⁻:
questions.why: I₃⁻ has a central I with 2 bonds and 3 lone pairs (steric number 5). The three lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, leaving a linear shape.

questions.q: Using Slater's rules, Zeff for a 2p electron of N (Z = 7):
questions.why: For a 2p electron in N: same-group electrons (4 others at 2s2p) contribute 0.35 each = 1.40 for 4... the given working S = 3.10 and Zeff = Z − S = 7 − 3.10 = 3.90.

questions.q: Case: For MgO, ΔH_sub = 148, IE₁ + IE₂ = 2188, ½D = 249, EA₁ + EA₂ = +603 (net), ΔH_f = −602 kJ/mol. Lattice energy:
Which species has bond order 2.5 and is paramagnetic?
questions.why: NO has 15 electrons: 10 bonding and 5 antibonding, so bond order = 2.5. The last electron is a single unpaired electron in π*, so it is paramagnetic. N₂, CO and CN⁻ are diamagnetic.

questions.q: Which pair are isostructural?
questions.why: XeF₂ and I₃⁻ both have steric number 5 with three lone pairs on the central atom, giving a linear shape. The other pairs differ in shape.

questions.q: Arrange in increasing bond length: O₂²⁻, O₂⁻, O₂, O₂⁺
questions.why: Bond order: O₂⁺ 2.5, O₂ 2, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1. Higher bond order means a shorter bond, so length increases as O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻.

questions.q: C₂ in its ground state (with s–p mixing) is:
questions.why: With s–p mixing C₂ fills π2p⁴ with σ2p empty. Bond order = (6 − 2)/2 = 2, and all electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic.

courses.title: Organic I · Electronic effects, intermediates, stereochemistry
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Inductive, resonance and hyperconjugation effects on acidity and basicity, carbocations and other intermediates, chirality with R/S and E/Z, and SN1/SN2/E1/E2 mechanisms.
outcomes: Learners can rank acids and bases using electronic effects
Learners can predict carbocation stability and rearrangements
Learners can assign R/S and E/Z and identify meso compounds
Learners can choose between SN1, SN2, E1 and E2

scenes.text: Neha wonders why chloroacetic acid, used in labs, is far more acidic than the acetic acid in vinegar.
The chlorine pulls electron density away and stabilises the anion — the inductive effect.

steps.title: Three electronic effects
steps.body:
- **Inductive (I)**: polarisation through σ bonds, fades with distance. −I: NO₂ > CN > F > Cl > Br > I > OH; +I: alkyl groups.
- **Resonance (R/M)**: delocalisation through π systems. +R: −OH, −OR, −NH₂ (lone pair donors); −R: −NO₂, −C=O, −CN.
- **Hyperconjugation**: σ(C–H) → empty p or π* donation; explains why more substituted alkenes and carbocations are more stable.

Rule: anything that stabilises the conjugate base increases acidity.

steps.title: Solved: ranking acids
steps.body:
- ClCH₂COOH (pKa ≈ 2.9) > CH₃COOH (≈ 4.8): −I of Cl
- Cl₃CCOOH is stronger still (three −I groups)
- Phenol (pKa ≈ 10) ≫ ethanol (≈ 16): phenoxide is resonance stabilised
- p-Nitrophenol (≈ 7.2) > phenol: −R of NO₂ delocalises the negative charge further

steps.title: Solved: ranking bases
steps.body:
- Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than aniline: in aniline the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
- In water, the usual order is (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃ — a balance of +I effects, solvation and steric hindrance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking −OH is only electron-withdrawing; on a benzene ring its +R dominates for ortho/para activation.
- Forgetting that inductive effects weaken quickly beyond 2–3 bonds.
- Comparing acidity by the acid's stability instead of the conjugate base's.
- Predicting gas-phase basicity order for amines in water.

activity.prompt: Arrange from MOST acidic to LEAST acidic.
items: Trichloroacetic acid
Chloroacetic acid
Acetic acid
Phenol
Ethanol

quiz.q: Which group shows +R effect?
quiz.why: −NH₂ has a lone pair on N that it donates into a conjugated system (+R effect). −CHO, −NO₂ and −CN withdraw electrons (−R).

quiz.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
options: phenol is aromatic so no reason
quiz.why: The phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised into the ring by resonance, making it stabler than ethoxide, so phenol loses H⁺ more easily.

quiz.q: Hyperconjugation involves:
quiz.why: Hyperconjugation is delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond next to a π bond, a radical or a positive carbon. It is sometimes called no-bond resonance.

quiz.q: Weakest base:
quiz.why: In aniline the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton. The alkylamines and ammonia are more basic.

quiz.q: Strongest acid:
quiz.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen and has the strongest −I effect, which stabilises the carboxylate and makes FCH₂COOH the strongest acid.

scenes.text: In practical class, Om adds HCl to 3-methylbut-1-ene and expects 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. The major product is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane.
The carbocation rearranged by a hydride shift to a more stable tertiary cation.

steps.title: Four intermediates
steps.body:
- **Carbocations** (sp², planar, empty p): stability 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺; allyl and benzyl are resonance stabilised. They rearrange by 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl shifts toward greater stability.
- **Carbanions** (usually sp³, pyramidal): stability order opposite to carbocations — CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3°; stabilised by −I/−R groups.
- **Free radicals** (≈ planar, 7 electrons): 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃•; allyl/benzyl extra stable.
- **Carbenes** (:CR₂): singlet (paired, sp²) or triplet (two unpaired).

steps.title: Solved: the hydride shift
steps.body:
3-methylbut-1-ene + H⁺ → secondary cation at C2.

- A hydride on C3 shifts to C2
- Positive charge moves to C3 — now tertiary
- Cl⁻ attacks → **2-chloro-2-methylbutane** (major)

steps.title: Solved: ranking cation stability
steps.body:
Benzyl ≈ allyl (resonance) vs tert-butyl:

- (C₆H₅)₃C⁺ > (C₆H₅)₂CH⁺ > C₆H₅CH₂⁺ — more rings, more delocalisation
- CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ (allyl) > CH₃CH₂⁺ (primary) by resonance
- A cation α to an electron-withdrawing group (e.g. next to C=O) is destabilised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying carbocation order to carbanions.
- Forgetting rearrangements in SN1/E1 and acid-catalysed additions.
- Drawing carbocations as tetrahedral (they are planar, which is why SN1 racemises).
- Thinking free radicals carry a charge.

activity.prompt: Most stable or least stable within its own class?

quiz.q: Hybridisation of carbon in a carbocation:
quiz.why: A carbocation carbon has three sigma bonds in a plane and an empty p orbital, so it is sp² hybridised and trigonal planar.

quiz.q: Most stable carbanion:
quiz.why: Alkyl groups donate electrons (+I), which intensifies the negative charge and destabilises carbanions. So the methyl carbanion with no alkyl groups is the most stable.

quiz.q: Benzyl cation is stable because of:
quiz.why: The benzyl cation's positive charge is delocalised over the ring through resonance, which makes it much more stable than simple primary cations.

quiz.q: Carbocation rearrangements occur by:
quiz.why: Carbocations rearrange by 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl (methyl) shifts to form a more stable cation, e.g. secondary to tertiary.

quiz.q: A triplet carbene has:
quiz.why: A triplet carbene has two unpaired electrons with parallel spins in different orbitals, so it behaves as a diradical. A singlet carbene has paired electrons.

scenes.text: Farah tries to put her left glove on her right hand. Mirror images that cannot be superimposed — chirality.
Many drugs are chiral, and the two mirror forms can act differently in the body. Naming them correctly matters.

steps.title: Key definitions
steps.body:
- **Chiral**: not superimposable on its mirror image; commonly a carbon with four different groups (stereocentre)
- **Enantiomers**: non-superimposable mirror images; same physical properties except the direction of rotating plane-polarised light
- **Diastereomers**: stereoisomers that are not mirror images; different physical properties
- **Meso**: has stereocentres but an internal plane of symmetry → achiral (meso-tartaric acid)
- Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ for n stereocentres (fewer if meso forms exist)
- Specific rotation [α] = α/(l × c), l in dm, c in g/mL

steps.title: CIP priority rules
steps.body:
1. Higher atomic number at the first point of difference gets higher priority.
2. If tied, move outward to the next atoms and compare sets.
3. Double bonds count as duplicated atoms.

**R/S**: point the lowest priority (4) away; 1 → 2 → 3 clockwise = R, anticlockwise = S. If 4 points toward you, reverse the answer.
**E/Z**: higher-priority groups on the same side = Z (zusammen), opposite = E (entgegen).

steps.title: Solved: counting stereoisomers
steps.body:
- 2,3-Dibromobutane: 2 stereocentres → 2² = 4 expected, but (2R,3S) is meso → only **3** stereoisomers (a pair of enantiomers + meso)
- 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane: 4 stereoisomers (no meso; ends differ)

steps.title: Solved: specific rotation and ee
steps.body:
A solution of 0.5 g/mL in a 1 dm tube rotates light +6.65°.

- [α] = 6.65/(1 × 0.5) = **+13.3°**
- If the pure enantiomer has [α] = +19.0°, enantiomeric excess = 13.3/19.0 × 100 = **70% ee** (85 : 15 mixture)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming R means (+) rotation — the R/S label and sign of rotation are unrelated.
- Forgetting to reverse when the lowest-priority group points toward you.
- Using cis/trans when E/Z is needed for tri- or tetra-substituted alkenes.
- Counting 2ⁿ isomers without checking for meso forms.

statements.s: A meso compound is optically inactive.

statements.why: Identical physical properties in an achiral environment.

statements.s: A racemic mixture shows zero net optical rotation.
An (R) compound always rotates light clockwise.
Diastereomers can be separated by ordinary distillation or crystallisation.

quiz.q: Number of stereoisomers of tartaric acid:
quiz.why: Tartaric acid has two stereocentres but is symmetric, so there are d, l and meso forms: 3 stereoisomers (not 4).

quiz.q: Higher CIP priority:
quiz.why: CIP priority goes by atomic number of the atom directly attached: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1), so −OH ranks highest.

quiz.q: Enantiomers differ in:
quiz.why: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except that they rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions.

quiz.q: If the lowest-priority group points toward the viewer and the sequence looks clockwise, the configuration is:
quiz.why: If the lowest-priority group faces the viewer, the apparent direction is reversed. A clockwise sequence would look R, but really it is S.

quiz.q: Specific rotation when α = −4°, l = 2 dm, c = 0.1 g/mL:
quiz.why: Specific rotation = α/(l × c) = −4/(2 × 0.1) = −20°.

lessons.title: Substitution and elimination: SN1, SN2, E1, E2

scenes.text: Two students treat 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with different reagents: one with water, one with hot ethanolic KOH.
One gets an alcohol (substitution); the other an alkene (elimination). Substrate, nucleophile/base, solvent and temperature decide.

steps.title: The four mechanisms
steps.body:
- **SN2**: one step, backside attack, rate = k[RX][Nu], **inversion** (Walden). Fastest for CH₃ > 1° > 2°; 3° essentially no. Favoured by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMSO, DMF).
- **SN1**: two steps via carbocation, rate = k[RX], **racemisation** (often with some inversion), possible rearrangement. 3° > 2°; polar protic solvents.
- **E2**: one step, strong base, **anti-periplanar** H and leaving group; usually **Zaitsev** (more substituted alkene), but bulky bases (t-BuO⁻) favour Hofmann (less substituted).
- **E1**: via carbocation, competes with SN1, favoured by heat.

steps.title: Solved: predicting the product
steps.body:
- (R)-2-bromobutane + NaI in acetone → **(S)-2-iodobutane** (SN2, inversion; Finkelstein)
- (CH₃)₃CBr in water/ethanol, warm → (CH₃)₃COH via SN1 (+ some alkene by E1)
- (CH₃)₃CBr + hot alcoholic KOH → **2-methylpropene** (E2)

steps.title: Solved: Zaitsev vs Hofmann
steps.body:
2-Bromobutane + base:

- Ethoxide (small) → but-2-ene major (more substituted, Zaitsev)
- tert-Butoxide (bulky) → but-1-ene proportion rises (Hofmann product), because the base reaches the less hindered H more easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Proposing SN2 at a tertiary carbon.
- Forgetting that SN1 gives (near) racemisation, not retention.
- Ignoring rearrangement possibilities in SN1/E1.
- Using a polar protic solvent to speed up SN2 (it solvates and slows the nucleophile).

a.text: Substrate: 1-bromobutane. Reagent: NaCN in DMSO. Which pathway dominates?

choices.label: SN2
choices.feedback: Yes — primary substrate, strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent.

choices.label: SN1
choices.feedback: A primary carbocation is too unstable.

a2.text: Think again: 1° substrates rarely ionise. Choose again.

b.text: Next: tert-butyl bromide in hot ethanolic KOH. Main pathway?

choices.label: E2
choices.feedback: Right — strong base, tertiary substrate, heat → elimination.

choices.label: SN2
choices.feedback: Backside attack is blocked at a 3° carbon.

b2.text: Tertiary carbons do not undergo SN2. Try again.

end.text: Rule of thumb: look at substrate class, then reagent strength/bulk, then solvent and temperature.

quiz.q: SN2 reactions proceed with:
quiz.why: SN2 involves backside attack by the nucleophile, so the configuration at the carbon is inverted (Walden inversion).

quiz.q: Rate law for SN1:
quiz.why: SN1 is unimolecular: the slow ionisation of RX to a carbocation is rate-determining, so rate = k[RX], independent of the nucleophile.

quiz.q: E2 requires the H and leaving group to be:
quiz.why: E2 is a one-step elimination needing the H and leaving group to be anti-periplanar so the orbitals overlap well as the π bond forms.

quiz.q: Best solvent for SN2:
quiz.why: Polar aprotic solvents like DMSO solvate cations but not the nucleophile, leaving it 'naked' and reactive, which suits SN2. Protic solvents hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile.

quiz.q: Bulky bases favour:
quiz.why: A bulky base cannot reach the more hindered hydrogen, so it removes the less hindered one and gives the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product).

questions.q: −NO₂ shows:
questions.why: −NO₂ strongly withdraws electrons both through sigma bonds (−I) and by resonance (−R), making it a strong electron-withdrawing group.

questions.q: A carbon with four different groups is a:
questions.why: A carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocentre (chiral centre) and can give enantiomers.

questions.q: Most stable carbocation:
questions.why: Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by three alkyl groups through +I and hyperconjugation, so they are more stable than secondary, primary and methyl.

questions.q: Racemic mixture rotation:
questions.why: A racemic mixture holds equal amounts of both enantiomers, and their rotations cancel, giving zero net rotation.

questions.q: Higher priority between −CH₂OH and −CH(CH₃)₂:
questions.why: Both carbons at the first point tie (C vs C). At the next set, −CH₂OH has (O, H, H) against (C, C, H), and O beats C, so −CH₂OH has higher priority.

questions.q: Aniline is less basic than methylamine due to:
questions.why: In aniline the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring by resonance, so it is less able to take up a proton than in methylamine, where +I raises basicity.

questions.q: Assertion: SN1 at a chiral centre gives mostly racemic product. Reason: The carbocation is planar and attacked from both faces.
questions.why: Both are true: SN1 proceeds via a planar carbocation attacked from either face, giving a mostly racemic mixture. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Number of stereoisomers of 2,3-dichlorobutane:
questions.why: 2,3-Dichlorobutane has two stereocentres, so 2² = 4 would be expected, but one form is meso, so only 3 stereoisomers: a pair of enantiomers and the meso form.

questions.q: Strongest acid:
questions.why: The nitro group at the para position withdraws electrons by −R, stabilising the phenoxide, so p-nitrophenol is the strongest acid. Methyl and methoxy donate electrons and weaken acidity.

questions.q: (S)-2-chlorobutane with NaSH in DMF gives:
questions.why: SH⁻ in the polar aprotic DMF gives an SN2 reaction, with inversion of configuration. Since priorities of the groups keep the same order, (S) becomes (R)-butane-2-thiol.

questions.q: Case: A sample of an enantiomer with [α]pure = +40° shows [α]obs = +10°. Percentage of the (+) form:
questions.why: Optical purity = 10/40 = 25% ee. The remainder 75% is racemic, 37.5% each, so (+) = 25 + 37.5 = 62.5%.

questions.q: Major product when 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene reacts with HBr:
questions.why: H⁺ adds to the terminal CH₂ to give a secondary cation, which undergoes a methyl shift to a tertiary cation. Br⁻ then attacks to give 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.q: Which conformation is required for E2 in a cyclohexyl halide?
options: axial leaving group with axial anti H
questions.why: E2 in cyclohexane requires the leaving group and the β-hydrogen to be trans-diaxial (anti-periplanar), so the leaving group must be axial with an axial anti H.

questions.q: Rank SN2 rates: CH₃Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr, CH₃CH₂Br, (CH₃)₃CBr
questions.why: SN2 rate falls as steric hindrance at the carbon increases: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary (which essentially does not react by SN2).

questions.q: Which statement on carbenes is correct?
options: Singlet carbenes add to cis-alkenes stereospecifically
Carbenes have 8 valence electrons on C
questions.why: Singlet carbenes (paired electrons) add in a concerted, stereospecific step, so cis alkene gives cis cyclopropane. Triplet carbenes react stepwise, and carbene carbon has 6, not 8, electrons.

courses.title: Physical I · Chemical thermodynamics and kinetics
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Thermochemistry with Hess and Kirchhoff, Gibbs energy and equilibrium, rate laws and integrated equations, and Arrhenius behaviour with collision and transition-state ideas.
outcomes: Learners can relate ΔH and ΔU and apply Hess's law
Learners can predict spontaneity and K from ΔG°
Learners can use integrated rate laws and half-lives
Learners can compute activation energy from rate data

lessons.title: Thermochemistry: ΔH, ΔU, Hess and Kirchhoff

scenes.text: Ananya wonders how much heat her family's LPG cylinder really gives.
Enthalpies of combustion and Hess's law answer it without burning anything in a calorimeter twice.

steps.title: Core relations
steps.body:
- ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT (Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − reactants)
- **Hess's law**: ΔH of a reaction is the same however it is carried out (state function)
- From formation enthalpies: ΔH° = ΣΔH_f°(products) − ΣΔH_f°(reactants)
- From bond enthalpies (gas phase, approximate): ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)
- **Kirchhoff**: ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔC_p (T₂ − T₁)

steps.title: Solved: Hess's law
steps.body:
Given C + O₂ → CO₂ (−393.5 kJ) and CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ (−283.0 kJ). Find ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO.

- Reverse the second: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂ (+283.0)
- Add to the first: C + ½O₂ → CO
- ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = **−110.5 kJ**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting liquids/solids in Δn_g.
- Mixing J and kJ when using R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
- Forgetting to multiply ΔH when scaling equations.
- Using bond enthalpies for liquids (they are gas-phase averages).

activity.prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ at 298 K. Find ΔU in kJ (R = 8.314 J/mol K).

quiz.q: Hess's law follows because enthalpy is a:
