scenes.text: A machinist is told the output must be within ε of target. She asks: then how precisely must I set the input?
That answer, δ, is exactly what the ε–δ definition asks you to produce.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means: for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε.

- f need not be defined at a; only nearby values matter.
- δ may depend on ε and a, never on x.
- One-sided limits: lim_{x→a⁻} and lim_{x→a⁺}. The limit exists iff both exist and are equal.

steps.title: Solved: a quadratic limit
steps.body:
Prove lim_{x→2} x² = 4.

- |x² − 4| = |x − 2|·|x + 2|.
- First restrict |x − 2| < 1, so 1 < x < 3 and |x + 2| < 5.
- Then |x² − 4| < 5|x − 2|; this is < ε if |x − 2| < ε/5.
- Choose δ = min(1, ε/5). ∎

steps.title: Standard limits
steps.body:
- lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1
- lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2
- lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x = 1
- lim_{x→0} ln(1 + x)/x = 1
- lim_{x→a} (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹
- lim_{x→∞} (1 + 1/x)ˣ = e

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing δ that depends on x.
- Forgetting the restriction step (like |x − 2| < 1) when the factor |x + 2| is not constant.
- Saying the limit equals f(a) when f is not continuous at a.
- Not checking both one-sided limits for piecewise functions or |x|.

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x². (Hint: 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2).)

quiz.q: For lim_{x→3} (2x + 5) = 11, a valid δ for a given ε is:
quiz.why: Since |(2x + 5) − 11| = 2|x − 3|, requiring this to be below ε gives |x − 3| < ε/2, so δ = ε/2 works.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} sin 5x / x equals:
quiz.why: Write sin 5x / x = 5·(sin 5x)/(5x); the bracket tends to 1, so the limit is 5.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} |x|/x:
quiz.why: The right-hand limit is 1 and the left-hand limit is −1; since they differ, the two-sided limit does not exist.

lessons.title: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem

scenes.text: A climber goes from 500 m to 900 m altitude along a trail.
Somewhere on the way she must have been at exactly 700 m — that is the intermediate value theorem.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
f is continuous at a if (i) f(a) is defined, (ii) lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and (iii) the limit equals f(a). In ε–δ form: for each ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε.

Types of discontinuity:
- Removable: limit exists but ≠ f(a) or f(a) undefined.
- Jump (first kind): both one-sided limits exist but differ.
- Second kind: at least one one-sided limit fails to exist (e.g. sin(1/x) at 0).

steps.title: Theorems on closed intervals
steps.body:
If f is continuous on [a, b]:
- f is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum.
- Intermediate value theorem: for every k between f(a) and f(b) there is c ∈ [a, b] with f(c) = k.
- Corollary (Bolzano): if f(a)·f(b) < 0, f has a root in (a, b).

steps.title: Solved: making a piecewise function continuous
steps.body:
f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 2, and f(x) = x² − 1 for x > 2.

- Left limit at 2: 2k + 1 = f(2).
- Right limit at 2: 4 − 1 = 3.
- Continuity needs 2k + 1 = 3 ⇒ k = 1.

steps.title: Solved: locating a root
steps.body:
Show x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root in (1, 2).

- f(1) = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 < 0; f(2) = 8 − 2 − 1 = 5 > 0.
- f is a polynomial, so continuous; by Bolzano a root lies in (1, 2).
- Halving: f(1.5) = 3.375 − 1.5 − 1 = 0.875 > 0, so the root is in (1, 1.5).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying IVT to a function that is discontinuous on the interval (1/x on [−1, 1] changes sign but has no root).
- Checking only one side of a piecewise junction.
- Calling a removable discontinuity a jump.

activity.prompt: f(x) = sin(3x)/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. Find k so that f is continuous at 0.

quiz.why: The limit at 2 is x + 2 → 4, which exists but differs from f(2) = 5, so redefining f(2) = 4 removes the discontinuity.

quiz.q: The greatest integer function [x] at x = 1 has:
quiz.why: The left limit is 0 and the right limit is 1; both exist but differ, which is a jump.

quiz.q: Which equation is guaranteed a root in (0, 1) by Bolzano's theorem?
quiz.why: For f(x) = x³ + 3x − 1, f(0) = −1 and f(1) = 3 have opposite signs, and f is continuous, so a root lies in (0, 1).

scenes.text: A road with a sharp corner is continuous — you never fall off — but your steering changes direction instantly.
A corner is where the left and right derivatives disagree.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
f'(a) = lim_{h→0} [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h.

- Right derivative Rf'(a): limit as h → 0⁺; left derivative Lf'(a): h → 0⁻.
- f is differentiable at a iff Lf'(a) and Rf'(a) exist, are finite and equal.
- Theorem: differentiable at a ⇒ continuous at a. Proof: f(a + h) − f(a) = h·[f(a + h) − f(a)]/h → 0·f'(a) = 0. The converse is false.

steps.title: Solved: |x| and x|x| at 0
steps.body:
- f(x) = |x|: Rf'(0) = lim h/h = 1, Lf'(0) = lim (−h)/h = −1 ⇒ not differentiable.
- g(x) = x|x|: [g(h) − g(0)]/h = |h| → 0 from both sides ⇒ g'(0) = 0, differentiable.

steps.title: Solved: a piecewise junction
steps.body:
f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1, f(x) = 2x − 1 for x > 1.

- Continuity: both pieces give 1 at x = 1. ✔
- Lf'(1) = derivative of x² at 1 = 2.
- Rf'(1) = lim_{h→0⁺} [2(1 + h) − 1 − 1]/h = 2.
- Equal ⇒ f is differentiable at 1 with f'(1) = 2.

steps.title: x^p sin(1/x) family
steps.body: With f(0) = 0: p = 1 gives continuous, not differentiable at 0; p = 2 gives differentiable at 0 (f'(0) = 0) but f' is not continuous at 0; p = 3 gives a continuously differentiable function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Differentiating each piece and comparing formulas without first checking continuity (a jump kills differentiability even if slopes match).
- Using the derivative formula of a piece at the endpoint where the other piece applies.
- Believing a continuous function must be differentiable.

activity.prompt: Classify each function at x = 0 (assume f(0) = 0 where needed).

quiz.q: For f(x) = |x − 3|, Rf'(3) − Lf'(3) equals:
quiz.why: The right derivative is +1 and the left derivative is −1, so their difference is 2, confirming a corner at x = 3.

quiz.q: Which statement is always true?
quiz.why: Differentiability forces f(a + h) − f(a) = h × (difference quotient) → 0, so f is continuous; the other statements have counterexamples.
The difference quotient h^(1/3)/h = h^(−2/3) → +∞, so the function is continuous but has an infinite derivative, i.e. a vertical tangent.

scenes.text: An exam asks for the 10th derivative of x³eˣ. Differentiating ten times by hand would take a page.
Leibniz's theorem does it in one line because x³ dies after three derivatives.

steps.title: Standard nth derivatives
Leibniz's theorem
steps.body:
If u and v have nth derivatives, (uv)_n = Σ_{r=0}^{n} C(n, r) u_{n−r} v_r = u_n v + n u_{n−1} v_1 + C(n,2) u_{n−2} v_2 + … + u vₙ.

Proof is by induction on n, using C(n, r) + C(n, r − 1) = C(n + 1, r). Choose v to be the polynomial factor so the series terminates.

steps.title: Solved: y = x² eˣ
steps.body:
Take u = eˣ, v = x² (v₁ = 2x, v₂ = 2, v₃ = 0).

yₙ = eˣ·x² + n·eˣ·2x + [n(n − 1)/2]·eˣ·2 = eˣ [x² + 2nx + n(n − 1)].

steps.title: Solved: recurrence for y = sin⁻¹x
steps.body:
- y₁ = 1/√(1 − x²) ⇒ (1 − x²) y₁² = 1.
- Differentiate: (1 − x²)·2y₁y₂ − 2x y₁² = 0 ⇒ (1 − x²) y₂ − x y₁ = 0.
- Apply Leibniz n times: (1 − x²) y_{n+2} − 2nx y_{n+1} − n(n − 1) y_n − x y_{n+1} − n y_n = 0.
- Hence (1 − x²) y_{n+2} − (2n + 1) x y_{n+1} − n² yₙ = 0.
- At x = 0: y_{n+2}(0) = n² yₙ(0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the polynomial as u (the series then never terminates).
- Dropping the binomial coefficients C(n, r).
- Sign errors in (−1)ⁿ for reciprocals and logarithms.
- Forgetting to split rational functions into partial fractions first.

activity.prompt: For y = x³ eˣ, find the 5th derivative y₅ at x = 0.

quiz.q: D⁴ sin x equals:
quiz.why: Dⁿ sin x = sin(x + nπ/2); for n = 4 the shift is 2π, which returns sin x.

quiz.q: The nth derivative of 1/(x + 2) is:
quiz.why: Each differentiation lowers the power by one and brings a negative factor, giving (−1)ⁿ n!/(x + 2)^{n+1}.

quiz.q: If y = sin⁻¹x, then y₄(0) equals (given y₂(0) = 0):
quiz.why: The recurrence at 0 is y_{n+2}(0) = n² yₙ(0); with n = 2, y₄(0) = 4·y₂(0) = 0.

questions.q: For lim_{x→2} (3x − 1) = 5, the largest valid δ for given ε is:
questions.why: |3x − 1 − 5| = 3|x − 2| < ε exactly when |x − 2| < ε/3.

questions.q: lim_{x→0} (e^{2x} − 1)/x equals:
questions.why: Write it as 2·(e^{2x} − 1)/(2x); the bracket tends to 1, so the limit is 2.

questions.q: lim_{x→0} tan 3x / sin 2x equals:
questions.why: tan 3x ≈ 3x and sin 2x ≈ 2x near 0, so the ratio tends to 3/2.

questions.q: f(x) = ax + 3 (x ≤ 1), f(x) = 2x² + 1 (x > 1) is continuous for a =
questions.why: Continuity at 1 requires a + 3 = 2 + 1 = 3, giving a = 0.

questions.q: The function f(x) = x − [x] at integer points has:
questions.why: At an integer n the left limit is 1 and the right limit is 0, so both exist and differ — a jump.

questions.q: Bolzano's theorem guarantees a root of x³ − 2x − 5 = 0 in:
questions.why: f(2) = 8 − 4 − 5 = −1 and f(3) = 27 − 6 − 5 = 16 have opposite signs, so a root lies in (2, 3).

questions.q: f(x) = |x| + |x − 1| is not differentiable at:
questions.why: Each absolute value term creates a corner where its inside is zero, so f has corners at both 0 and 1.

questions.q: f(x) = x² sin(1/x), f(0) = 0. Then:
options: f'(0) = 0 but f' is not continuous at 0
questions.why: The difference quotient h sin(1/h) → 0, so f'(0) = 0, but for x ≠ 0 f'(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x), which has no limit at 0.

questions.q: Dⁿ ln(2x + 3) equals:
questions.why: The first derivative is 2/(2x + 3); differentiating that n − 1 more times gives (−1)^{n−1}(n − 1)! 2ⁿ/(2x + 3)ⁿ.

questions.q: For y = x² e^{x}, y₃ at x = 0 equals:
questions.why: yₙ = eˣ[x² + 2nx + n(n − 1)]; at x = 0 with n = 3 this is 3·2 = 6.

questions.q: If y = e^{a sin⁻¹x}, then (1 − x²)y₂ − x y₁ equals:
questions.why: y₁ = a y/√(1 − x²), so (1 − x²)y₁² = a²y²; differentiating and dividing by 2y₁ gives (1 − x²)y₂ − x y₁ = a² y.

questions.q: The 10th derivative of x³ eˣ at x = 0 is:
questions.why: Only the term with x³ differentiated three times survives at 0: C(10, 3)·6 = 120·6 = 720.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Mean value theorems, expansions and extrema
courses.summary: Rolle's, Lagrange's and Cauchy's mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin's theorems with remainders, indeterminate forms by L'Hôpital's rule, and maxima–minima of functions of one variable.
outcomes: State and verify Rolle's, Lagrange's and Cauchy's mean value theorems
Use the MVT to prove inequalities
Expand functions in Taylor and Maclaurin series and estimate remainders
Evaluate all seven indeterminate forms
Find and classify extrema and solve optimisation problems

scenes.text: A car enters an expressway at 10:00 and exits 120 km later at 11:00.
Lagrange's theorem says the speedometer read exactly 120 km/h at some instant — average speed is achieved.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
Let f (and g) be continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b).

- Rolle: if f(a) = f(b) then f'(c) = 0 for some c ∈ (a, b).
- Lagrange: f'(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) for some c ∈ (a, b).
- Cauchy: if g'(x) ≠ 0 on (a, b), [f(b) − f(a)]/[g(b) − g(a)] = f'(c)/g'(c) for some c.

Geometry: Rolle — a horizontal tangent; Lagrange — a tangent parallel to the chord.

steps.title: Proof of Lagrange from Rolle
steps.body:
Define φ(x) = f(x) − f(a) − k(x − a) with k = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a). Then φ(a) = φ(b) = 0, φ is continuous and differentiable, so by Rolle φ'(c) = f'(c) − k = 0 for some c. ∎

Cauchy is proved the same way with φ(x) = f(x) − k g(x), k chosen so φ(a) = φ(b).

steps.title: Solved: an inequality
steps.body:
Show x/(1 + x) < ln(1 + x) < x for x > 0.

- Apply Lagrange to ln t on [1, 1 + x]: ln(1 + x) = x·(1/c) with 1 < c < 1 + x.
- Then 1/(1 + x) < 1/c < 1, so x/(1 + x) < ln(1 + x) < x. ∎

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body:
- f' = 0 on an interval ⇒ f constant.
- f' > 0 ⇒ f strictly increasing; f' < 0 ⇒ strictly decreasing.
- Between two roots of f there is a root of f'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Rolle to |x| on [−1, 1] (not differentiable at 0).
- Accepting a c that lies outside the open interval.
- Forgetting the hypothesis g'(x) ≠ 0 in Cauchy's theorem.

activity.prompt: Find c given by Lagrange's MVT for f(x) = x² + 3x on [1, 5].

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem for f(x) = sin x on [0, π] gives c =
quiz.why: f(0) = f(π) = 0 and f'(c) = cos c = 0 in (0, π) gives c = π/2.

quiz.q: Lagrange's c for f(x) = √x on [1, 4] is:
quiz.why: The chord slope is (2 − 1)/3 = 1/3, and 1/(2√c) = 1/3 gives √c = 3/2, so c = 9/4.

quiz.q: If f'(x) = 0 for all x in (a, b), then f is:
quiz.why: For any two points the MVT gives f(x) − f(y) = f'(c)(x − y) = 0, so all values are equal.

scenes.text: A calculator has no table of eˣ; it adds a few terms of a polynomial.
Taylor's theorem tells it exactly how many terms are enough.

steps.title: Taylor's theorem with remainder
steps.body:
If f⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾ is continuous on [a, a + h] and f⁽ⁿ⁾ exists on (a, a + h):

f(a + h) = f(a) + h f'(a) + h²/2! f''(a) + … + hⁿ⁻¹/(n − 1)! f⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾(a) + Rₙ

- Lagrange form: Rₙ = hⁿ/n! · f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh), 0 < θ < 1.
- Cauchy form: Rₙ = hⁿ(1 − θ)ⁿ⁻¹/(n − 1)! · f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh).
- Maclaurin: a = 0, h = x.

steps.title: Solved: e^{sin x} up to x³
steps.body:
Let u = sin x = x − x³/6 + …

- e^u = 1 + u + u²/2 + u³/6 + …
- u² = x² + (terms of degree 4), u³ = x³ + …
- e^{sin x} = 1 + x − x³/6 + x²/2 + x³/6 + … = 1 + x + x²/2 + 0·x³ + …

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln(1 + x) series for x > 1 (it diverges).
- Dropping factorials in the denominators.
- Truncating a composition too early (keep all terms up to the required degree in each power of u).

activity.prompt: Use the first four terms of the Maclaurin series of eˣ to estimate e^{0.2} (four decimals).

quiz.q: The coefficient of x⁴ in cos x is:
quiz.why: cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …, and 1/4! = 1/24 with a positive sign.

quiz.q: The coefficient of x³ in tan x is:
quiz.why: tan x = x + x³/3 + 2x⁵/15 + …, so the x³ coefficient is 1/3.

quiz.q: In the Lagrange remainder Rₙ = hⁿ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh)/n!, θ satisfies:
quiz.why: θ locates an unknown point strictly between a and a + h, so 0 < θ < 1.

scenes.text: Plugging x = 0 into (x − sin x)/x³ gives 0/0 — no information.
L'Hôpital's rule compares how fast numerator and denominator vanish.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body:
If f(a) = g(a) = 0 (or both → ∞), f, g differentiable near a, g'(x) ≠ 0, and lim f'/g' exists, then lim f/g = lim f'/g'. It follows from Cauchy's MVT.

Seven forms: 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰.
- 0·∞ and ∞ − ∞: rewrite as a quotient.
- Exponent forms: take y = f^g, ln y = g ln f, find lim ln y = L, answer e^L.

steps.title: Solved: (x − sin x)/x³
steps.body:
- 0/0 ⇒ (1 − cos x)/(3x²) still 0/0
- ⇒ sin x/(6x) → 1/6.
- Answer 1/6 (also visible from sin x = x − x³/6 + …).

steps.title: Solved: x ln x as x → 0⁺
steps.body: 0·(−∞). Write ln x/(1/x): ∞/∞ ⇒ (1/x)/(−1/x²) = −x → 0. So lim x ln x = 0, and hence lim xˣ = e⁰ = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the quotient rule instead of differentiating numerator and denominator separately.
- Applying the rule when the form is not indeterminate (e.g. (x + 1)/x at 0).
- Forgetting to exponentiate at the end for 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰.

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1 − x)/x².

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} (1/x − 1/sin x) equals:
quiz.why: Combining gives (sin x − x)/(x sin x) ≈ (−x³/6)/x², which tends to 0.

quiz.q: lim_{x→∞} x/eˣ equals:
quiz.why: ∞/∞, and one application of L'Hôpital gives 1/eˣ → 0; exponentials beat polynomials.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} (1 + 2x)^{1/x} equals:
quiz.why: ln y = ln(1 + 2x)/x → 2 by L'Hôpital, so y → e².

lessons.title: Maxima and minima of one variable

scenes.text: A tinsmith cuts equal squares from the corners of a 12 cm square sheet and folds up a box.
Too small a cut gives a flat tray, too big a narrow tower; calculus finds the best cut.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
- Critical points: f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist.
- First-derivative test: f' changes + to − ⇒ local max; − to + ⇒ local min.
- Second-derivative test: f'(c) = 0, f''(c) < 0 ⇒ max; f''(c) > 0 ⇒ min; f''(c) = 0 ⇒ test higher derivatives: if the first nonzero derivative is of even order n, extremum (max if f⁽ⁿ⁾(c) < 0); if odd order, no extremum.
- Absolute extrema on [a, b]: compare f at critical points and endpoints.

steps.title: Solved: the open box
steps.body:
Cut x from each corner of a 12 × 12 sheet: V = x(12 − 2x)², 0 < x < 6.

- V' = (12 − 2x)² − 4x(12 − 2x) = (12 − 2x)(12 − 6x).
- V' = 0 ⇒ x = 2 (x = 6 gives V = 0).
- V(2) = 2·8² = 128 cm³, a maximum.

steps.title: Solved: higher-derivative test
steps.body: f(x) = x⁴: f'(0) = f''(0) = f'''(0) = 0, f⁽⁴⁾(0) = 24 > 0, even order ⇒ minimum. f(x) = x³: first nonzero is f'''(0) = 6, odd order ⇒ no extremum (point of inflection).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting endpoints when asked for absolute extrema.
- Ignoring points where f' does not exist (|x| has a minimum at 0).
- Calling every critical point an extremum (x³ at 0).

activity.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 40 m. What is the largest possible area (m²)?

quiz.q: f(x) = x³ − 3x has a local maximum at:
quiz.why: f'(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1 and f''(−1) = −6 < 0, so x = −1 is a local maximum.

quiz.q: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) = 0 but f'''(c) ≠ 0, then at c:
quiz.why: The first nonvanishing derivative has odd order, so f changes sign of f − f(c) across c and there is no extremum.

quiz.q: The minimum value of x + 1/x for x > 0 is:
quiz.why: f'(x) = 1 − 1/x² = 0 gives x = 1, f''(1) = 2 > 0, so the minimum is 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.q: Rolle's c for f(x) = x² − 4x on [0, 4] is:
questions.why: f(0) = f(4) = 0 and f'(c) = 2c − 4 = 0 gives c = 2.

questions.q: Lagrange's c for f(x) = x² on [a, b] is:
questions.why: (b² − a²)/(b − a) = a + b = 2c, so c is the arithmetic mean.

questions.q: Cauchy's c for f = eˣ, g = e^{−x} on [a, b] is:
Rolle's theorem cannot be applied to f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] because:
questions.why: |x| has a corner at 0, so the differentiability hypothesis fails.

questions.q: The Maclaurin coefficient of x² in ln(1 + x) is:
questions.why: ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − …, so the coefficient is −1/2.

questions.q: The Maclaurin series of e^{x} cos x up to x² is:
lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³ equals:
questions.why: sin x = x − x³/6 + …, so the numerator is x³/6 + … and the limit is 1/6.

questions.q: lim_{x→0⁺} xˣ equals:
questions.why: ln y = x ln x → 0, so y → e⁰ = 1.

questions.q: lim_{x→0} (tan x − x)/x³ equals:
questions.why: tan x = x + x³/3 + …, so (tan x − x)/x³ → 1/3.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x has a local minimum value:
The largest volume of an open box from a 12 cm square sheet is:
questions.why: V = x(12 − 2x)² is maximised at x = 2, giving 2 × 64 = 128 cm³.

questions.q: f(x) = x⁴ at x = 0 has:
questions.why: The first nonzero derivative at 0 is f⁽⁴⁾(0) = 24 > 0, of even order, so x = 0 is a minimum.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Asymptotes, curvature and curve tracing
courses.summary: Finding vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes of algebraic curves, concavity and points of inflection, radius of curvature in Cartesian, parametric and polar forms, and systematic tracing of standard curves.
outcomes: Find all asymptotes of rational and algebraic curves
Locate points of inflection and intervals of concavity
Compute the radius of curvature in Cartesian, parametric and polar forms
Trace standard Cartesian and polar curves using symmetry, tangents at the origin and asymptotes

scenes.text: Railway tracks seem to meet at the horizon but never do.
An asymptote is a line the curve approaches ever more closely as it runs off to infinity.

steps.title: Types and formulas
steps.body:
- Vertical: x = a if y → ±∞ as x → a (zeros of the denominator, or coefficient of the highest power of y set to zero).
- Horizontal: y = b if y → b as x → ±∞.
- Oblique y = mx + c: m = lim_{x→∞} y/x, c = lim_{x→∞} (y − mx).

steps.title: Method for algebraic curves
steps.body:
Write the curve as φₙ(x, y) + φₙ₋₁(x, y) + … = 0 (homogeneous parts). Put x = 1, y = m to get φₙ(m), φₙ₋₁(m).

- Slopes: roots of φₙ(m) = 0.
- Intercepts: c = −φₙ₋₁(m)/φₙ'(m).
- If φₙ'(m) = 0 for a repeated root, use c²/2·φₙ''(m) + c·φₙ₋₁'(m) + φₙ₋₂(m) = 0.

steps.title: Solved: a rational function
steps.body:
y = (x² + 1)/(x − 1).

- Vertical: x = 1.
- Divide: x² + 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1) + 2 ⇒ y = x + 1 + 2/(x − 1).
- As x → ±∞, 2/(x − 1) → 0, so the oblique asymptote is y = x + 1.

steps.title: Solved: folium of Descartes x³ + y³ = 3axy
steps.body:
- φ₃(m) = 1 + m³ = 0 ⇒ m = −1 (only real root).
- φ₂(m) = −3am, φ₃'(m) = 3m².
- c = −φ₂(m)/φ₃'(m) = 3am/(3m²) = a/m = −a.
- Asymptote: y = −x − a, i.e. x + y + a = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking only x → +∞ when the behaviour at −∞ differs (e.g. y = √(x² + 1) has y = x and y = −x).
- Forgetting that a curve may cross its oblique asymptote at finite points.
- Using the c-formula when φₙ'(m) = 0.

activity.prompt: y = (2x² + 3x)/(x + 1) has an oblique asymptote y = 2x + c. Find c.

quiz.q: y = (3x + 1)/(x − 2) has horizontal asymptote:
quiz.why: As x → ∞ the ratio of leading coefficients gives 3x/x = 3, so y = 3.

quiz.q: The slopes of asymptotes of a curve of degree n come from:
quiz.why: For large x the highest-degree part dominates, so the directions to infinity satisfy φₙ(m) = 0.

quiz.q: The curve x²y = x² + 1 has vertical asymptote:
quiz.why: Solving gives y = 1 + 1/x², which blows up as x → 0, so x = 0 is a vertical asymptote.

scenes.text: A hill road curves left, straightens for an instant, then curves right.
That instant is a point of inflection — the sign of y'' changes.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Concave upward (convex) on I if y'' > 0 there: the curve lies above its tangents.
- Concave downward if y'' < 0.
- Point of inflection: where concavity changes. Necessary: y'' = 0 or undefined. Sufficient: y'' changes sign (or y'' = 0, y''' ≠ 0).

steps.title: Solved: y = x³ − 3x²
steps.body:
- y' = 3x² − 6x, y'' = 6x − 6.
- y'' < 0 for x < 1 (concave down), > 0 for x > 1 (concave up).
- Inflection at (1, −2).

steps.title: Solved: y = x⁴ and y = x^{1/3}
steps.body:
- y = x⁴: y'' = 12x² = 0 at 0 but does not change sign ⇒ no inflection.
- y = x^{1/3}: y'' = −(2/9)x^{−5/3} is undefined at 0 and changes sign ⇒ inflection at the origin with a vertical tangent.

steps.title: Solved: the bell curve y = e^{−x²}
steps.body:
- y' = −2x e^{−x²}, y'' = (4x² − 2)e^{−x²}.
- y'' = 0 at x = ±1/√2 and changes sign there.
- Inflections at (±1/√2, e^{−1/2}) ≈ (±0.707, 0.607).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring every zero of y'' an inflection point.
- Missing points where y'' is undefined.
- Confusing extremum (y' changes sign) with inflection (y'' changes sign).

activity.prompt: Find the x-coordinate of the point of inflection of y = x³ − 6x² + 5.

quiz.q: y = sin x on (0, π) is:
quiz.why: y'' = −sin x < 0 on (0, π), so the arc is concave downward throughout.

quiz.q: A sufficient condition for an inflection at x = a is:
quiz.why: If y''(a) = 0 and y'''(a) ≠ 0, then y'' is strictly monotone near a and changes sign, giving an inflection.

quiz.q: y = eˣ has how many points of inflection?
quiz.why: y'' = eˣ > 0 everywhere, so the curve is always concave up and never changes concavity.

scenes.text: Highway engineers need the tightness of every bend to set speed limits and banking.
The radius of curvature is the radius of the circle that best hugs the curve at a point.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Curvature κ = dψ/ds, radius ρ = 1/κ.

- Cartesian: ρ = (1 + y₁²)^{3/2}/|y₂|.
- Parametric: ρ = (x'² + y'²)^{3/2}/|x'y'' − y'x''|.
- Polar r = f(θ): ρ = (r² + r₁²)^{3/2}/|r² + 2r₁² − r r₂|.
- Pedal p = f(r): ρ = r dr/dp.
- At the origin, if the x-axis is tangent: ρ = lim x²/(2y) (Newton's formula).

steps.title: Solved: parabola and circle
steps.body:
- y = x² at the origin: y₁ = 0, y₂ = 2 ⇒ ρ = 1/2. Newton: x²/(2y) = 1/2 ✔.
- Circle x = a cos t, y = a sin t: x'² + y'² = a², x'y'' − y'x'' = a² ⇒ ρ = a³/a² = a.

steps.title: Solved: cardioid r = a(1 − cos θ)
steps.body:
- r₁ = a sin θ, r₂ = a cos θ.
- r² + r₁² = 2a²(1 − cos θ) = 2ar; r² + 2r₁² − r r₂ = 3a²(1 − cos θ) = 3ar.
- ρ = (2ar)^{3/2}/(3ar) = (2√2/3)√(ar), so ρ² ∝ r.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the exponent 3/2.
- Dropping the absolute value in the denominator (ρ is positive).
- Using the Cartesian formula where y₁ is infinite (vertical tangent) — switch to dx/dy form or parametric.

activity.prompt: Find the radius of curvature of y = eˣ at (0, 1) (three decimals).

quiz.q: The radius of curvature of a straight line is:
quiz.why: A line has y'' = 0, so κ = 0 and ρ = 1/κ is infinite.

quiz.q: For y = x²/2 at the origin, ρ equals:
quiz.why: y₁ = 0 and y₂ = 1 at the origin, so ρ = 1/1 = 1.

quiz.q: For r = a (a circle in polar form), ρ equals:
quiz.why: r₁ = r₂ = 0, so ρ = (a²)^{3/2}/a² = a, as expected for a circle of radius a.

scenes.text: An examiner asks you to sketch y²(a − x) = x³ — no calculator, no table of values.
A checklist of symmetry, origin, tangents, asymptotes and region gives the full picture in minutes.

steps.title: Cartesian checklist
steps.body:
1. Symmetry: only even powers of y ⇒ about x-axis; only even powers of x ⇒ about y-axis; unchanged under (x, y) → (−x, −y) ⇒ opposite quadrants; x ↔ y ⇒ about y = x.
2. Origin: no constant term ⇒ passes through O; tangents at O from the lowest-degree terms set to zero.
3. Intercepts with axes and tangents there.
4. Asymptotes.
5. Region: where y is real (y² ≥ 0).
6. Special points: dy/dx = 0 or ∞.

steps.title: Solved: cissoid y²(a − x) = x³
steps.body:
- Even powers of y ⇒ symmetric about the x-axis.
- Passes through O; lowest terms a y² = 0 ⇒ tangent y = 0 twice ⇒ cusp at O.
- y² = x³/(a − x) ≥ 0 ⇒ 0 ≤ x < a.
- Vertical asymptote x = a (coefficient of y² vanishes).
- Shape: two branches leaving O tangent to the x-axis and rising to ±∞ along x = a.

steps.title: Polar checklist
steps.body:
- Symmetry about the initial line if θ → −θ leaves the equation unchanged; about θ = π/2 if θ → π − θ does.
- Pole: values of θ with r = 0 give tangents at the pole.
- Range of r (|r| ≤ max), and tan φ = r dθ/dr for the angle between radius and tangent.

steps.title: Solved: cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ)
steps.body:
- Symmetric about the initial line.
- r = 2a at θ = 0, r = a at θ = π/2, r = 0 at θ = π (cusp at the pole, tangent θ = π).
- tan φ = r/(dr/dθ) = −cot(θ/2) ⇒ φ = π/2 + θ/2.
- Heart shape, enclosed area 3πa²/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the region test can exclude whole strips of the plane.
- Taking all terms instead of the lowest-degree terms for tangents at the origin.
- Plotting negative r for curves like r = a cos 2θ in the wrong direction.

activity.prompt: Match each curve to its symmetry.

quiz.q: Tangents at the origin of y²(a + x) = x²(a − x) are:
quiz.why: The lowest-degree terms are a y² = a x², i.e. y² = x², giving tangents y = ±x (a node).

quiz.q: r = a(1 + cos θ) passes through the pole at θ =
quiz.why: r = 0 needs cos θ = −1, i.e. θ = π.

quiz.q: The curve y²(a − x) = x³ exists only for:
quiz.why: y² = x³/(a − x) must be non-negative, which requires x and a − x to have the same sign, so 0 ≤ x < a.

questions.q: The oblique asymptote of y = (x² + 1)/(x − 1) is:
questions.why: Division gives y = x + 1 + 2/(x − 1), and the last term tends to 0.

questions.q: The asymptote of x³ + y³ = 3axy is:
questions.why: m = −1 from 1 + m³ = 0 and c = a/m = −a, so y = −x − a.

questions.q: y = 1/(x² − 4) has vertical asymptotes:
questions.why: The denominator vanishes at x = ±2 while the numerator does not.

questions.q: The inflection point of y = x³ − 3x² is:
questions.why: y'' = 6x − 6 changes sign at x = 1, where y = 1 − 3 = −2.

questions.q: y = e^{−x²} has inflection points at x =
questions.why: y'' = (4x² − 2)e^{−x²} vanishes and changes sign at x² = 1/2.

questions.q: The radius of curvature of y = x³ at (1, 1) is about:
For a circle of radius 5, the curvature is:
questions.why: Curvature is the reciprocal of the radius: 1/5 = 0.2.

questions.q: Newton's formula gives ρ at the origin of y² = 4ax (tangent x = 0) as:
questions.why: With the y-axis as tangent, ρ = lim y²/(2x) = 4ax/(2x) = 2a.

questions.q: For the cardioid r = a(1 − cos θ), ρ² is proportional to:
questions.why: ρ = (2√2/3)√(ar), so ρ² = (8a/9) r, proportional to r.

questions.q: A curve whose equation has only even powers of y is symmetric about:
questions.why: Replacing y by −y leaves the equation unchanged, so every point (x, y) has its mirror (x, −y).

questions.q: The cissoid y²(a − x) = x³ has at the origin:
questions.why: The lowest terms give y² = 0, a repeated real tangent, and the curve lies on one side, which is a cusp.

questions.q: The area enclosed by r = a(1 + cos θ) is:
questions.why: Area = ½∫₀^{2π} a²(1 + cos θ)² dθ = ½a²(2π + π) = 3πa²/2.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Functions of several variables
courses.summary: Limits and partial derivatives of functions of two variables, Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions, total derivatives and the chain rule, Jacobians, and extrema with and without constraints (Lagrange multipliers).
outcomes: Compute first and higher partial derivatives and test two-variable limits along paths
Apply Euler's theorem, including its second-order form
Use the chain rule, implicit differentiation and Jacobians
Classify critical points using rt − s²
Solve constrained optimisation with Lagrange multipliers

scenes.text: Standing on a hillside, walking east feels steep but walking north feels gentle.
Each direction has its own slope — those are the partial derivatives.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For u = f(x, y):
- u_x = ∂u/∂x = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h, y) − f(x, y)]/h (y held fixed); similarly u_y.
- Second order: u_xx, u_yy, u_xy = ∂/∂y(∂u/∂x).
- Schwarz/Clairaut: if u_xy and u_yx are continuous, they are equal.
- lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f = L must be the same along every path; two paths with different limits prove the limit does not exist.

steps.title: Solved: a path test
steps.body:
f(x, y) = xy/(x² + y²) at (0, 0).

- Along y = mx: f = m x²/((1 + m²)x²) = m/(1 + m²).
- This depends on m (0 along the x-axis, 1/2 along y = x), so the limit does not exist and f is discontinuous at O even though f_x(0, 0) = f_y(0, 0) = 0 exist.

steps.title: Solved: Laplace's equation
steps.body:
Show u = ln(x² + y²) satisfies u_xx + u_yy = 0.

- u_x = 2x/(x² + y²), u_xx = 2(y² − x²)/(x² + y²)².
- By symmetry u_yy = 2(x² − y²)/(x² + y²)².
- Sum = 0. ∎

steps.title: Solved: mixed partials
steps.body: u = x²y + y³: u_x = 2xy, u_y = x² + 3y², u_xy = 2x = u_yx, u_yy = 6y.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing only straight lines and concluding a limit exists (try y = x² too).
- Treating y as a function of x while computing u_x.
- Assuming existence of partial derivatives implies continuity (false in two variables).

activity.prompt: For u = x³y², find u_xy at (1, 2).

quiz.q: For u = eˣ sin y, u_yy equals:
quiz.why: Differentiating sin y twice with respect to y gives −sin y, while eˣ is a constant factor.

quiz.q: lim_{(x,y)→(0,0)} x²y/(x⁴ + y²) along y = x² equals:
quiz.why: Substituting y = x² gives x⁴/(2x⁴) = 1/2, while along y = 0 the value is 0, so the full limit does not exist.

quiz.q: u_xy = u_yx is guaranteed when:
quiz.why: Schwarz's theorem guarantees equality of mixed partials when they are continuous near the point.

scenes.text: Double every ingredient and a cook's cost doubles; the cost is homogeneous of degree 1.
Euler's theorem turns that scaling property into an identity between partial derivatives.

steps.title: Statement and proof
steps.body:
u(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if u(tx, ty) = tⁿ u(x, y), equivalently u = xⁿ φ(y/x).

Euler: x u_x + y u_y = n u.
Proof: differentiate u(tx, ty) = tⁿu with respect to t: x u_x(tx, ty) + y u_y(tx, ty) = n tⁿ⁻¹ u; put t = 1. ∎

Second order: x²u_xx + 2xy u_xy + y²u_yy = n(n − 1)u.

steps.title: Solved: direct verification
steps.body: u = x³ + y³ (n = 3): x·3x² + y·3y² = 3(x³ + y³) = 3u ✔

steps.title: Solved: a non-homogeneous u
steps.body:
u = sin⁻¹[(x² + y²)/(x + y)]. Show x u_x + y u_y = tan u.

- z = sin u = (x² + y²)/(x + y) is homogeneous of degree 1.
- Euler on z: x z_x + y z_y = z ⇒ cos u (x u_x + y u_y) = sin u.
- Hence x u_x + y u_y = tan u. ∎

steps.title: General rule
steps.body: If f(u) is homogeneous of degree n, then x u_x + y u_y = n f(u)/f'(u) = g(u), and x²u_xx + 2xy u_xy + y²u_yy = g(u)[g'(u) − 1].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Euler to u itself when only sin u (or tan u, eᵘ) is homogeneous.
- Miscounting the degree of a quotient (degree of numerator minus degree of denominator).
- Writing n² instead of n(n − 1) in the second-order form.

activity.prompt: u = (x⁴ + y⁴)/(x + y). Evaluate x u_x + y u_y at (1, 1).

quiz.q: The degree of homogeneity of u = (x² + y²)/√(x + y) is:
quiz.why: Numerator degree 2 minus denominator degree 1/2 gives 3/2.

quiz.q: If u = x⁵ φ(y/x), then x u_x + y u_y =
quiz.why: xⁿφ(y/x) is homogeneous of degree n = 5, so Euler gives 5u.

quiz.q: For u homogeneous of degree 3, x²u_xx + 2xy u_xy + y²u_yy equals:
quiz.why: The second-order Euler identity gives n(n − 1)u = 3·2·u = 6u.

lessons.title: Chain rule, implicit functions and Jacobians

scenes.text: Temperature depends on position, and a drone's position depends on time.
The chain rule adds up how each coordinate's motion changes the reading.

steps.title: Chain rule and total derivative
steps.body:
- If u = f(x, y), x = x(t), y = y(t): du/dt = u_x dx/dt + u_y dy/dt.
- If x = x(s, t), y = y(s, t): u_s = u_x x_s + u_y y_s, u_t = u_x x_t + u_y y_t.
- Total differential: du = u_x dx + u_y dy.
- Implicit f(x, y) = 0: dy/dx = −f_x/f_y (f_y ≠ 0).

steps.title: Solved: checking the chain rule
steps.body:
u = x²y, x = t², y = t³.

- Directly: u = t⁷ ⇒ du/dt = 7t⁶.
- Chain: 2xy·2t + x²·3t² = 2t⁵·2t + t⁴·3t² = 4t⁶ + 3t⁶ = 7t⁶ ✔

steps.title: Solved: implicit derivative
steps.body: x³ + y³ − 3axy = 0: f_x = 3x² − 3ay, f_y = 3y² − 3ax ⇒ dy/dx = −(x² − ay)/(y² − ax).

steps.title: Jacobians
steps.body:
J = ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = det [[u_x, u_y], [v_x, v_y]].

- Polar: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ ⇒ ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r.
- Spherical: ∂(x, y, z)/∂(r, θ, φ) = r² sin θ.
- JJ' = 1 where J' is the inverse Jacobian; J(u, v)/J(x, y) chain: ∂(u, v)/∂(r, s) = ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)·∂(x, y)/∂(r, s).
- u, v functionally dependent ⇔ J = 0 identically.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign in dy/dx = −f_x/f_y.
- Writing the Jacobian matrix transposed (harmless for the determinant but confusing in chains).
- Writing the polar Jacobian as 1/r (that is ∂(r, θ)/∂(x, y)).

activity.prompt: Find ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) for u = x + y, v = x − y.

quiz.q: For x² + y² = 25, dy/dx at (3, 4) is:
∂(r, θ)/∂(x, y) for polar coordinates equals:
quiz.why: It is the reciprocal of ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r, since JJ' = 1.

quiz.q: u = x + y, v = (x + y)² have Jacobian:
quiz.why: v = u², so u and v are functionally dependent and the Jacobian vanishes identically.

lessons.title: Extrema of two variables and Lagrange multipliers

scenes.text: A factory needs a box-shaped tank of fixed volume with the least sheet metal.
That is a minimum under a constraint — the job of Lagrange's multiplier.

steps.title: Second-derivative test
steps.body:
At a critical point f_x = f_y = 0, let r = f_xx, s = f_xy, t = f_yy.

- rt − s² > 0 and r < 0 ⇒ maximum.
- rt − s² > 0 and r > 0 ⇒ minimum.
- rt − s² < 0 ⇒ saddle point.
- rt − s² = 0 ⇒ further investigation.

steps.title: Lagrange's method
steps.body: To extremise f(x, y, z) subject to φ(x, y, z) = 0, form F = f + λφ and solve F_x = F_y = F_z = 0 with φ = 0. Geometrically ∇f ∥ ∇φ at the extremum.

steps.title: Solved: maximum product
steps.body:
Maximise xyz with x + y + z = 12 (x, y, z > 0).

- F = xyz + λ(x + y + z − 12).
- yz + λ = 0, xz + λ = 0, xy + λ = 0 ⇒ yz = xz = xy ⇒ x = y = z.
- x = y = z = 4, maximum xyz = 64.

steps.title: Solved: open box of volume 32
steps.body: Minimise S = xy + 2xz + 2yz with xyz = 32. Symmetry and Lagrange give x = y = 2z; then 4z³ = 32 ⇒ z = 2, x = y = 4, S = 16 + 16 + 16 = 48.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r alone without checking rt − s².
- Missing critical points by dividing by a variable that may be zero.
- Forgetting that λ itself is not the answer.

activity.prompt: Find the minimum of x² + y² subject to x + y = 4.

quiz.q: f = x² − y² at the origin has:
quiz.why: r = 2, t = −2, s = 0, so rt − s² = −4 < 0, which is a saddle.

quiz.q: f = x² + xy + y² − 3x has its minimum at:
quiz.why: f_x = 2x + y − 3 = 0 and f_y = x + 2y = 0 give x = 2, y = −1, and rt − s² = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 with r > 0.

quiz.q: In Lagrange's method, at an extremum ∇f is:
quiz.why: The level curve of f must be tangent to the constraint, so their normals ∇f and ∇φ are parallel.

questions.q: For u = x²y³, u_xy equals:
questions.why: u_x = 2xy³ and differentiating with respect to y gives 6xy².
Along y = 0 the value is 1 and along x = 0 it is −1, so the limit does not exist.

questions.q: Which function satisfies Laplace's equation?
questions.why: For x² − y², u_xx = 2 and u_yy = −2, which sum to 0.

questions.q: u = x² tan⁻¹(y/x) is homogeneous of degree:
questions.why: It has the form x²φ(y/x), so its degree is 2.

questions.q: If u = tan⁻¹[(x³ + y³)/(x − y)], then x u_x + y u_y =
questions.why: tan u is homogeneous of degree 2, so x u_x + y u_y = 2 tan u/sec²u = 2 sin u cos u = sin 2u.

questions.q: For u homogeneous of degree 4, x u_x + y u_y equals:
questions.why: Euler's theorem gives n u = 4u.

questions.q: If u = x² + y², x = cos t, y = sin t, then du/dt =
questions.why: u = cos²t + sin²t = 1 for all t, so its derivative is 0 (the chain rule gives −2xy·… which cancels).

questions.q: ∂(x, y, z)/∂(r, θ, φ) in spherical coordinates is:
questions.why: The standard spherical Jacobian is r² sin θ, which appears as dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ.

questions.q: For x y = c, dy/dx equals:
questions.why: f_x = y and f_y = x, so dy/dx = −y/x.

questions.q: f = x³ + y³ − 3xy has a local minimum value:
The maximum of xyz subject to x + y + z = 12 (positive) is:
questions.why: Lagrange's conditions force x = y = z = 4, giving 64.

questions.q: For a critical point with rt − s² = 0:
questions.why: When rt − s² = 0 the second-derivative test gives no conclusion and higher-order or direct analysis is needed.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Integral calculus and its applications
courses.summary: Reduction formulae and Wallis's formula, rectification and quadrature, volumes and surfaces of solids of revolution, double integrals with change of order and polar coordinates, and the Beta and Gamma functions.
outcomes: Derive and apply reduction formulae including Wallis's formula
Find arc lengths and plane areas in Cartesian, parametric and polar forms
Compute volumes and surface areas of revolution
Evaluate double integrals, change the order of integration and switch to polar coordinates
Use Beta and Gamma functions to evaluate definite integrals

scenes.text: ∫ sin⁸x dx looks frightening, but it is linked to ∫ sin⁶x, which is linked to ∫ sin⁴x, and so on.
A reduction formula lets you climb down the ladder one rung at a time.

steps.title: Derivation for sinⁿx
steps.body:
Let Iₙ = ∫ sinⁿx dx. Write sinⁿx = sinⁿ⁻¹x·sin x and integrate by parts:

Iₙ = −sinⁿ⁻¹x cos x + (n − 1)∫ sinⁿ⁻²x cos²x dx = −sinⁿ⁻¹x cos x + (n − 1)(Iₙ₋₂ − Iₙ).

Hence n Iₙ = −sinⁿ⁻¹x cos x + (n − 1)Iₙ₋₂. On [0, π/2] the boundary term vanishes: Iₙ = [(n − 1)/n] Iₙ₋₂.

steps.title: Wallis's formula
steps.body:
∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿx dx = ∫₀^{π/2} cosⁿx dx =
- n even: [(n − 1)(n − 3)…1]/[n(n − 2)…2] · π/2
- n odd: [(n − 1)(n − 3)…2]/[n(n − 2)…3]

Other standard reductions:
- ∫ xⁿeˣ dx: Iₙ = xⁿeˣ − n Iₙ₋₁
- ∫ tanⁿx dx: Iₙ = tanⁿ⁻¹x/(n − 1) − Iₙ₋₂
- ∫₀^{π/2} sin^m x cos^n x dx = [(m − 1)(m − 3)…][(n − 1)(n − 3)…]/[(m + n)(m + n − 2)…] × (π/2 only if both m, n even)

steps.title: Solved: ∫₀¹ x³eˣ dx
steps.body:
Iₙ = [xⁿeˣ]₀¹ − n Iₙ₋₁ = e − n Iₙ₋₁ (n ≥ 1), I₀ = e − 1.

- I₁ = e − (e − 1) = 1
- I₂ = e − 2
- I₃ = e − 3(e − 2) = 6 − 2e ≈ 0.5634

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the factor π/2 for odd n.
- Using Wallis's formula on limits other than 0 to π/2 without first adjusting (e.g. ∫₀^π sinⁿx = 2∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿx).
- Sign errors in the boundary term of integration by parts.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} cos⁴x dx (three decimals).

quiz.q: ∫₀^{π/2} sin³x dx equals:
quiz.why: For odd n = 3 Wallis gives 2/3 with no π/2 factor.

quiz.q: ∫₀^{π} sin⁴x dx equals:
quiz.why: By symmetry it is 2∫₀^{π/2} sin⁴x dx = 2·(3/4)(1/2)(π/2) = 3π/8.

quiz.q: For Iₙ = ∫ tanⁿx dx, Iₙ + Iₙ₋₂ equals:
quiz.why: tanⁿx + tanⁿ⁻²x = tanⁿ⁻²x sec²x, whose integral is tanⁿ⁻¹x/(n − 1).

scenes.text: A surveyor knows the equation of a river bank and needs its true length for fencing.
Adding up tiny hypotenuses √(dx² + dy²) gives the arc length exactly.

steps.title: Rectification formulas
steps.body:
- y = f(x): s = ∫ √(1 + y'²) dx
- x = x(t), y = y(t): s = ∫ √(x'² + y'²) dt
- r = f(θ): s = ∫ √(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ

Area: ∫ (y₁ − y₂) dx between curves; polar ½∫ r² dθ; parametric ∫ y x'(t) dt.

steps.title: Solved: perimeter of the cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ)
steps.body:
- r² + r₁² = a²[(1 + cos θ)² + sin²θ] = 2a²(1 + cos θ) = 4a² cos²(θ/2).
- s = 2∫₀^π 2a cos(θ/2) dθ = 4a[2 sin(θ/2)]₀^π = 8a.

steps.title: Solved: area between y = x and y = x²
steps.body: They meet at x = 0 and 1. Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

steps.title: Results worth remembering
steps.body:
- Astroid x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = a^{2/3}: perimeter 6a, area 3πa²/8.
- One arch of the cycloid x = a(t − sin t), y = a(1 − cos t): length 8a, area 3πa².
- Ellipse area πab.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply by the number of symmetric pieces.
- Taking √(r² + r₁²) as r + r₁.
- Using area formulas where the curves cross inside the interval (split at crossing points).

activity.prompt: Find the area enclosed between y = x² and y = 2x (three decimals).

quiz.q: The area of the circle r = 2a cos θ is:
quiz.why: It is a circle of diameter 2a, i.e. radius a; indeed ½∫_{−π/2}^{π/2} 4a²cos²θ dθ = πa².

quiz.q: The length of one arch of the cycloid x = a(t − sin t), y = a(1 − cos t) is:
quiz.why: x'² + y'² = 4a² sin²(t/2), so s = ∫₀^{2π} 2a sin(t/2) dt = 8a.

quiz.q: The arc-length element in polar coordinates is:
quiz.why: ds² = dr² + r²dθ², so ds = √(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ.

scenes.text: A potter spins a profile curve and a pot appears.
Revolving a curve about an axis creates a solid whose volume is a sum of thin discs.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
About the x-axis, a ≤ x ≤ b:
- Volume (discs): V = π∫ y² dx
- Washers: V = π∫ (y₁² − y₂²) dx
- Surface: S = 2π∫ y ds = 2π∫ y√(1 + y'²) dx

About the y-axis by shells: V = 2π∫ x y dx.
Pappus: V = (area) × (distance travelled by centroid); S = (arc length) × (distance travelled by its centroid).

steps.title: Solved: the sphere
steps.body:
Revolve y = √(a² − x²), −a ≤ x ≤ a.

- V = π∫ (a² − x²) dx = π[2a³ − 2a³/3] = 4πa³/3.
- y√(1 + y'²) = a, so S = 2π∫_{−a}^{a} a dx = 4πa².

steps.body: z = x + iy, x = Re z, y = Im z, conjugate z̄ = x − iy, modulus |z| = √(x² + y²). z z̄ = |z|², |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|, |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂| (triangle inequality). 1/z = z̄/|z|².

scenes.text: On the real line you approach a point from the left or the right. In the plane you can spiral in from infinitely many directions.

steps.title: Sets in the plane
steps.body: |z − a| < r: open disc; |z − a| = r: circle; Re z > 0: right half-plane; 1 < |z| < 2: annulus. A domain is an open connected set. |z − 1| = |z + 1| is the perpendicular bisector of −1 and 1, i.e. the imaginary axis.

steps.title: Functions and limits
steps.body: f(z) = u(x, y) + iv(x, y). lim_{z→z₀} f(z) = L if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |f(z) − L| < ε whenever 0 < |z − z₀| < δ. f is continuous at z₀ iff u and v are. Polynomials and rational functions (away from zeros of the denominator) are continuous.

steps.title: Worked example: a limit that fails
steps.body: f(z) = z̄/z near 0. Along the real axis z = x: f = x/x = 1. Along the imaginary axis z = iy: f = −iy/(iy) = −1. Different values ⇒ the limit does not exist.

steps.title: Extended plane
steps.body: ℂ ∪ {∞} is modelled by the Riemann sphere via stereographic projection. z → ∞ means |z| → ∞; f(z) → ∞ at z₀ iff 1/f(z) → 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes

lessons.title: Complex differentiability and the Cauchy–Riemann equations

scenes.text: A real function can be smooth along x and along y separately yet behave badly in diagonal directions.
Complex differentiability demands the same derivative from every direction — and the Cauchy–Riemann equations encode exactly that.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: f′(z₀) = lim_{h→0} [f(z₀ + h) − f(z₀)]/h, h complex. f is analytic (holomorphic) at z₀ if it is differentiable in a neighbourhood of z₀; entire if analytic on all of ℂ. Sum, product, quotient and chain rules hold as in real calculus.

steps.title: Cauchy–Riemann equations
steps.body: If f = u + iv is differentiable at z₀ then u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x there, and f′ = u_x + iv_x. Conversely, if u, v have continuous first partials near z₀ satisfying CR, f is differentiable at z₀. Polar form: u_r = (1/r)v_θ, v_r = −(1/r)u_θ.

steps.title: Worked example: f(z) = z²
steps.body: u = x² − y², v = 2xy. u_x = 2x = v_y; u_y = −2y = −v_x. CR hold everywhere with continuous partials, so z² is entire and f′ = u_x + iv_x = 2x + 2iy = 2z.

steps.title: Worked example: z̄ and |z|²
steps.body: f = z̄: u = x, v = −y, u_x = 1 ≠ v_y = −1, so z̄ is nowhere differentiable. f = |z|² = x² + y²: u_x = 2x, v_y = 0, u_y = 2y, −v_x = 0. CR hold only at (0,0), so |z|² is differentiable only at 0 and analytic nowhere.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: CR equations alone (without continuity of partials) do not guarantee differentiability. Differentiable at a point ≠ analytic at that point.

activity.prompt: Where is f analytic?

quiz.q: The CR equations are:
quiz.why: Equating derivatives along the real and imaginary directions gives u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x.

quiz.q: Re z = x is:
quiz.why: u = x, v = 0 gives u_x = 1 ≠ v_y = 0, so CR fail everywhere.

quiz.q: f′(z) in terms of u, v:
quiz.why: Taking h real in the difference quotient gives f′ = u_x + iv_x.

quiz.q: |z|² is differentiable:
quiz.why: The CR equations 2x = 0 and 2y = 0 hold only at the origin.

scenes.text: A metal plate at steady temperature has a temperature field u(x, y) with u_xx + u_yy = 0.
Every such harmonic u is the real part of some analytic function.

steps.title: Harmonic functions
steps.body: u is harmonic if u_xx + u_yy = 0 (Laplace's equation). If f = u + iv is analytic, both u and v are harmonic, and v is called a harmonic conjugate of u. Level curves u = c and v = c cut at right angles.

steps.title: Worked example: find v
steps.body: u = 2x − x³ + 3xy². u_xx = −6x, u_yy = 6x, so u is harmonic. v_y = u_x = 2 − 3x² + 3y² ⇒ v = 2y − 3x²y + y³ + g(x). v_x = −6xy + g′(x) must equal −u_y = −6xy, so g′ = 0. v = 2y − 3x²y + y³, and f = 2z − z³ + ic.

steps.title: Milne-Thomson method
steps.body: Given u, write φ₁(x,y) = u_x, φ₂(x,y) = u_y. Then f′(z) = φ₁(z, 0) − iφ₂(z, 0); integrate in z. Example: u = eˣ cos y: u_x = eˣ cos y → e^z, u_y = −eˣ sin y → 0. f′ = e^z, f = e^z + c.

steps.title: Worked example: not harmonic
steps.body: u = x² + y² gives u_xx + u_yy = 4 ≠ 0, so it is not the real part of any analytic function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the function of x (or y) after partial integration. The harmonic conjugate of v is −u, not u.

steps.title: Exponential
steps.body: e^z = eˣ(cos y + i sin y). It is entire, (e^z)′ = e^z, |e^z| = eˣ, e^z ≠ 0, and e^z is periodic with period 2πi. e^z = 1 ⇔ z = 2kπi.

steps.title: Trig and hyperbolic
steps.body: sin z = (e^{iz} − e^{−iz})/(2i), cos z = (e^{iz} + e^{−iz})/2, sinh z = (e^z − e^{−z})/2, cosh z = (e^z + e^{−z})/2. sin(iy) = i sinh y, cos(iy) = cosh y. sin(x + iy) = sin x cosh y + i cos x sinh y. |sin z|² = sin²x + sinh²y — unbounded.

steps.title: Definitions

story.title: Walking a path in the plane

scenes.text: A complex integral adds up f(z) dz as you walk along a path — the path matters, unless f is very nice.
The ML-inequality bounds the total using the path length and the largest |f|.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: For a smooth contour C: z(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, ∫_C f(z) dz = ∫ₐᵇ f(z(t)) z′(t) dt. Reversing direction changes the sign; integrals over pieces add.

steps.title: Worked example: ∮ dz/z on |z| = 1
steps.body: z = e^{it}, dz = ie^{it} dt, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. ∫₀^{2π} (1/e^{it}) ie^{it} dt = ∫₀^{2π} i dt = 2πi. More generally ∮_{|z−a|=r} (z − a)ⁿ dz = 2πi if n = −1 and 0 for every other integer n.

steps.title: Worked example: z̄ on two paths
steps.body: From 0 to 1 + i. Path 1, straight line z = (1 + i)t: z̄ dz = (1 − i)t(1 + i)dt = 2t dt, integral = 1. Path 2, 0 → 1 → 1 + i: first leg ∫₀¹ x dx = ½; second leg z = 1 + it, dz = i dt: ∫₀¹ (1 − it) i dt = i + ½. Total 1 + i ≠ 1. Path dependence shows z̄ has no antiderivative.

steps.title: ML-inequality
steps.body: If |f(z)| ≤ M on C and C has length L, then |∫_C f dz| ≤ ML. Example: on |z| = 2, |1/(z² + 1)| ≤ 1/(|z|² − 1) = 1/3, L = 4π, so |∮ dz/(z² + 1)| ≤ 4π/3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the factor z′(t). Using |z² + 1| ≥ |z|² + 1 — the reverse triangle inequality gives |z² + 1| ≥ |z|² − 1.

activity.prompt: Evaluate the imaginary part of ∫_C z̄ dz where C is the path 0 → 1 → 1 + i (two straight segments).

story.title: When the path does not matter

scenes.text: Walking between two villages on a hill, the height you gain does not depend on the route.
For analytic functions on simply connected domains, contour integrals behave the same way.

steps.title: Antiderivatives
steps.body: If F′ = f on a domain containing C from z₁ to z₂, then ∫_C f dz = F(z₂) − F(z₁), and ∮ f dz = 0 on closed contours. Example: ∫ z² dz from 0 to 1 + i = (1 + i)³/3 = (−2 + 2i)/3.

steps.title: Cauchy–Goursat theorem
steps.body: If f is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour C, then ∮_C f dz = 0. On a simply connected domain, every analytic function has an antiderivative and integrals are path-independent.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=1} e^z/(z − 3) dz = 0: the only singularity, z = 3, lies outside the unit circle, so the integrand is analytic on and inside C.

steps.title: Deformation of contours
steps.body: If f is analytic in the region between two simple closed contours C₁ and C₂ (same orientation), then ∮_{C₁} f = ∮_{C₂} f. So ∮ dz/(z − a) = 2πi for every simple closed C enclosing a.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying Cauchy–Goursat when a singularity lies inside C — e.g. ∮_{|z|=1} dz/z = 2πi ≠ 0. 1/z has no antiderivative on ℂ \ {0} (Log has a branch cut).

activity.prompt: Value of ∮ f dz around |z| = 2 (counter-clockwise).

quiz.q: ∫ from 0 to i of 2z dz:
quiz.why: An antiderivative is z², so the integral is i² − 0 = −1.

The singularities ±2 lie outside the unit circle.
This is the basic integral ∮ dz/(z − a) = 2πi with a = 2 inside.

scenes.text: Measure an analytic function only on a circle, and you can compute its value — and every derivative — at any point inside.
This makes many hard-looking integrals one-line computations.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: If f is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour C (positively oriented) and z₀ is inside, then f(z₀) = (1/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z − z₀) dz, and f⁽ⁿ⁾(z₀) = (n!/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z − z₀)ⁿ⁺¹ dz.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=2} e^z/(z − 1) dz: f = e^z, z₀ = 1 inside. Value 2πi f(1) = 2πie.

steps.title: Worked example 2: derivative form
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=2} e^{2z}/(z − 1)² dz = 2πi f′(1) with f = e^{2z}, f′ = 2e^{2z}. Value 2πi · 2e² = 4πie².

steps.title: Worked example 3: partial fractions
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=3} dz/((z − 1)(z − 2)). 1/((z − 1)(z − 2)) = 1/(z − 2) − 1/(z − 1). Both points are inside, each term contributes ±2πi: total 2πi − 2πi = 0.

steps.title: Worked example 4: one point inside
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=1} cos z/(z(z − 3)) dz: only 0 is inside. Take f = cos z/(z − 3), analytic inside. Value 2πi f(0) = 2πi · (1/(−3)) = −2πi/3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting n! in the derivative formula, or the power n + 1. Putting into f a factor that vanishes inside C.

quiz.why: Differentiating 1/(z − z₀) n times under the integral gives n!/(z − z₀)ⁿ⁺¹.

lessons.title: Liouville, Morera and the fundamental theorem of algebra

scenes.text: An entire function trapped inside a bounded box cannot move at all — it must be constant.
From this one fact follows the fundamental theorem of algebra.

steps.title: Cauchy's estimate
steps.body: If |f| ≤ M on |z − z₀| = R, then |f⁽ⁿ⁾(z₀)| ≤ n! M / Rⁿ.

steps.title: Liouville's theorem
steps.body: A bounded entire function is constant. Proof: |f′(z₀)| ≤ M/R for every R; let R → ∞ to get f′ ≡ 0.

steps.title: Fundamental theorem of algebra
steps.body: Every non-constant polynomial p has a root in ℂ. Proof: if p had no zero, 1/p would be entire and bounded (|p| → ∞ as |z| → ∞), hence constant — contradiction. So a degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity.

steps.title: Morera's theorem
steps.body: If f is continuous on a domain D and ∮_C f dz = 0 for every closed contour C in D, then f is analytic in D (converse of Cauchy–Goursat).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: sin z is entire but not bounded on ℂ, so Liouville does not force it to be constant. Liouville needs boundedness on the whole plane, not just on the real axis.

activity.prompt: Order the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.
items: Suppose p is a non-constant polynomial with no zero
Then g = 1/p is entire
Since |p(z)| → ∞ as |z| → ∞, g is bounded
By Liouville, g is constant
So p is constant — contradiction

courses.title: Unit 4 · Power series, Taylor and Laurent series, singularities
courses.summary: Convergence of sequences and series of complex numbers, power series and radius of convergence, Taylor's theorem, zeros of analytic functions, Laurent series in annuli, and the classification of isolated singularities as removable, poles and essential.
outcomes: Find the radius of convergence of a power series
Expand functions in Taylor series about a point
Find Laurent expansions valid in specified annuli
Determine the order of zeros and poles
Classify isolated singularities

lessons.title: Power series and radius of convergence

scenes.text: A power series Σaₙ(z − z₀)ⁿ converges inside a disc and diverges outside it.
The radius of that disc reaches exactly to the nearest point where the function breaks down.

steps.title: Radius of convergence
steps.body: For Σaₙ(z − z₀)ⁿ, R = 1/limsup |aₙ|^{1/n} (Cauchy–Hadamard), or R = lim |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| when this limit exists. The series converges absolutely for |z − z₀| < R and diverges for |z − z₀| > R. Inside the disc it is analytic and can be differentiated term by term.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body: Σ zⁿ/n!: |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = n + 1 → ∞, so R = ∞. Σ n! zⁿ: ratio 1/(n + 1) → 0, R = 0. Σ zⁿ/3ⁿ: R = 3. Σ zⁿ/n²: R = 1, and it converges at every point of |z| = 1 since Σ1/n² converges.

steps.title: Worked example: lacunary-type series
steps.body: Σ z^{2n}/4ⁿ = Σ (z²/4)ⁿ, a geometric series converging when |z²/4| < 1, i.e. |z| < 2. So R = 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the ratio test formula directly on series with missing powers — substitute w = z² first. On the circle |z − z₀| = R the behaviour must be checked separately.

activity.prompt: Find the radius of convergence of Σ (n + 1) zⁿ / 5ⁿ.

quiz.q: R for Σ zⁿ:
quiz.why: The geometric series converges exactly for |z| < 1.

quiz.q: R for Σ n! zⁿ:
quiz.why: |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = 1/(n + 1) → 0, so it converges only at z = 0.

quiz.q: R for Σ 2ⁿ zⁿ:
quiz.why: Σ(2z)ⁿ converges for |2z| < 1, i.e. |z| < 1/2.

quiz.q: Inside its disc of convergence a power series is:
quiz.why: Power series can be differentiated term by term within the disc, so they define analytic functions there.

story.title: Analytic means locally a power series

scenes.text: Zoom into any point where f is analytic and f looks exactly like a convergent power series.
The disc of validity extends to the nearest singularity.

steps.title: Taylor's theorem
steps.body: If f is analytic in |z − z₀| < R then f(z) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(z₀)/n! (z − z₀)ⁿ there. Standard series: e^z = Σ zⁿ/n!, sin z = Σ (−1)ⁿ z^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)!, cos z = Σ (−1)ⁿ z^{2n}/(2n)!, 1/(1 − z) = Σ zⁿ (|z| < 1).

steps.title: Worked example: 1/z about z₀ = 1
steps.body: 1/z = 1/(1 + (z − 1)) = Σ (−1)ⁿ (z − 1)ⁿ, valid for |z − 1| < 1 — the distance from 1 to the singularity 0.

steps.title: Worked example: 1/(1 + z²)
steps.body: = Σ (−1)ⁿ z^{2n} for |z| < 1. Real-variable puzzle solved: the real function 1/(1 + x²) is smooth everywhere, but its series has R = 1 because of the complex singularities ±i.

steps.title: Zeros
steps.body: z₀ is a zero of order m if f(z₀) = … = f⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾(z₀) = 0 ≠ f⁽ᵐ⁾(z₀); then f = (z − z₀)ᵐ g with g(z₀) ≠ 0. Zeros of a non-zero analytic function are isolated. Example: sin z − z = −z³/6 + … has a zero of order 3 at 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Giving the wrong region of validity — always measure to the nearest singularity. Forgetting factorials when computing coefficients.

activity.prompt: What is the order of the zero of f(z) = 1 − cos z at z = 0?

quiz.q: Taylor series of 1/(1 − z) about 0 is valid for:
quiz.why: The singularity at z = 1 is at distance 1 from 0.

quiz.q: Coefficient of z³ in e^z:
Radius of the Taylor series of 1/(z − 3) about z = 1:
quiz.why: The distance from 1 to the singularity 3 is 2.

quiz.q: Order of the zero of z² sin z at 0:
quiz.why: z² sin z = z³ − z⁵/6 + …, whose lowest term is z³.

scenes.text: Near a singularity, a Taylor series is impossible — but a series with negative powers works in a ring around it.
Different rings give different Laurent series for the same function.

steps.title: Laurent's theorem
steps.body: If f is analytic in the annulus r < |z − z₀| < R, then f(z) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} aₙ(z − z₀)ⁿ there, with aₙ = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − z₀)ⁿ⁺¹ dz. The negative-power part is the principal part; a₋₁ is the residue.

steps.title: Worked example: e^{1/z}
steps.body: e^{1/z} = Σ 1/(n! zⁿ) = 1 + 1/z + 1/(2z²) + …, valid for |z| > 0. Infinitely many negative powers.

steps.title: Worked example: sin z / z³
steps.body: = (z − z³/6 + z⁵/120 − …)/z³ = 1/z² − 1/6 + z²/120 − …, valid for |z| > 0. Coefficient of 1/z is 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Expanding 1/(z − 1) as Σ zⁿ in a region where |z| > 1 — there you must factor out z. Always check which ratio has modulus less than 1.

activity.prompt: Laurent series of e^z/z² about 0.
activity.text: e^z/z² = 1/z² + 1/z + ___ + z/6 + …, and the residue at 0 is ___.

quiz.q: In 1 < |z| < 2, 1/(z − 1) should be expanded as:
Principal part of e^{1/z} at 0 has:
quiz.why: Every negative power 1/(n! zⁿ) appears with a non-zero coefficient.

quiz.q: Coefficient of 1/z in sin z/z³:
quiz.why: Only even powers z^{−2}, z⁰, z², … occur, so the 1/z coefficient is 0.

quiz.q: Laurent series in an annulus are:
quiz.why: The coefficients are determined by the contour-integral formula, so the expansion in a given annulus is unique.

scenes.text: Some 'holes' can be patched (removable), some blow up in a controlled way (poles), and some are wild (essential).
Near an essential singularity f takes almost every value infinitely often (Picard).

steps.title: Classification by the principal part
steps.body: Removable: no negative powers (lim f exists). Pole of order m: finitely many, lowest a₋ₘ(z − z₀)^{−m} ≠ 0 (|f| → ∞). Essential: infinitely many negative powers.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: sin z/z at 0: 1 − z²/6 + … → removable. (1 − cos z)/z²: ½ − z²/24 + … → removable. 1/(z²(z − 1)): pole of order 2 at 0, simple pole at 1. e^{1/z}, sin(1/z) at 0: essential. z/sin z at π: sin z has a simple zero at π, z ≠ 0 there → simple pole.

steps.title: Shortcut with zeros
steps.body: If f = g/h with g(z₀) ≠ 0 and h having a zero of order m at z₀, then f has a pole of order m. If both vanish, compare orders: zero of order k over zero of order m gives a pole of order m − k (or removable if k ≥ m).

steps.title: Casorati–Weierstrass
steps.body: Near an essential singularity, f comes arbitrarily close to every complex value. This is how examiners distinguish essential singularities from poles conceptually.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling 1/sin z's singularity at 0 'essential' — it is a simple pole. Non-isolated singularities (e.g. 0 for 1/sin(1/z)) fall outside this classification.

activity.prompt: Classify the singularity at z = 0.

quiz.why: z³ sin z = z⁴ − …, a zero of order 4, so the reciprocal has a pole of order 4.

quiz.q: (e^z − 1)/z² at 0 has:
quiz.why: e^z − 1 has a simple zero, z² a double zero, so the quotient has a pole of order 2 − 1 = 1.

quiz.q: f has an essential singularity iff its Laurent series has:
quiz.why: That is exactly the definition in terms of the principal part.

quiz.q: tan z at π/2 has:
quiz.why: cos z has a simple zero at π/2 while sin(π/2) = 1 ≠ 0.

questions.why: |3 + 4i| = 5, so the series converges for |5z| < 1.

questions.why: The nearest singularity (branch point) is at z = −1.

In |z| > 2, the coefficient of z^{−3} in 1/((z − 1)(z − 2)) is:
questions.why: The coefficient is 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 with n = 3: 4 − 1 = 3.

questions.why: sin z − z has a zero of order 3, so 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.q: cos(1/z) at 0:
questions.why: cos(1/z) = Σ (−1)ⁿ/((2n)! z^{2n}) has infinitely many negative powers.

questions.q: Zero of order of e^z − 1 − z at 0:
Singularities of 1/(z² + 4):
Radius of the Taylor series of 1/(z² + 4) about 0:
questions.why: The nearest singularities ±2i lie at distance 2.

questions.why: Riemann's theorem: bounded near z₀ ⇔ removable.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Residues, real integrals and exam revision
courses.summary: Residues at poles, the residue theorem, evaluation of trigonometric integrals over [0, 2π], improper rational integrals and Fourier-type integrals using Jordan's lemma, the argument principle and Rouché's theorem, followed by a formula sheet and exam-style practice.
outcomes: Compute residues at simple and higher-order poles
Evaluate contour integrals with the residue theorem
Evaluate ∫₀^{2π} R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ and ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P/Q dx
Use Jordan's lemma for integrals with cos x or sin x
Count zeros with the argument principle and Rouché's theorem

scenes.text: A closed contour integral of a meromorphic function depends only on the singularities inside — each contributes its residue.
So ∮ f dz = 2πi × (sum of residues inside).

steps.title: Computing residues
steps.body: Res(f, z₀) = a₋₁. Simple pole: Res = lim (z − z₀) f(z); if f = g/h with h(z₀) = 0, h′(z₀) ≠ 0, g(z₀) ≠ 0 then Res = g(z₀)/h′(z₀). Pole of order m: Res = (1/(m − 1)!) lim dᵐ⁻¹/dzᵐ⁻¹ [(z − z₀)ᵐ f(z)].

steps.title: Residue theorem
steps.body: If f is analytic on and inside a simple closed positively oriented C except at finitely many points z₁, …, zₙ inside C, then ∮_C f dz = 2πi Σ Res(f, z_k).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=2} z/((z − 1)(z − 3)) dz. Only z = 1 is inside. Res = 1/(1 − 3) = −½. Integral = 2πi(−½) = −πi.

steps.title: Worked example 2: double pole
steps.body: f = e^z/(z − 1)² at z = 1: Res = d/dz[e^z] at 1 = e. So ∮_{|z|=2} f dz = 2πie (agreeing with Cauchy's derivative formula).

steps.title: Worked example 3: g/h′
steps.body: Res of 1/(z⁴ + 1) at z₀ = e^{iπ/4}: g/h′ = 1/(4z₀³) = z₀/(4z₀⁴) = −z₀/4, using z₀⁴ = −1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including residues of poles outside C. Using the simple-pole formula at a double pole. Forgetting (m − 1)! in the higher-order formula.

activity.prompt: Find Res(e^z/z³, 0).

quiz.why: g/h′ = 1/(2z) at z = i gives 1/(2i) = −i/2.

quiz.q: Res(cot z, 0):
quiz.why: cot z = cos z/sin z, and g/h′ = cos 0/cos 0 = 1.
Only z = 0 is inside, with residue 1/(0 − 2) = −1/2, giving 2πi(−1/2) = −πi.

quiz.q: Res(1/z², 0):
quiz.why: The Laurent series is just z^{−2}, with no 1/z term.

story.title: A detour through the complex plane

scenes.text: Some real integrals resist every substitution — until you detour through the complex plane.
∫ dx/(x² + 1) over ℝ falls out as π from a single residue.

steps.title: Type 1: ∫₀^{2π} R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ
steps.body: Put z = e^{iθ}, dθ = dz/(iz), cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2, sin θ = (z − 1/z)/(2i), and integrate over |z| = 1.

steps.title: Type 2: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P(x)/Q(x) dx
steps.body: If deg Q ≥ deg P + 2 and Q has no real zeros, the integral = 2πi Σ residues in the upper half-plane (the integral over the large semicircle → 0).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body: ∫ dx/(x² + 1) = 2πi · 1/(2i) = π. ∫ dx/(x² + 1)²: double pole at i, Res = d/dz[(z + i)^{−2}] at i = −2/(2i)³ = −2/(−8i) = 1/(4i). Integral = 2πi/(4i) = π/2.

steps.title: Type 3: Jordan's lemma
steps.body: For ∫ P/Q cos(mx) dx with m > 0 and deg Q ≥ deg P + 1, use f = P/Q · e^{imz} and take the real part. ∫_{−∞}^{∞} cos x/(x² + 1) dx = Re[2πi · e^{−1}/(2i)] = π/e.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using cos z directly — it grows in the upper half-plane; use e^{iz}. Counting lower half-plane poles. In Type 1, forgetting the factor 1/(iz).

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x² + 4). Give the answer to 4 decimal places.

quiz.why: The residue at i is 1/(2i), so 2πi/(2i) = π.

quiz.q: In Type 1, dθ is replaced by:
quiz.why: z = e^{iθ} gives dz = iz dθ.
Re[2πi Res(e^{iz}/(z² + 1), i)] = Re[2πi e^{−1}/(2i)] = π/e.

quiz.q: For Type 2 we need deg Q ≥ deg P +
quiz.why: This makes the semicircle contribution decay like 1/R.

scenes.text: A control engineer needs to know how many roots of a polynomial lie inside the unit disc — not their values.
Rouché's 'dog-walking' theorem answers this by comparing with a simpler function.

steps.title: Argument principle
steps.body: If f is meromorphic inside and on C with no zeros or poles on C, then (1/2πi)∮_C f′/f dz = N − P, the number of zeros minus poles inside C (with multiplicity).

steps.title: Rouché's theorem
steps.body: If f, g are analytic on and inside C and |g| < |f| on C, then f and f + g have the same number of zeros inside C.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How many zeros of z⁵ + 3z + 1 lie in |z| < 1? Take f = 3z, g = z⁵ + 1. On |z| = 1, |g| ≤ 2 < 3 = |f|. f has one zero inside, so z⁵ + 3z + 1 has exactly one zero in |z| < 1.

steps.title: Worked example: annulus
steps.body: Zeros of z⁴ − 6z + 3 in |z| < 2: f = z⁴, g = −6z + 3, on |z| = 2: |g| ≤ 15 < 16 = |f| → 4 zeros. In |z| < 1: f = −6z, g = z⁴ + 3, |g| ≤ 4 < 6 → 1 zero. So 3 zeros in 1 < |z| < 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Choosing the 'big' function wrongly — test the inequality on the whole contour. Rouché needs strict inequality.

activity.prompt: How many zeros does z⁷ − 5z³ + 1 have in |z| < 1? (Compare with −5z³.)

quiz.q: (1/2πi)∮ f′/f dz counts:
quiz.why: Each zero contributes +1 and each pole −1, counted with multiplicity.

quiz.q: Zeros of z³ + 10z + 1 inside |z| = 1:
quiz.why: With f = 10z and g = z³ + 1, |g| ≤ 2 < 10 on |z| = 1, so there is one zero.

quiz.q: Rouché's theorem requires on C:
quiz.why: The strict inequality guarantees f + g never vanishes on C and has the same zero count as f.
Inside |z| = 2 there are 3 zeros (0 twice, 1 once) and no poles, since 3 is outside.

lessons.title: Revision: formula sheet and previous-year-style problems

story.title: One page to rule the paper

scenes.text: Most Complex Analysis papers mix CR equations, Cauchy's formula, Laurent series and residue integrals.
Here is the sheet and a full model answer.

steps.title: Formula sheet
steps.body: CR: u_x = v_y, u_y = −v_x. f′ = u_x + iv_x. ∮ (z − a)ⁿ dz = 2πi if n = −1, else 0. f⁽ⁿ⁾(z₀) = n!/(2πi) ∮ f/(z − z₀)ⁿ⁺¹. Liouville. R = lim|aₙ/aₙ₊₁|. Res at simple pole g/h′; order m: (1/(m−1)!) dᵐ⁻¹[(z − z₀)ᵐ f]. Residue theorem 2πi Σ Res. Type 1 z = e^{iθ}; Type 2 upper half-plane; Jordan e^{imz}.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Evaluate ∮_{|z|=3} (z² + 1)/(z(z − 2)) dz. A: Poles 0 and 2, both inside. Res at 0 = (0 + 1)/(0 − 2) = −½. Res at 2 = (4 + 1)/2 = 5/2. Sum = 2. Integral = 2πi · 2 = 4πi.
