uni-bsc-math-differential-equations.title: B.Sc Mathematics · Differential Equations (full paper)
uni-bsc-math-differential-equations.description: First-order equations (separable, homogeneous, exact, linear, Bernoulli, Clairaut), applications, higher-order linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy–Euler equations, variation of parameters, simultaneous and total equations, series solutions and first-order partial differential equations, with solved problems and unit exams. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Mathematics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · First-order, first-degree equations
courses.summary: Order, degree and formation of differential equations; variables separable; homogeneous equations; exact equations and integrating factors; linear and Bernoulli equations, with initial value problems.
outcomes: Find order and degree and form an equation by eliminating constants
Solve separable and homogeneous equations
Test exactness and find integrating factors
Solve linear and Bernoulli equations with the integrating factor e^{∫P dx}
Apply initial conditions to obtain particular solutions

scenes.text: A cup of chai cools fast at first, then slowly — the rate depends on how hot it still is.
A relation between a quantity and its rate of change is a differential equation.

steps.title: Basic terms
steps.body:
- Order: highest derivative present. Degree: power of that derivative once the equation is free of radicals and fractions in derivatives.
- General solution: contains as many arbitrary constants as the order; particular solution: constants fixed by conditions.
- Formation: eliminate n constants by differentiating n times. Example: y = Ae^{2x} + Be^{−2x} gives y'' = 4y, i.e. y'' − 4y = 0.

steps.title: Variables separable
steps.body: If dy/dx = f(x)g(y), write dy/g(y) = f(x)dx and integrate both sides: ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx + C. Check separately for constant solutions where g(y) = 0.

steps.title: Solved: two separable equations
steps.body:
- dy/dx = xy ⇒ dy/y = x dx ⇒ ln|y| = x²/2 + c ⇒ y = Ce^{x²/2}.
- (1 + x²)dy = (1 + y²)dx ⇒ dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²) ⇒ tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + C, equivalently (y − x)/(1 + xy) = constant.

steps.title: Solved: an initial value problem
steps.body:
dy/dx = 2xy², y(0) = 1.

- dy/y² = 2x dx ⇒ −1/y = x² + C.
- y(0) = 1 ⇒ C = −1 ⇒ y = 1/(1 − x²), valid for |x| < 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the constant of integration, or adding it on both sides separately.
- Losing solutions when dividing by g(y) (y = 0 also solves dy/dx = xy).
- Confusing degree with order.

activity.prompt: For dy/dx = 2xy², y(0) = 1, find y(0.5) (three decimals).

quiz.q: The order and degree of (y'')³ + (y')⁴ + y = 0 are:
quiz.why: The highest derivative is y'' (order 2) and it appears to the third power (degree 3).

quiz.q: Eliminating A from y = Ax² gives:
quiz.why: y' = 2Ax and A = y/x², so y' = 2y/x, i.e. xy' = 2y.

quiz.q: The general solution of dy/dx = e^{x − y} is:
quiz.why: Separating gives eʸ dy = eˣ dx, and integrating both sides gives eʸ = eˣ + C.

scenes.text: Zoom a family of curves in or out from the origin and it looks the same.
Such equations depend only on y/x — the substitution y = vx unlocks them.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
dy/dx = f(x, y) is homogeneous if f(tx, ty) = f(x, y), i.e. f depends only on y/x.

Put y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. Then x dv/dx = F(v) − v, which separates: dv/(F(v) − v) = dx/x.

Reducible case: dy/dx = (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/(a₂x + b₂y + c₂) with a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂: shift x = X + h, y = Y + k to kill the constants.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(2xy)
steps.body:
- y = vx: v + xv' = (1 + v²)/(2v) ⇒ xv' = (1 − v²)/(2v).
- 2v dv/(1 − v²) = dx/x ⇒ −ln|1 − v²| = ln|x| + c.
- x(1 − v²) = C ⇒ x(1 − y²/x²) = C ⇒ x² − y² = Cx.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = (x + y)/(x − y)
steps.body:
- v + xv' = (1 + v)/(1 − v) ⇒ xv' = (1 + v²)/(1 − v).
- (1 − v)dv/(1 + v²) = dx/x ⇒ tan⁻¹v − ½ln(1 + v²) = ln|x| + C.
- Hence tan⁻¹(y/x) = ln√(x² + y²) + C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the v term in dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
- Not substituting back v = y/x at the end.
- Calling an equation homogeneous because each term has the same degree when there is a constant term.

activity.prompt: The curve x² − y² = Cx passes through (1, 0). Find y > 0 on it at x = 2 (three decimals).

quiz.q: Which equation is homogeneous?
quiz.why: (x² + xy)/y² is unchanged when x, y are replaced by tx, ty, so it depends only on y/x.

quiz.q: For a homogeneous equation the substitution is:
quiz.why: y = vx turns a function of y/x into a function of v alone and makes the equation separable.

quiz.q: After y = vx, the equation dy/dx = y/x + 1 becomes:
quiz.why: v + x v' = v + 1 gives x v' = 1, so v = ln|x| + C and y = x ln|x| + Cx.

scenes.text: Contour lines on a map are curves where altitude F(x, y) is constant.
An exact equation is just dF = 0 — find F and the solution is F = C.

steps.title: Exactness
steps.body:
M dx + N dy = 0 is exact iff ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x. Then there is F with F_x = M, F_y = N and the solution is F(x, y) = C.

Practical rule: ∫M dx (treating y constant) + ∫(terms of N not containing x) dy = C.

steps.title: Solved: an exact equation
steps.body:
(2xy + 3)dx + (x² + 4y)dy = 0.

- M_y = 2x = N_x ✔ exact.
- ∫M dx = x²y + 3x; N's term without x: 4y ⇒ ∫4y dy = 2y².
- Solution: x²y + 3x + 2y² = C.

steps.title: Integrating factor rules
steps.body:
If not exact:
- (M_y − N_x)/N = f(x) ⇒ IF = e^{∫f dx}.
- (N_x − M_y)/M = g(y) ⇒ IF = e^{∫g dy}.
- M, N homogeneous with Mx + Ny ≠ 0 ⇒ IF = 1/(Mx + Ny).
- Form y f(xy)dx + x g(xy)dy with Mx − Ny ≠ 0 ⇒ IF = 1/(Mx − Ny).

steps.title: Solved: finding an IF
steps.body:
(x² + y² + x)dx + xy dy = 0.

- M_y = 2y, N_x = y ⇒ (M_y − N_x)/N = y/(xy) = 1/x ⇒ IF = x.
- Exact form: (x³ + xy² + x²)dx + x²y dy = 0.
- Solution: x⁴/4 + x²y²/2 + x³/3 = C (check: F_y = x²y ✔).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing M_x = N_y instead of M_y = N_x.
- Integrating N fully with respect to y, double-counting terms that contain x.
- Using an IF formula whose expression is not purely a function of one variable.

activity.prompt: For (2xy + 3)dx + (x² + 4y)dy = 0, find C for the solution curve through (1, 1).

quiz.q: (y cos x + 2x)dx + (sin x + 1)dy = 0 is:
quiz.why: M_y = cos x and N_x = cos x are equal.

quiz.q: For y dx − x dy = 0, an integrating factor is:
quiz.why: Dividing by x² gives (y dx − x dy)/x² = −d(y/x), which is exact.

quiz.q: If (M_y − N_x)/N = 2, an integrating factor is:
quiz.why: A function of x alone (here the constant 2) gives IF = e^{∫2 dx} = e^{2x}.

scenes.text: Brine flows into a tank while mixed solution flows out at the same rate.
The salt amount obeys a linear equation y' + Py = Q, solved by one integrating factor.

steps.title: Linear equations
steps.body:
dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). IF = e^{∫P dx}. Then d/dx(y·IF) = Q·IF, so

y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.

Linear in x: dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y), IF = e^{∫P dy}.

steps.title: Solved: y' + y = x
steps.body:
- IF = eˣ ⇒ (yeˣ)' = xeˣ.
- ∫xeˣ dx = (x − 1)eˣ ⇒ yeˣ = (x − 1)eˣ + C.
- y = x − 1 + Ce^{−x}.

steps.title: Solved: xy' + 2y = x²
steps.body:
- Standard form y' + (2/x)y = x, IF = e^{2 ln x} = x².
- (x²y)' = x³ ⇒ x²y = x⁴/4 + C ⇒ y = x²/4 + C/x².

steps.title: Bernoulli equations
steps.body: y' + Py = Qyⁿ (n ≠ 0, 1). Divide by yⁿ and put z = y^{1−n}: z' + (1 − n)Pz = (1 − n)Q, which is linear.

steps.title: Solved: y' + y/x = xy²
steps.body:
- Divide by y²: y⁻²y' + (1/x)y⁻¹ = x. Put z = 1/y, z' = −y⁻²y'.
- −z' + z/x = x ⇒ z' − z/x = −x; IF = 1/x.
- (z/x)' = −1 ⇒ z/x = −x + C ⇒ 1/y = −x² + Cx.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not putting the equation in standard form (coefficient of y' must be 1) before finding P.
- Forgetting to multiply Q by the IF.
- Using z = yⁿ instead of z = y^{1−n} for Bernoulli.

activity.prompt: Solve y' + y = x with y(0) = 0 and find y(1) (three decimals).

quiz.q: The IF of y' + (tan x)y = sec x is:
quiz.why: e^{∫tan x dx} = e^{ln sec x} = sec x.

quiz.q: For Bernoulli y' + Py = Qy³, the substitution is:
quiz.why: z = y^{1−n} with n = 3 gives z = y⁻².

quiz.q: The general solution of y' − 2y = 0 is:
quiz.why: IF = e^{−2x} gives (ye^{−2x})' = 0, so y = Ce^{2x}.

questions.q: Eliminating A and B from y = Ae^{2x} + Be^{−2x} gives:
questions.why: Differentiating twice gives y'' = 4Ae^{2x} + 4Be^{−2x} = 4y.

questions.q: The solution of dy/dx = xy is:
questions.why: Separating gives ln|y| = x²/2 + c.

questions.q: For dy/dx = 2xy², y(0) = 1, the solution is:
questions.why: −1/y = x² + C with C = −1 gives y = 1/(1 − x²).

questions.q: The solution of dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(2xy) is:
questions.why: With y = vx the equation separates to x(1 − v²) = C, i.e. x² − y² = Cx.

questions.q: For dy/dx = (x + 2y − 3)/(2x + y − 3), a suitable shift is x = X + h, y = Y + k with (h, k) =
questions.why: Solving h + 2k = 3 and 2h + k = 3 gives h = k = 1, which removes the constants.

questions.q: (2xy + 3)dx + (x² + 4y)dy = 0 has solution:
questions.why: It is exact; ∫M dx = x²y + 3x and the remaining y-term of N integrates to 2y².

questions.q: For (x² + y² + x)dx + xy dy = 0, an integrating factor is:
questions.why: (M_y − N_x)/N = (2y − y)/(xy) = 1/x, so IF = e^{ln x} = x.

questions.q: For homogeneous M dx + N dy = 0 with Mx + Ny ≠ 0, an IF is:
questions.why: This is the standard integrating factor for homogeneous equations.

questions.q: The solution of y' + y = x is:
questions.why: With IF eˣ, ye^{x} = (x − 1)eˣ + C.

questions.q: The solution of xy' + 2y = x² is:
questions.why: IF = x² gives (x²y)' = x³, so x²y = x⁴/4 + C.

questions.q: The equation dx/dy + x/y = y² is linear in x with IF:
questions.why: P(y) = 1/y, so IF = e^{∫dy/y} = y.

questions.q: For y' + y/x = xy², the general solution is:
questions.why: With z = 1/y the equation becomes z' − z/x = −x, whose solution is z = −x² + Cx.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Higher-degree equations, trajectories and applications
courses.summary: First-order equations of higher degree solvable for p, x or y, Clairaut's equation and singular solutions, orthogonal trajectories in Cartesian and polar form, and applications to growth and decay, Newton's law of cooling and electric circuits.
outcomes: Solve equations solvable for p and for y
Find general and singular solutions of Clairaut's equation
Find orthogonal trajectories of Cartesian and polar families
Model and solve growth, decay, cooling and RL-circuit problems

lessons.title: Equations solvable for p, y or x

scenes.text: An equation quadratic in p = dy/dx gives two slopes through each point.
Factorising splits it into two ordinary first-order equations, each with its own family of curves.

steps.title: Methods (p = dy/dx)
steps.body:
- Solvable for p: factor F(x, y, p) = (p − f₁)(p − f₂)… = 0; solve each p = fᵢ(x, y) to get φᵢ(x, y, c) = 0; the general solution is the product φ₁φ₂… = 0 (same c).
- Solvable for y: y = f(x, p). Differentiate w.r.t. x: p = f_x + f_p dp/dx, a first-order equation in x and p. Eliminate p between its solution and y = f(x, p).
- Solvable for x: x = f(y, p). Differentiate w.r.t. y: 1/p = f_y + f_p dp/dy.

steps.title: Solved: p² − 5p + 6 = 0
steps.body:
(p − 2)(p − 3) = 0 ⇒ y = 2x + c or y = 3x + c.
General solution: (y − 2x − c)(y − 3x − c) = 0.

steps.title: Solved: p² − (x + y)p + xy = 0
steps.body:
(p − x)(p − y) = 0.
- p = x ⇒ y = x²/2 + c.
- p = y ⇒ y = ceˣ.
General solution: (2y − x² − c)(y − ceˣ) = 0 (constants absorbed).

steps.title: Solved: solvable for y
steps.body:
y = 2px − p². (This is not Clairaut's form, because the coefficient of x is 2p, not p.)

- Differentiate: p = 2p + 2x p' − 2p p' ⇒ −p = 2p'(x − p) ⇒ dx/dp + 2x/p = 2 (linear in x).
- IF = p² ⇒ xp² = 2p³/3 + c ⇒ x = 2p/3 + c/p².
- Together with y = 2px − p² this gives the solution in parametric form.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using different constants in different factors of the general solution.
- Forgetting that p is a function of x when differentiating y = f(x, p).
- Dropping the parametric form when p cannot be eliminated (it is a valid answer).

activity.prompt: For p² − 5p + 6 = 0, the solution branch y = 3x + c passes through (1, 4). Find c.

quiz.q: p² − 9 = 0 has general solution:
quiz.why: p = ±3 gives y = ±3x + c, combined into one product with the same constant.

quiz.q: For y = f(x, p), we differentiate with respect to:
quiz.why: Differentiating w.r.t. x replaces dy/dx by p and gives an equation in x and p only.

quiz.q: p = y gives:
quiz.why: dy/dx = y separates to ln|y| = x + c, i.e. y = ceˣ.

story.title: A curve drawn by its tangents

scenes.text: Draw many straight lines, each obeying one rule; their outline is a smooth curve.
Clairaut's family of lines is the general solution; the outline (envelope) is the singular solution.

steps.title: Clairaut's equation
steps.body:
y = px + f(p).

- Differentiate: p = p + x p' + f'(p) p' ⇒ p'(x + f'(p)) = 0.
- p' = 0 ⇒ p = c ⇒ general solution y = cx + f(c) (straight lines).
- x + f'(p) = 0 ⇒ eliminating p gives the singular solution (envelope of the lines), which contains no arbitrary constant.

The singular solution also appears via the p-discriminant (or c-discriminant) — but check it actually satisfies the equation.

steps.title: Solved: y = px + a/p
steps.body:
- General: y = cx + a/c.
- Singular: x − a/p² = 0 ⇒ p = √(a/x); y = √(ax) + √(ax) = 2√(ax) ⇒ y² = 4ax (parabola, envelope of its tangent lines).

steps.title: Solved: y = px + p²
steps.body:
- General: y = cx + c².
- Singular: x + 2p = 0 ⇒ p = −x/2 ⇒ y = −x²/2 + x²/4 = −x²/4, i.e. x² + 4y = 0.

steps.title: Reducible to Clairaut
steps.body: Substitutions such as X = x², Y = y² (for equations in x, y, p with xy-type terms) or X = eˣ, Y = eʸ convert some equations into Clairaut form; then solve and substitute back.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the singular solution as a particular case of the general solution (it is not obtained for any c).
- Accepting every factor of a discriminant as a singular solution (tac-loci and cusp-loci are not solutions).
- Forgetting to check the singular solution in the original equation.

activity.prompt: For y = px + p², find y on the singular solution at x = 2.

quiz.q: The general solution of y = px + √(1 + p²) is:
quiz.why: It is Clairaut's form, so replace p by c.

quiz.q: The singular solution of y = px + a/p is:
quiz.why: Eliminating p from y = px + a/p and x = a/p² gives y² = 4ax.

quiz.q: A singular solution:
options: contains no arbitrary constant and is not a particular case
quiz.why: It satisfies the equation but cannot be obtained from the general solution by choosing c.

scenes.text: On a heated plate, curves of equal temperature form one family.
Heat flows along curves that cut every isotherm at right angles — the orthogonal trajectories.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Cartesian: from the family f(x, y, c) = 0, eliminate c to get dy/dx = F(x, y). Replace dy/dx by −dx/dy and solve.

Polar: from f(r, θ, c) = 0 get r dθ/dr = G(r, θ); replace r dθ/dr by −dr/(r dθ) and solve.

Self-orthogonal families (e.g. confocal parabolas y² = 4a(x + a)) give back the same family.

steps.title: Solved: parabolas y = cx²
steps.body:
- dy/dx = 2cx = 2y/x.
- Orthogonal: dy/dx = −x/(2y) ⇒ 2y dy = −x dx ⇒ y² = −x²/2 + k.
- Trajectories: x² + 2y² = k (ellipses).

steps.title: Solved: circles and lines
steps.body: x² + y² = c²: dy/dx = −x/y ⇒ orthogonal dy/dx = y/x ⇒ y = kx (lines through the origin).

steps.title: Solved: the cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ)
steps.body:
- ln r = ln a + ln(1 + cos θ) ⇒ (1/r) dr/dθ = −sin θ/(1 + cos θ) = −tan(θ/2).
- Replace (1/r) dr/dθ by −r dθ/dr: −r dθ/dr = −tan(θ/2) ⇒ dr/r = cot(θ/2) dθ.
- ln r = 2 ln sin(θ/2) + c ⇒ r = b sin²(θ/2) = (b/2)(1 − cos θ): the cardioids r = k(1 − cos θ).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not eliminating c before replacing the slope.
- Using −dy/dx instead of −dx/dy.
- In polar form, replacing dr/dθ by −dr/dθ (the correct swap is r dθ/dr → −dr/(r dθ)).

activity.prompt: The orthogonal trajectories of y = cx² are x² + 2y² = k. Find k for the trajectory through (2, 1).

quiz.q: The orthogonal trajectories of y = cx are:
quiz.why: dy/dx = y/x becomes −x/y, which integrates to x² + y² = k.

quiz.q: The orthogonal trajectories of xy = c are:
quiz.why: dy/dx = −y/x becomes x/y, so y dy = x dx and x² − y² = k.

quiz.q: A self-orthogonal family is one whose orthogonal trajectories are:
quiz.why: Confocal parabolas, for example, cut members of their own family at right angles.

lessons.title: Applications: growth, decay, cooling and circuits

scenes.text: Investigators estimate time of death from body temperature readings.
Newton's law of cooling, a first-order linear ODE, turns two temperatures into a time.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- Growth/decay: dN/dt = kN ⇒ N = N₀e^{kt}. Half-life T: k = −ln 2/T. Doubling time: k = ln 2/T.
- Newton's law of cooling: dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ) ⇒ T − Tₛ = (T₀ − Tₛ)e^{−kt}.
- RL circuit: L di/dt + Ri = E ⇒ i = (E/R)(1 − e^{−Rt/L}) with i(0) = 0. Time constant L/R.
- RC circuit: R dq/dt + q/C = E ⇒ q = CE(1 − e^{−t/(RC)}).

steps.title: Solved: cooling
steps.body:
Tea at 100 °C cools to 60 °C in 10 min in a 20 °C room. When will it reach 30 °C?

- 60 − 20 = 80e^{−10k} ⇒ e^{−10k} = 1/2 ⇒ k = ln 2/10.
- 30 − 20 = 80e^{−kt} ⇒ e^{−kt} = 1/8 = (1/2)³ ⇒ t = 30 min.

steps.title: Solved: radioactive decay
steps.body: Radium's half-life is about 1600 years. Fraction left after 400 years: (1/2)^{400/1600} = 2^{−1/4} ≈ 0.841, i.e. about 84%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying cooling to T instead of T − Tₛ.
- Sign of k in decay problems.
- Mixing time units (minutes vs hours) inside the exponent.

activity.prompt: A bacterial culture doubles every 3 hours. How many hours until it is 8 times its initial size?

quiz.q: The solution of dN/dt = kN with N(0) = N₀ is:
quiz.why: Separating gives ln N = kt + c, so N = N₀e^{kt}.

quiz.q: In Newton's law of cooling, the quantity that decays exponentially is:
quiz.why: The rate is proportional to the temperature excess, so T − Tₛ = (T₀ − Tₛ)e^{−kt}.

quiz.q: The time constant of an RL circuit is:
quiz.why: i = (E/R)(1 − e^{−t/(L/R)}), so L/R sets the time scale.

questions.q: The general solution of p² − 5p + 6 = 0 is:
questions.why: Factorising gives p = 2 or 3, each giving a family of lines with the same constant.

questions.q: p² − (x + y)p + xy = 0 factorises as:
questions.why: Expanding (p − x)(p − y) gives p² − (x + y)p + xy.

questions.q: Clairaut's equation has the form:
questions.why: Clairaut's equation is y = px + f(p), whose general solution is y = cx + f(c).

questions.q: The singular solution of y = px + p² is:
questions.why: x + 2p = 0 gives p = −x/2, and substituting gives y = −x²/4.

questions.q: The singular solution of y = px + a/p is:
questions.why: Eliminating p using x = a/p² gives y = 2√(ax), i.e. y² = 4ax.

questions.q: The orthogonal trajectories of y = cx² are:
questions.why: Replacing 2y/x by −x/(2y) and integrating gives x² + 2y² = k.

questions.q: The orthogonal trajectories of x² − y² = c are:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Linear equations with constant coefficients
courses.summary: Higher-order linear equations with constant coefficients: the auxiliary equation and complementary function, particular integrals by operator methods for exponential, trigonometric, polynomial and eᵃˣV inputs, and the Cauchy–Euler equation.
outcomes: Write the complementary function for real, repeated and complex roots
Find particular integrals for eᵃˣ, sin ax and cos ax, including failure cases
Find particular integrals for polynomials and eᵃˣV
Solve Cauchy–Euler equations by x = eᶻ
Solve initial value problems for second-order equations

scenes.text: After a speed bump, a car's body bounces and settles.
Whether it oscillates or settles smoothly depends on the roots of an auxiliary equation.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For f(D)y = 0 with D = d/dx, solve the auxiliary equation f(m) = 0.

- Distinct real roots m₁, m₂, …: y = c₁e^{m₁x} + c₂e^{m₂x} + …
- Repeated root m (k times): (c₁ + c₂x + … + c_k x^{k−1})e^{mx}.
- Complex pair α ± iβ: e^{αx}(c₁ cos βx + c₂ sin βx).

General solution of f(D)y = X: y = CF + PI.

steps.title: Solved: a higher-order case
steps.body:
(D³ − D)y = 0: m(m − 1)(m + 1) = 0 ⇒ y = c₁ + c₂eˣ + c₃e^{−x}.
(D⁴ + 2D² + 1)y = 0: (m² + 1)² = 0 ⇒ y = (c₁ + c₂x)cos x + (c₃ + c₄x)sin x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the factor x for repeated roots.
- Writing e^{βx} instead of cos βx, sin βx for complex roots.
- Having fewer constants than the order of the equation.

activity.prompt: For y = e^{3x} − e^{2x} (the IVP above), find y(1) (three decimals).

options: e^{3x}(c₁ cos x + c₂ sin x)
quiz.why: (m − 3)² = 0 is a repeated root, so the second solution carries a factor x.

quiz.q: A third-order linear ODE has a general solution with how many constants?
quiz.why: The number of arbitrary constants equals the order of the equation.

lessons.title: Particular integrals for exponential and trigonometric inputs

scenes.text: Push a swing at a random rhythm and it barely moves; push at its natural rhythm and it soars.
That is resonance — the 'failure case' where the PI picks up a factor of x.

steps.title: Operator rules
steps.body:
- 1/f(D) eᵃˣ = eᵃˣ/f(a) if f(a) ≠ 0.
- If f(a) = 0: 1/f(D) eᵃˣ = x eᵃˣ/f'(a) (and x²eᵃˣ/f''(a) if f'(a) = 0 too).
- 1/f(D²) sin ax = sin ax/f(−a²) if f(−a²) ≠ 0; same for cos ax.
- Failure case: 1/(D² + a²) sin ax = −x cos ax/(2a); 1/(D² + a²) cos ax = x sin ax/(2a).
- If f has odd powers of D, write f(D) = g(D²) + D h(D²), replace D² by −a², then rationalise.

steps.title: Solved: exponential inputs
steps.body:
- (D² − 5D + 6)y = eˣ: PI = eˣ/(1 − 5 + 6) = eˣ/2.
- (D² − 5D + 6)y = e^{2x}: f(2) = 0, f'(D) = 2D − 5, f'(2) = −1 ⇒ PI = −x e^{2x}.
- Full solution of the second: y = c₁e^{2x} + c₂e^{3x} − xe^{2x}.

steps.title: Solved: trigonometric inputs
steps.body:
- (D² + 4)y = sin x: PI = sin x/(−1 + 4) = (1/3) sin x.
- (D² + 4)y = sin 2x (resonance): PI = −x cos 2x/4.
- (D² + D + 1)y = sin x: replace D² by −1: 1/D sin x = −cos x. So PI = −cos x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Replacing D (not D²) by −a² for trig inputs.
- Missing the failure case when the input matches a CF term.
- Forgetting that 1/D means integration.

lessons.title: Particular integrals for polynomials and eᵃˣV

scenes.text: A beam carries a load that grows linearly along its length.
Expanding 1/f(D) as a power series in D handles polynomial inputs exactly.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Polynomial X: write 1/f(D) = [1 ± φ(D)]⁻¹ (after factoring out the lowest term) and expand by the binomial series up to D^k where k = degree of X.
- Exponential shift: 1/f(D) (eᵃˣV) = eᵃˣ · 1/f(D + a) V.
- xV: 1/f(D)(xV) = x·(1/f(D))V − (f'(D)/f(D)²)V.

steps.title: Solved: (D² + 1)y = x²
steps.body:
PI = (1 + D²)⁻¹x² = (1 − D² + D⁴ − …)x² = x² − 2.

Check: (x² − 2)'' + (x² − 2) = 2 + x² − 2 = x² ✔

steps.title: Solved: (D² − 2D + 1)y = xeˣ
steps.body:
f(D) = (D − 1)². Shift: eˣ · 1/(D + 1 − 1)² x = eˣ · (1/D²)x = eˣ x³/6.

General solution: y = (c₁ + c₂x)eˣ + x³eˣ/6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expanding beyond what is needed or stopping too early (keep up to D^{deg X}).
- Forgetting to shift D → D + a in the operator when using eᵃˣV.
- Losing the 1/D integration when f(D) has a factor D.

scenes.text: In x²y'' + axy' + by = 0, coefficients change with x, so eᵐˣ guesses fail.
The substitution x = eᶻ turns it into a constant-coefficient equation in z.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
aₙxⁿyⁿ + … + a₁xy' + a₀y = X(x).

Put x = eᶻ, θ = d/dz. Then xD = θ, x²D² = θ(θ − 1), x³D³ = θ(θ − 1)(θ − 2).

Solve the constant-coefficient equation in z, then replace z = ln x. Equivalently, try y = xᵐ in the homogeneous equation.

steps.title: Solved: x²y'' − 2xy' + 2y = 0
steps.body: θ(θ − 1) − 2θ + 2 = θ² − 3θ + 2 = (θ − 1)(θ − 2) ⇒ y = c₁eᶻ + c₂e^{2z} = c₁x + c₂x².

steps.title: Solved: x²y'' + xy' + y = 0
steps.body: θ(θ − 1) + θ + 1 = θ² + 1 ⇒ y = c₁ cos z + c₂ sin z = c₁ cos(ln x) + c₂ sin(ln x).

steps.title: Solved: a non-homogeneous case
steps.body:
x²y'' − 2xy' + 2y = x³ ⇒ (θ² − 3θ + 2)y = e^{3z}.

PI = e^{3z}/(9 − 9 + 2) = e^{3z}/2 = x³/2.

y = c₁x + c₂x² + x³/2. Check PI: y = x³/2, y' = 3x²/2, y'' = 3x ⇒ 3x³ − 3x³ + x³ = x³ ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing x²D² = θ² (it is θ(θ − 1)).
- Forgetting to convert X(x) to a function of z.
- Leaving the answer in z.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Variation of parameters, systems and total equations
courses.summary: The Wronskian and variation of parameters, reduction of order when one solution is known, simultaneous linear equations and the symmetric form dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R, and total differential equations with the integrability condition.
outcomes: Compute Wronskians and test linear independence
Find particular integrals by variation of parameters
Find a second solution by reduction of order
Solve simultaneous linear systems and symmetric-form equations
Test and solve total differential equations P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0

scenes.text: The input sec x has no neat operator rule — 1/f(D) shortcuts give up.
Lagrange's variation of parameters works for any continuous input once the CF is known.

steps.title: The Wronskian
steps.body: W(y₁, y₂) = y₁y₂' − y₂y₁'. For solutions of y'' + P y' + Q y = 0 on an interval, W ≠ 0 ⇔ y₁, y₂ are linearly independent (Abel: W = C e^{−∫P dx}, so W is either never zero or always zero).

steps.title: Variation of parameters
steps.body:
For y'' + P y' + Q y = X with CF c₁y₁ + c₂y₂, seek y = u₁y₁ + u₂y₂ with

u₁ = −∫ y₂X/W dx, u₂ = ∫ y₁X/W dx.

(The equation must have leading coefficient 1.)

steps.title: Solved: y'' + y = sec x
steps.body:
y₁ = cos x, y₂ = sin x, W = cos²x + sin²x = 1.

- u₁ = −∫ sin x sec x dx = −∫ tan x dx = ln|cos x|.
- u₂ = ∫ cos x sec x dx = x.
- y = c₁ cos x + c₂ sin x + cos x ln|cos x| + x sin x.

steps.title: Solved: y'' − 2y' + y = eˣ/x
steps.body:
y₁ = eˣ, y₂ = xeˣ, W = e^{2x}.

- u₁ = −∫ xeˣ·(eˣ/x)/e^{2x} dx = −x.
- u₂ = ∫ eˣ·(eˣ/x)/e^{2x} dx = ln x.
- PI = −xeˣ + xeˣ ln x; the −xeˣ part can be absorbed into the CF, so y = (c₁ + c₂x)eˣ + xeˣ ln x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign in u₁.
- Applying the formula before dividing by the coefficient of y''.
- Writing W = y₁'y₂ − y₁y₂' (wrong sign; it changes u₁ and u₂).

activity.prompt: Compute the Wronskian W(x, x²) at x = 2.

quiz.q: W(eˣ, e^{−x}) equals:
If W(y₁, y₂) ≡ 0 for two solutions of a linear ODE, they are:
quiz.why: For solutions of the same linear ODE, a vanishing Wronskian means one is a constant multiple of the other.

quiz.q: For y'' + y = tan x, the Wronskian of cos x and sin x is:
quiz.why: cos x·cos x − sin x·(−sin x) = 1.

story.title: One key opens the second door

scenes.text: Guessing one solution of a variable-coefficient equation is often easy (try x, eˣ, xᵐ).
Writing y = v·y₁ reduces the problem to a first-order equation for v'.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
If y₁ solves y'' + P y' + Q y = 0, put y = v y₁. The equation reduces to y₁v'' + (2y₁' + P y₁)v' = 0, first-order in v'.

Formula: y₂ = y₁ ∫ e^{−∫P dx}/y₁² dx.

Quick guesses: y₁ = x works if P + xQ = 0; y₁ = eˣ works if 1 + P + Q = 0; y₁ = e^{−x} if 1 − P + Q = 0.

steps.title: Solved: x²y'' + xy' − y = 0 with y₁ = x
steps.body:
- Check: 0 + x − x = 0 ✔.
- y = vx: y' = v'x + v, y'' = v''x + 2v'.
- x²(v''x + 2v') + x(v'x + v) − vx = x³v'' + 3x²v' = 0 ⇒ v''/v' = −3/x ⇒ v' = c/x³ ⇒ v = −c/(2x²).
- y₂ = 1/x. General solution y = c₁x + c₂/x.

steps.title: Solved: using the formula
steps.body:
Same equation in standard form: y'' + (1/x)y' − (1/x²)y = 0, P = 1/x.

e^{−∫P} = 1/x, so y₂ = x ∫ (1/x)/x² dx = x·(−1/(2x²)) = −1/(2x) — a multiple of 1/x ✔

steps.title: Solved: guessing eˣ
steps.body: y'' − (1 + x)y'/x + y/x = 0 has P = −(1 + x)/x, Q = 1/x: 1 + P + Q = 1 − 1/x − 1 + 1/x = 0 ⇒ y₁ = eˣ. Also P + xQ = −1/x − 1 + 1 ≠ 0 here; reduction of order then gives y₂ = −(1 + x), so y = c₁eˣ + c₂(1 + x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P from an equation not in standard form.
- Forgetting the y₁ factor outside the integral.
- Reporting a y₂ that is just a multiple of y₁.

activity.prompt: For x²y'' + xy' − y = 0 with y₁ = x, reduction of order gives y₂ = xᵏ. Find k.

quiz.why: Substituting y = x gives 0 + P + Qx = 0.

quiz.why: After y = vy₁, v itself does not appear, only v' and v''.

lessons.title: Simultaneous equations and the symmetric form

scenes.text: Two populations affect each other's rate of change.
A pair of coupled ODEs can be decoupled by eliminating one unknown.

steps.title: Linear systems
steps.body:
For equations like dx/dt = f(x, y), dy/dt = g(x, y) with constant coefficients, write them with D = d/dt and eliminate one variable (like solving linear equations), obtaining a single higher-order ODE.

Symmetric form dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R: find two independent integrals u = c₁, v = c₂ using multipliers (l, m, n) with lP + mQ + nR = 0, so l dx + m dy + n dz = 0 is exact.

steps.title: Solved: dx/dt = y, dy/dt = x
steps.body:
- Differentiate the first: x'' = y' = x ⇒ x = c₁eᵗ + c₂e^{−t}.
- y = x' = c₁eᵗ − c₂e^{−t}.
- With x(0) = 1, y(0) = 0: c₁ = c₂ = 1/2 ⇒ x = cosh t, y = sinh t.

steps.title: Solved: dx/dt = y, dy/dt = −x
steps.body: x'' = −x ⇒ x = c₁ cos t + c₂ sin t, y = x' = −c₁ sin t + c₂ cos t. Note x² + y² = c₁² + c₂²: the motion is a circle.

steps.title: Solved: dx/(yz) = dy/(zx) = dz/(xy)
steps.body:
- From the first two: x dx = y dy ⇒ x² − y² = c₁.
- From the last two: y dy = z dz ⇒ y² − z² = c₂.
- Multipliers (x, −y, 0) and (0, y, −z) were used implicitly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Solving for y independently and introducing extra constants (y must come from x via the equations).
- Finding two integrals that are not independent.
- Dividing by expressions that may vanish without noting it.

activity.prompt: For dx/dt = y, dy/dt = x with x(0) = 1, y(0) = 0, find x(1) (three decimals).

quiz.q: Eliminating y from dx/dt = y, dy/dt = −4x gives:
quiz.why: x'' = y' = −4x, so x'' + 4x = 0 with solutions cos 2t, sin 2t.

quiz.q: For dx/x = dy/y = dz/z, one integral is:
quiz.why: dx/x = dy/y integrates to ln y = ln x + c, i.e. y = cx (and similarly z = c'x).

quiz.q: In the symmetric form, multipliers l, m, n are chosen so that:
quiz.why: Then l dx + m dy + n dz = 0 along solutions and, if it is exact, integrates to an integral.

scenes.text: An equation P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0 asks for surfaces whose normal points along (P, Q, R).
Such surfaces exist only when an integrability condition holds.

steps.title: Integrability
steps.body:
P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0 has a solution family φ(x, y, z) = c iff

P(Q_z − R_y) + Q(R_x − P_z) + R(P_y − Q_x) = 0.

If it is exact (curl of (P, Q, R) = 0), integrate directly. Otherwise try an integrating factor, or treat z as constant, solve P dx + Q dy = 0, then find the z-dependence of the constant.

steps.title: Solved: exact cases
steps.body:
- yz dx + zx dy + xy dz = 0 is d(xyz) = 0 ⇒ xyz = c.
- (y + z)dx + (z + x)dy + (x + y)dz = 0 is d(xy + yz + zx) = 0 ⇒ xy + yz + zx = c.

steps.title: Solved: dividing by xyz
steps.body: yz dx + 2zx dy − 3xy dz = 0. Divide by xyz: dx/x + 2dy/y − 3dz/z = 0 ⇒ ln x + 2 ln y − 3 ln z = ln c ⇒ xy² = cz³.

steps.title: Solved: a non-integrable equation
steps.body:
z dx + x dy + y dz = 0: P = z, Q = x, R = y.

Q_z − R_y = −1, R_x − P_z = −1, P_y − Q_x = −1 ⇒ condition = −(x + y + z) ≠ 0 ⇒ no single family of surfaces satisfies it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the cyclic order in the integrability condition.
- Concluding non-integrable from non-exactness alone (an integrating factor may exist).
- Forgetting the dependence of the 'constant' on z in the method of treating z as constant.

activity.prompt: For z dx + x dy + y dz = 0, evaluate the integrability expression P(Q_z − R_y) + Q(R_x − P_z) + R(P_y − Q_x) at (1, 1, 1).

quiz.q: The solution of yz dx + zx dy + xy dz = 0 is:
quiz.why: The left side is exactly d(xyz).

quiz.q: The solution of x dx + y dy + z dz = 0 is:
quiz.why: It is ½d(x² + y² + z²) = 0, giving spheres centred at the origin.

quiz.q: If the integrability condition fails, then:
options: no family φ(x, y, z) = c satisfies the equation
quiz.why: The condition is necessary and sufficient for the existence of integral surfaces.

questions.why: u₁ = ln|cos x| and u₂ = x, so PI = cos x ln|cos x| + x sin x.

questions.why: Reduction of order gives v' = c/x³, so v ∝ 1/x² and y₂ = 1/x.

questions.why: W' = −PW for two solutions, so W = Ce^{−∫P dx}.

x + y = c₁, y + z = c₂

questions.q: The solution of yz dx + 2zx dy − 3xy dz = 0 is:
questions.why: Dividing by xyz gives dx/x + 2dy/y − 3dz/z = 0, which integrates to xy²/z³ = c.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Series solutions and first-order PDEs
courses.summary: Power-series solutions about ordinary points, the Frobenius method and indicial equation at regular singular points, formation of partial differential equations, and Lagrange's method for linear first-order PDEs Pp + Qq = R.
outcomes: Find power-series solutions and recurrence relations about an ordinary point

lessons.title: Power-series solutions about an ordinary point

scenes.text: Airy's equation y'' = xy describes light near a rainbow's edge, yet has no elementary solution.
A power series builds the solution term by term from a recurrence.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0, x₀ is an ordinary point if P and Q are analytic there. Then two independent solutions y = Σaₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ exist, converging at least up to the nearest singularity.

1. Substitute y = Σaₙxⁿ, y' = Σnaₙxⁿ⁻¹, y'' = Σn(n − 1)aₙxⁿ⁻².
2. Shift indices so every sum shows xⁿ.
3. Equate coefficients to get a recurrence; a₀, a₁ stay arbitrary.

steps.title: Solved: y'' + y = 0
steps.body:
Σ(n + 2)(n + 1)aₙ₊₂xⁿ + Σaₙxⁿ = 0 ⇒ aₙ₊₂ = −aₙ/((n + 2)(n + 1)).

- Even terms: a₂ = −a₀/2!, a₄ = a₀/4!, … ⇒ a₀ cos x.
- Odd terms: a₃ = −a₁/3!, … ⇒ a₁ sin x.

steps.title: Solved: Airy's equation y'' − xy = 0
steps.body:
Σ(n + 2)(n + 1)aₙ₊₂xⁿ − Σaₙ₋₁xⁿ = 0 (n ≥ 1), and the x⁰ term gives 2a₂ = 0.

- a₂ = 0, aₙ₊₂ = aₙ₋₁/((n + 2)(n + 1)).
- a₃ = a₀/6, a₄ = a₁/12, a₅ = 0, a₆ = a₀/180.
- y = a₀(1 + x³/6 + x⁶/180 + …) + a₁(x + x⁴/12 + …).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shifting the index in one sum but not adjusting its lower limit.
- Forgetting the leftover low-order terms (like 2a₂ = 0) before the recurrence starts.
- Expanding about a singular point with this method (Frobenius is needed there).

activity.prompt: Solve y' = y with y = Σaₙxⁿ and a₀ = 1. Find a₃ (three decimals).

quiz.q: For y' = y, the recurrence is:
quiz.why: Σ(n + 1)aₙ₊₁xⁿ = Σaₙxⁿ gives aₙ₊₁ = aₙ/(n + 1), so aₙ = a₀/n! and y = a₀eˣ.

quiz.q: x = 0 is an ordinary point of:
quiz.why: Here P = x and Q = 1 are analytic at 0; the others have P or Q blowing up at 0.

quiz.q: In Airy's equation y'' = xy, the coefficient a₂ is:
quiz.why: The constant term gives 2a₂ = 0 because the right side xy has no constant term.

lessons.title: Regular singular points and the Frobenius method

scenes.text: A circular drumhead vibrates in patterns described by Bessel's equation.
At its centre the equation is singular, so Frobenius adds a power xʳ to the series.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
x = 0 is a regular singular point of y'' + Py' + Qy = 0 if xP and x²Q are analytic at 0 (but P or Q is not).

Frobenius: try y = Σaₙx^{n+r}, a₀ ≠ 0. The lowest power gives the indicial equation r(r − 1) + p₀r + q₀ = 0, where p₀ = lim xP, q₀ = lim x²Q.

- Roots differing by a non-integer: two Frobenius series.
- Equal roots or roots differing by an integer: the second solution may contain a log term.

steps.title: Solved: 4xy'' + 2y' + y = 0
steps.body:
Standard form: P = 1/(2x), Q = 1/(4x) ⇒ p₀ = 1/2, q₀ = 0.

- Indicial: r(r − 1) + r/2 = 0 ⇒ r(r − 1/2) = 0 ⇒ r = 0, 1/2.
- The series sum to cos√x and sin√x (substituting t = √x turns the equation into d²y/dt² + y = 0).

steps.title: Solved: Bessel and Legendre
steps.body:
- Bessel x²y'' + xy' + (x² − n²)y = 0: p₀ = 1, q₀ = −n² ⇒ r² − n² = 0 ⇒ r = ±n; one solution is Jₙ(x).
- Legendre (1 − x²)y'' − 2xy' + n(n + 1)y = 0: x = 0 is ordinary; x = ±1 are regular singular points. For integer n one solution is the polynomial Pₙ(x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Frobenius at an irregular singular point (e.g. x³y'' + y = 0 at 0).
- Computing p₀, q₀ before dividing by the coefficient of y''.
- Assuming two series solutions always exist (integer-differing roots may need a log).

activity.prompt: Find the larger root of the indicial equation for 4xy'' + 2y' + y = 0.

quiz.q: x = 0 for x²y'' + xy' + (x² − 1)y = 0 is:
quiz.why: P = 1/x and Q = (x² − 1)/x² are singular, but xP = 1 and x²Q = x² − 1 are analytic.

quiz.q: The indicial roots of Bessel's equation of order n are:
quiz.why: p₀ = 1 and q₀ = −n² give r² − n² = 0.

quiz.q: For roots differing by a non-integer, Frobenius gives:
quiz.why: Each root gives its own series, and they are linearly independent when r₁ − r₂ is not an integer.

scenes.text: All spheres of radius 1 centred on the xy-plane form a family with two parameters.
Eliminating those parameters leaves one PDE every such sphere satisfies.

steps.title: Notation and methods
steps.body:
z = z(x, y), p = ∂z/∂x, q = ∂z/∂y, r = z_xx, s = z_xy, t = z_yy.

- Eliminating arbitrary constants: differentiate w.r.t. x and y and eliminate. Two constants usually give a first-order PDE.
- Eliminating an arbitrary function: z = f(u) gives p = f'(u)u_x, q = f'(u)u_y; divide to remove f'. φ(u, v) = 0 gives a linear first-order PDE.

steps.title: Solved: eliminating constants
steps.body:
- z = (x − a)² + (y − b)²: p = 2(x − a), q = 2(y − b) ⇒ z = p²/4 + q²/4 ⇒ p² + q² = 4z.
- z = ax + by + ab: p = a, q = b ⇒ z = px + qy + pq (a Clairaut-type PDE).

steps.title: Solved: eliminating a function
steps.body:
z = f(x² + y²): p = 2x f', q = 2y f' ⇒ p/q = x/y ⇒ yp − xq = 0.

z = f(x + ct) + g(x − ct) (two functions): eliminating both gives the wave equation z_tt = c² z_xx (second order).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the chain-rule factor u_x, u_y when differentiating f(u).
- Keeping a constant in the final PDE.
- Expecting a first-order PDE when two arbitrary functions are eliminated.

activity.prompt: For the family z = (x − a)² + (y − b)², at a point where p = 2 and q = 4, what is z?

quiz.q: Eliminating a, b from z = ax + by gives:
quiz.why: p = a and q = b, so z = px + qy.

quiz.q: z = f(y/x) satisfies:
quiz.why: p = −(y/x²)f' and q = (1/x)f', so xp + yq = −(y/x)f' + (y/x)f' = 0.

quiz.q: Eliminating two arbitrary functions usually gives a PDE of order:
quiz.why: Each function needs one further differentiation to eliminate, leading to second-order derivatives.

lessons.title: Lagrange's linear equation Pp + Qq = R

scenes.text: Dye dropped in a steady stream travels along fixed paths.
Lagrange's method finds those characteristic curves and builds every solution from them.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For Pp + Qq = R (P, Q, R functions of x, y, z):

1. Write the auxiliary equations dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R.
2. Find two independent integrals u(x, y, z) = c₁ and v(x, y, z) = c₂ (by grouping pairs or using multipliers).
3. The general solution is φ(u, v) = 0, or equivalently v = f(u).

steps.title: Solved: xp + yq = z
steps.body: dx/x = dy/y = dz/z ⇒ y/x = c₁, z/x = c₂ ⇒ φ(y/x, z/x) = 0, i.e. z = x f(y/x).

steps.title: Solved: p + q = 1 with a condition
steps.body:
dx/1 = dy/1 = dz/1 ⇒ x − y = c₁, z − x = c₂ ⇒ z = x + f(x − y).

If z(x, 0) = 0: x + f(x) = 0 ⇒ f(u) = −u ⇒ z = x − (x − y) = y.

steps.title: Solved: multipliers
steps.body:
(y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y.

- Multipliers 1, 1, 1: dx + dy + dz = 0 ⇒ x + y + z = c₁.
- Multipliers x, y, z: x dx + y dy + z dz = 0 ⇒ x² + y² + z² = c₂.
- Solution φ(x + y + z, x² + y² + z²) = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R with P, Q, R in the wrong places.
- Giving only one integral (two independent ones are needed).
- Writing the answer as u = c₁, v = c₂ instead of φ(u, v) = 0.

activity.prompt: For p + q = 1 with z(x, 0) = 0, the solution is z = y. Evaluate z at (3, 2).

quiz.q: The auxiliary equations of yzp + zxq = xy are:
quiz.why: They are dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R with P = yz, Q = zx, R = xy.

quiz.q: The general solution of yzp + zxq = xy is:
quiz.why: Pairs give x dx = y dy and y dy = z dz, so x² − y² and y² − z² are the integrals.

quiz.q: The general solution of p = 2q (i.e. p − 2q = 0) is:
quiz.why: dx/1 = dy/(−2) = dz/0 gives z = c₁ and 2x + y = c₂, so z = f(2x + y).

questions.q: For y'' + y = 0 with y = Σaₙxⁿ, the recurrence is:
questions.why: Equating coefficients of xⁿ gives (n + 2)(n + 1)aₙ₊₂ + aₙ = 0.

questions.why: With n = 1 the recurrence gives 3·2·a₃ = a₀.

options: eˣ and sin x are analytic at 0
questions.why: P and Q have convergent Taylor series at 0, which is the definition of an ordinary point.

questions.why: For x³y'' + y = 0, Q = 1/x³ and x²Q = 1/x is not analytic at 0.

questions.why: p₀ = 1/2 and q₀ = 0 give r(r − 1) + r/2 = r(r − 1/2) = 0.

questions.why: With t = √x the equation becomes y_tt + y = 0, giving cos t and sin t.

questions.why: p = 2(x − a) and q = 2(y − b), so p²/4 + q²/4 = z.

questions.q: z = f(x² + y²) satisfies:
questions.why: p = 2xf' and q = 2yf', so yp = xq.

questions.q: The general solution of xp + yq = z is:
questions.why: The integrals y/x = c₁ and z/x = c₂ give z/x = f(y/x).

questions.q: The general solution of p + q = 1 is:
questions.why: From dx = dy = dz the integrals x − y and z − x combine into z − x = f(x − y).

questions.q: For (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y, suitable multipliers are:
questions.why: Both give zero denominators: (y − z) + (z − x) + (x − y) = 0 and x(y − z) + y(z − x) + z(x − y) = 0.

questions.q: Lagrange's general solution is written as:
questions.why: Any relation between the two independent integrals u and v solves the PDE.

uni-bsc-math-group-theory.title: Group Theory (B.Sc Mathematics)
uni-bsc-math-group-theory.description: Groups, subgroups, cyclic and permutation groups, cosets and Lagrange, normal subgroups, quotient groups, homomorphisms, isomorphism theorems, Cayley, direct products and Sylow basics. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc (Hons) Mathematics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Groups: definitions, examples and elementary properties
courses.summary: Binary operations, the group axioms, standard examples (ℤ, ℤₙ, U(n), GL(2,ℝ), D₄, symmetries), elementary properties such as uniqueness of identity and inverses, cancellation laws and order of elements.
outcomes: State the group axioms and test whether a given set with an operation is a group
Work with the standard examples ℤₙ, U(n), GL(2,ℝ) and dihedral groups
Prove uniqueness of identity and inverses and the cancellation laws
Compute the order of an element and use (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹

lessons.title: Binary operations and the group axioms

scenes.text: Meera is laying square tiles and notices she can rotate a tile by 0°, 90°, 180° or 270° and it still fits the slot.
Doing two rotations one after another is again a rotation; doing nothing is a rotation; every rotation can be undone. These are exactly the group axioms.

steps.title: Binary operation
steps.body: A binary operation on a set G is a function * : G × G → G. The key word is closure: a*b must again lie in G. Subtraction is a binary operation on ℤ but not on ℕ, since 2 − 5 ∉ ℕ.

steps.title: Definition of a group
steps.body: (G, *) is a group if (G1) * is associative: (a*b)*c = a*(b*c); (G2) there is e ∈ G with e*a = a*e = a for all a; (G3) every a has an inverse a⁻¹ with a*a⁻¹ = a⁻¹*a = e. If also a*b = b*a for all a, b, the group is abelian. The order |G| is the number of elements.

steps.title: Worked example: ℤₙ and U(n)
steps.body: ℤₙ = {0, 1, …, n−1} under addition mod n is an abelian group with identity 0; the inverse of k is n − k. U(n) = {k : 1 ≤ k < n, gcd(k, n) = 1} under multiplication mod n is a group. U(10) = {1, 3, 7, 9}: 3·7 = 21 ≡ 1, so 3⁻¹ = 7; 9·9 = 81 ≡ 1, so 9⁻¹ = 9. |U(n)| = φ(n).

steps.title: Worked example: a non-standard operation
steps.body: On ℤ define a*b = a + b − 1. Closure: clear. Associative: (a*b)*c = a + b + c − 2 = a*(b*c). Identity: a*e = a + e − 1 = a gives e = 1. Inverse: a*a' = a + a' − 1 = 1 gives a' = 2 − a. So (ℤ, *) is an abelian group with identity 1.

steps.title: Worked example: GL(2, ℝ)
steps.body: The set of 2 × 2 real matrices with non-zero determinant is a group under multiplication: det(AB) = det A · det B ≠ 0 (closure), matrix multiplication is associative, I is the identity, and A⁻¹ exists because det A ≠ 0. It is non-abelian: [[1,1],[0,1]]·[[1,0],[1,1]] = [[2,1],[1,1]] but the reverse product is [[1,1],[1,2]].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: (1) Forgetting closure — (ℤ₆ \ {0}, × mod 6) fails since 2·3 = 0. (2) Checking a*e = a only on one side for a non-abelian candidate. (3) Assuming the identity is 0 or 1 — it depends on the operation (it was 1 for a + b − 1 above). (4) Thinking (ℤ, ×) is a group: 2 has no integer inverse.

activity.prompt: Is it a group?

quiz.q: Identity of (ℤ, a*b = a + b − 1):
quiz.why: Solving a + e − 1 = a gives e = 1, so 1 is the identity for this operation.

quiz.q: Inverse of 7 in U(15):
|U(20)| equals:
(ℤ, −) is not a group because:
options: no identity on both sides and not associative
quiz.why: Subtraction is not associative ((5−3)−1 ≠ 5−(3−1)) and 0 is only a right identity, so the axioms fail.

scenes.text: A hostel warden claims there are two different master keys that both 'do nothing' to any lock. A maths student proves that can't happen.
If e and e' are both identities, then e = e*e' = e'. Short proofs like this are the backbone of Unit 1 exam questions.

steps.title: Uniqueness of identity
steps.body: If e and e' are identities, e = e*e' (since e' is an identity) and e*e' = e' (since e is an identity), so e = e'.

steps.title: Uniqueness of inverse
steps.body: If b and c are inverses of a, then b = b*e = b*(a*c) = (b*a)*c = e*c = c. Associativity is used in the middle step.

steps.title: Cancellation and socks–shoes
steps.body: Left cancellation: ab = ac ⇒ b = c (multiply on the left by a⁻¹). Right cancellation similarly. Also (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹, because (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹) = a(bb⁻¹)a⁻¹ = e. And (a⁻¹)⁻¹ = a. Consequence: in a Cayley table each element appears exactly once in every row and column (Latin square).

steps.title: Worked example: a² = e for all a ⇒ abelian
steps.body: Suppose every element satisfies a² = e, so a = a⁻¹. For any a, b: ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba. Hence G is abelian. Example: U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7} where every square is 1.

steps.title: Worked example: (ab)² = a²b² ⇒ abelian
steps.body: abab = aabb. Cancel a on the left: bab = abb. Cancel b on the right: ba = ab. So G is abelian.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing (ab)⁻¹ = a⁻¹b⁻¹ — true only in abelian groups. Cancelling 'diagonally' (ab = ca ⇒ b = c) is invalid in non-abelian groups.

activity.prompt: Order the proof that the inverse is unique.
items: Assume b and c are both inverses of a
Write b = b*e
Replace e by a*c to get b*(a*c)
Use associativity: (b*a)*c
Since b*a = e, this is e*c = c, so b = c

quiz.q: (ab)⁻¹ in any group equals:
quiz.why: (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹) = a(bb⁻¹)a⁻¹ = aa⁻¹ = e, so the inverse of ab is b⁻¹a⁻¹ with order reversed.

quiz.q: Which property guarantees a Cayley table is a Latin square?
quiz.why: If an element appeared twice in row a, we would have ab = ac with b ≠ c, contradicting left cancellation.

quiz.q: If x² = e for all x in G, then G is:
quiz.why: Each element is its own inverse, so ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba, which makes G abelian.

quiz.q: Uniqueness of the inverse uses which axiom essentially?
quiz.why: The step b(ac) = (ba)c regroups the product, which is exactly associativity.

lessons.title: Order of an element and the dihedral group

scenes.text: On a 12-hour clock, adding 4 hours repeatedly returns to the start after 3 steps: 4, 8, 12.
We say 4 has order 3 in ℤ₁₂. The smallest positive n with aⁿ = e is the order of a.

steps.title: Order of an element
steps.body: |a| is the least n ≥ 1 with aⁿ = e (written na = 0 additively); if none exists, a has infinite order. In ℤₙ, |k| = n / gcd(k, n). In ℤ every non-zero element has infinite order.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body: If |a| = n then aᵐ = e ⇔ n | m. |a⁻¹| = |a|. |ab| = |ba|. If |a| = n then |aᵏ| = n / gcd(n, k).

steps.title: Worked example: orders in ℤ₁₂ and U(15)
Dihedral group Dₙ
steps.body: Dₙ is the symmetry group of a regular n-gon: n rotations R₀, R, …, Rⁿ⁻¹ (R = rotation by 360°/n) and n reflections. |Dₙ| = 2n. Presentation: Rⁿ = e, F² = e, FRF = R⁻¹. Every reflection has order 2; D₃ (order 6) is the smallest non-abelian group.

steps.title: Worked example: D₄
steps.body: D₄ has 8 elements: R₀, R₉₀, R₁₈₀, R₂₇₀, H, V, D, D'. Orders: R₉₀ and R₂₇₀ have order 4; R₁₈₀, H, V, D, D' have order 2; R₀ has order 1. HV = R₁₈₀ but H R₉₀ ≠ R₉₀ H, so D₄ is non-abelian.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using additive notation but writing powers: in ℤₙ, 'a³' means a + a + a. Do not confuse the order of an element with the order of the group.

lessons.title: Lab: Building and reading Cayley tables

scenes.text: An exam hands you a half-filled 4 × 4 Cayley table and asks you to finish it.
Using the Latin-square property and the identity row, you can complete it like a Sudoku.

steps.title: Reading a Cayley table
steps.body: Row a, column b holds a*b. The identity's row and column copy the header. The inverse of a is the column where e appears in row a. The group is abelian iff the table is symmetric about the main diagonal.

steps.title: Worked example: U(8)
steps.body: U(8) = {1,3,5,7}: 3·3 = 9 ≡ 1, 3·5 = 15 ≡ 7, 3·7 = 21 ≡ 5, 5·5 = 25 ≡ 1, 5·7 = 35 ≡ 3, 7·7 = 49 ≡ 1. Every element is self-inverse, the table is symmetric, so U(8) is abelian but not cyclic (no element of order 4). It is the Klein four-group V₄.

steps.title: Worked example: U(10) is cyclic
steps.body: U(10) = {1,3,7,9}: 3¹=3, 3²=9, 3³=27≡7, 3⁴=81≡1. So 3 generates all of U(10), which is cyclic of order 4, unlike U(8).

steps.title: Sudoku strategy
steps.body: Fill the identity row and column first, then use 'each element exactly once per row and column', then associativity checks for any remaining choices.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Build the Cayley table of ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ and compare with U(8). Matching 1↔(0,0), 3↔(1,0), 5↔(0,1), 7↔(1,1) gives the same pattern — they are isomorphic.

quiz.why: a*b = b*a for all a, b means entry (a,b) equals entry (b,a), which is symmetry about the main diagonal.

quiz.why: All three non-identity elements of U(8) have order 2, which is the defining pattern of the Klein four-group.

quiz.q: A generator of U(10) is:
quiz.why: The powers of 3 mod 10 are 3, 9, 7, 1, covering all of U(10).

quiz.q: In row a of the table, the column containing e gives:
quiz.why: If a*b = e then b is the inverse of a, so the column where e sits in row a is a⁻¹.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Subgroups and cyclic groups
courses.summary: Subgroup tests, centre and centraliser, cyclic groups, the fundamental theorem of cyclic groups, generators and the Euler phi function.
outcomes: Apply the one-step and finite subgroup tests
Compute centres and centralisers in small groups
Prove that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic
Count generators and subgroups of ℤₙ using φ and divisors
Draw the subgroup lattice of ℤₙ

scenes.text: A robot on the integer line may only take even-sized steps. Wherever it goes, it stays on even numbers.
The even integers 2ℤ form a group inside ℤ — a subgroup.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: H ⊆ G is a subgroup (H ≤ G) if H is itself a group under the operation of G. Every group has the trivial subgroup {e} and G itself; others are proper non-trivial subgroups.

steps.title: One-step and two-step tests
steps.body: One-step test: H non-empty and a, b ∈ H ⇒ ab⁻¹ ∈ H. Two-step test: H non-empty, closed under products and inverses. Finite subgroup test: if H is finite, non-empty and closed under the operation, then H ≤ G (inverses come free since aⁿ = e for some n).

steps.title: Worked example: nℤ ≤ ℤ
steps.body: Take a = nx, b = ny in nℤ. Then a − b = n(x − y) ∈ nℤ, and 0 ∈ nℤ. By the one-step test (additive form a − b), nℤ ≤ ℤ. In fact these are all the subgroups of ℤ.

steps.title: Worked example: SL(2, ℝ) ≤ GL(2, ℝ)
steps.body: SL(2,ℝ) = {A : det A = 1} contains I. If det A = det B = 1, then det(AB⁻¹) = det A / det B = 1. So SL(2,ℝ) is a subgroup.

steps.title: Worked example: a union that fails
steps.body: 2ℤ ∪ 3ℤ is not a subgroup of ℤ: 2 and 3 lie in it, but 2 + 3 = 5 does not. In general H ∪ K is a subgroup iff H ⊆ K or K ⊆ H, whereas H ∩ K is always a subgroup.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting to show H ≠ ∅ (usually by e ∈ H). Applying the finite subgroup test to an infinite set: ℕ is closed under + in ℤ but is not a subgroup.

activity.prompt: Is H a subgroup of G?

quiz.q: One-step test condition:
quiz.why: Together with non-emptiness, closure under ab⁻¹ gives the identity, inverses and closure.

quiz.q: Intersection of two subgroups is:
quiz.why: If a, b lie in both H and K, then ab⁻¹ lies in both, so H ∩ K passes the one-step test.

quiz.q: The finite subgroup test needs only:
options: non-empty and closed under the operation
quiz.why: For a finite set, closure forces each element to have finite order n, so a⁻¹ = aⁿ⁻¹ is automatically in H.

quiz.q: {0, 3, 6, 9} in ℤ₁₂ is:
quiz.why: It is ⟨3⟩, closed under addition mod 12 (e.g. 6 + 9 = 15 ≡ 3), hence a subgroup by the finite subgroup test.

scenes.text: Some elements commute with everyone in the group — like a friend who gets along with the entire class.
Collecting them gives the centre Z(G), always a subgroup and, as we will see later, always normal.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Z(G) = {a ∈ G : ax = xa for all x ∈ G}. For a fixed a, the centraliser C(a) = {g ∈ G : ga = ag}. Both are subgroups. Z(G) = ∩ C(a) over all a, and G is abelian iff Z(G) = G.

steps.title: Worked example: Z(D₄)
steps.body: In D₄ with rotations R₀, R₉₀, R₁₈₀, R₂₇₀ and reflections, R₁₈₀ commutes with every element (rotating by 180° is −I as a matrix). R₉₀ does not commute with H. Hence Z(D₄) = {R₀, R₁₈₀}. More generally Z(Dₙ) = {R₀, R₁₈₀} for even n ≥ 4 and {R₀} for odd n.

steps.title: Worked example: Z(GL(2,ℝ))
steps.body: A matrix commuting with every invertible matrix must be scalar: Z(GL(2,ℝ)) = {λI : λ ≠ 0}. Check with A = [[a,b],[c,d]] commuting with [[1,1],[0,1]]: this forces c = 0 and a = d; commuting with [[1,0],[1,1]] forces b = 0.

steps.title: Worked example: centraliser in D₄
steps.body: C(H) for a horizontal reflection H in D₄: H commutes with R₀, R₁₈₀, H and V. So C(H) = {R₀, R₁₈₀, H, V}, a subgroup of order 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing C(a) (depends on a) with Z(G) (commutes with everything). Z(G) is never empty: e ∈ Z(G).

quiz.why: Every element commutes with every other element precisely when the group is abelian.

quiz.why: For odd n there is no 180° rotation in Dₙ, and no other element commutes with all reflections, so the centre is trivial.

quiz.why: Commuting with all elementary matrices forces A to be a non-zero multiple of the identity.

quiz.why: aa = aa trivially, so every element lies in its own centraliser.

lessons.title: Cyclic groups and the fundamental theorem

scenes.text: A Ferris wheel with 12 cabins: pressing 'advance 1' repeatedly reaches every cabin. So does 'advance 5', but 'advance 4' only reaches three cabins.
That is ℤ₁₂: generators are the k with gcd(k, 12) = 1.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: G is cyclic if G = ⟨a⟩ = {aⁿ : n ∈ ℤ} for some a. Every cyclic group is abelian. Infinite cyclic groups are ≅ ℤ; finite cyclic groups of order n are ≅ ℤₙ.

steps.title: Theorem: subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic
steps.body: Proof sketch: let G = ⟨a⟩ and H ≤ G, H ≠ {e}. Let m be the least positive integer with aᵐ ∈ H. For any aᵏ ∈ H write k = qm + r with 0 ≤ r < m. Then aʳ = aᵏ(aᵐ)⁻ᑫ ∈ H, so minimality gives r = 0. Hence H = ⟨aᵐ⟩.

steps.title: Fundamental theorem of finite cyclic groups
steps.body: If |⟨a⟩| = n, then for each divisor k of n there is exactly one subgroup of order k, namely ⟨a^(n/k)⟩. ⟨aᵏ⟩ = ⟨a^gcd(n,k)⟩. aᵏ generates G iff gcd(k, n) = 1, so there are φ(n) generators. The number of elements of order d (d | n) is φ(d).

steps.title: Worked example: ℤ₃₀
steps.body: Divisors of 30: 1,2,3,5,6,10,15,30 → 8 subgroups. Generators: φ(30) = 30·(1/2)(2/3)(4/5) = 8, namely 1,7,11,13,17,19,23,29. The subgroup of order 5 is ⟨6⟩ = {0,6,12,18,24}. Elements of order 6: φ(6) = 2 (they are 5 and 25).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Abelian does not imply cyclic: U(8) ≅ V₄ is abelian but not cyclic. The number of generators of ℤ is 2 (namely ±1), not φ of anything.

scenes.text: Subgroups of ℤ₁₂ can be drawn as a diagram: ⟨1⟩ at the top, {0} at the bottom, joined by containment.

steps.title: Recipe
steps.body: For each divisor d of n, the unique subgroup of order d is ⟨n/d⟩. ⟨n/d₁⟩ ⊆ ⟨n/d₂⟩ iff d₁ | d₂.

steps.title: Worked example: ℤ₂₀
steps.body: Divisors 1,2,4,5,10,20 → 6 subgroups. Order-10 subgroup ⟨2⟩, order-4 ⟨5⟩ = {0,5,10,15}, order-5 ⟨4⟩, order-2 ⟨10⟩.

steps.title: Exam shortcut
steps.body: Number of subgroups of ℤₙ = τ(n), the number of divisors. If n = p₁^a₁ ⋯ p_k^a_k then τ(n) = (a₁+1)⋯(a_k+1). For 36 = 2²·3²: τ = 9.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Permutation groups, cosets and Lagrange's theorem
courses.summary: Cycle notation, order of a permutation, even and odd permutations, the alternating group Aₙ, cosets, Lagrange's theorem and its corollaries including Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem.
outcomes: Write permutations in cycle notation and multiply them
Find the order and parity of a permutation
Describe Sₙ and Aₙ and their orders
Prove Lagrange's theorem using cosets
Apply Fermat's and Euler's theorems to compute remainders

lessons.title: Cycle notation and products in Sₙ

scenes.text: Five friends swap seats: 1 moves to 3's chair, 3 to 5's, 5 back to 1's, while 2 and 4 swap.
We write this compactly as (1 3 5)(2 4) — a product of disjoint cycles.

steps.title: Sₙ
steps.body: Sₙ is the group of all bijections of {1, …, n} under composition; |Sₙ| = n!. Sₙ is non-abelian for n ≥ 3.

steps.title: Cycle notation and composition
steps.body: (a₁ a₂ … a_k) sends a₁→a₂→…→a_k→a₁. Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles, unique up to order. Disjoint cycles commute. Convention used here: compose right to left, so in στ apply τ first.

steps.title: Order of a permutation
steps.body: The order of a product of disjoint cycles is the lcm of the cycle lengths. (1 2 3)(4 5) has order lcm(3, 2) = 6. A k-cycle has order k.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing left-to-right and right-to-left conventions — state yours. The order of non-disjoint cycles is NOT the lcm of their lengths: (1 3)(1 2) = (1 2 3) has order 3, not 2.

activity.prompt: What is the largest possible order of an element of S₇? (Hint: maximise the lcm of cycle lengths summing to at most 7.)

quiz.q: Order of (1 2 3 4)(5 6) in S₆:
quiz.why: For disjoint cycles the order is lcm(4, 2) = 4.

quiz.q: |S₅| equals:
(1 3)(1 2), composed right to left, equals:
Disjoint cycles:
quiz.why: They move different symbols, so applying them in either order gives the same result.

scenes.text: Any shuffle can be achieved by swapping two cards at a time.
Remarkably, the number of swaps is always even or always odd for a given shuffle — never both.

steps.title: Transpositions
steps.body: A 2-cycle is a transposition. Every permutation is a product of transpositions: (a₁ a₂ … a_k) = (a₁ a_k)(a₁ a_{k−1})⋯(a₁ a₂), which uses k − 1 transpositions.

steps.title: Parity theorem
steps.body: If e = τ₁τ₂⋯τ_r with transpositions τᵢ, then r is even. Hence a permutation cannot be both even and odd. A k-cycle is even iff k is odd.

steps.title: Alternating group
steps.body: Aₙ = set of even permutations in Sₙ is a subgroup of order n!/2 (n ≥ 2). Multiplying by (1 2) is a bijection between even and odd permutations, giving the count.

steps.title: Worked example: parity
steps.body: σ = (1 2 5)(3 4 6 7): a 3-cycle (2 transpositions) and a 4-cycle (3 transpositions) → 5 transpositions → odd. Its order is lcm(3,4) = 12.

steps.title: Worked example: elements of A₄
steps.body: |A₄| = 12: identity, eight 3-cycles such as (1 2 3), and three double transpositions (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3). A₄ has no subgroup of order 6 — the standard counterexample to the converse of Lagrange.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling a 3-cycle odd because 3 is odd — it is even (two transpositions). Odd permutations do not form a subgroup (no identity).

activity.prompt: Even or odd?

quiz.q: |A₅| equals:
A 6-cycle is:
quiz.why: A k-cycle is a product of k − 1 = 5 transpositions, an odd number.

quiz.q: A₄ has no subgroup of order:
quiz.why: Although 6 divides 12, A₄ has no subgroup of order 6, showing that the converse of Lagrange fails.

quiz.q: Which set is NOT a subgroup of Sₙ?
quiz.why: The product of two odd permutations is even, and the identity is even, so odd permutations are not closed and lack e.

scenes.text: A class of 12 students forms identical-sized teams by shifting one team around.
Every team has the same size, so the team size must divide 12 — that is Lagrange's theorem.

steps.title: Cosets
steps.body: For H ≤ G and a ∈ G, the left coset aH = {ah : h ∈ H}. Properties: a ∈ aH; aH = H iff a ∈ H; aH = bH iff a⁻¹b ∈ H; any two left cosets are equal or disjoint; |aH| = |H| (h ↦ ah is a bijection).

steps.title: Lagrange's theorem
steps.body: If G is finite and H ≤ G then |H| divides |G|, and the number of distinct left cosets is [G : H] = |G|/|H|. Proof: the left cosets partition G into blocks each of size |H|.

steps.title: Corollaries
steps.body: (1) |a| divides |G|. (2) a^|G| = e. (3) A group of prime order is cyclic. (4) Fermat: aᵖ ≡ a (mod p). (5) Euler: if gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), applying (2) to U(n).

steps.title: Worked example: cosets of H = {0, 4, 8} in ℤ₁₂
Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming the converse: |G| divisible by d does not guarantee a subgroup of order d (A₄, d = 6). Using Euler's theorem when gcd(a, n) ≠ 1.

quiz.why: Element orders must divide 35, and 7 is the only option that does.

scenes.text: University papers love 'find all left cosets of H in G' and 'use Lagrange to show …'.
This lab drills the procedure until it is automatic.

steps.title: Procedure for listing cosets
steps.body: Write H. Pick an element not yet covered, multiply it by every element of H, record the coset. Repeat until all of G is covered. Check: number of cosets × |H| = |G|.

steps.title: Worked example: cosets of H = {e, (1 2)} in S₃
steps.body: (1 3)H = {(1 3), (1 3)(1 2)} = {(1 3), (1 2 3)}. (2 3)H = {(2 3), (2 3)(1 2)} = {(2 3), (1 3 2)}. Together with H these are three left cosets of size 2. Right coset H(1 3) = {(1 3), (1 2)(1 3)} = {(1 3), (1 3 2)} ≠ (1 3)H — so left and right cosets can differ.

steps.title: Worked example: order of an element in U(n)
steps.body: |U(21)| = φ(21) = 12, so any element's order divides 12. For 2: 2² = 4, 2³ = 8, 2⁴ = 16, 2⁶ = 64 = 3·21 + 1 ≡ 1. Since 2¹, 2², 2³, 2⁴ ≢ 1, |2| = 6.

steps.title: Viva tip
steps.body: Lagrange is about subgroups; the converse holds for cyclic groups (a unique subgroup for each divisor) and for prime powers via Sylow (Unit 5).

courses.title: Unit 4 · Normal subgroups, quotient groups and homomorphisms
courses.summary: Normal subgroups and tests, factor groups, homomorphisms and kernels, isomorphisms, Cayley's theorem and the three isomorphism theorems with standard applications.
outcomes: Test normality using gHg⁻¹ ⊆ H or index 2
Construct quotient groups and compute their orders and element orders
Find kernels and images of homomorphisms
State and prove the first isomorphism theorem
Apply Cayley's theorem and the second and third isomorphism theorems

story.title: Rules that survive a change of viewpoint

scenes.text: Rotations of a triangle stay rotations even if you first flip the triangle, rotate, then flip back.
A subgroup that survives every such 'conjugation' is called normal.

steps.title: Definition and tests
steps.body: H ≤ G is normal (H ⊴ G) if gH = Hg for all g ∈ G, equivalently gHg⁻¹ ⊆ H for all g. Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal. {e}, G and Z(G) are always normal.

steps.title: Index-2 theorem
steps.body: If [G : H] = 2 then H ⊴ G: the two left cosets are H and G \ H, and so are the two right cosets, hence gH = Hg. So Aₙ ⊴ Sₙ and the rotation subgroup is normal in Dₙ.

steps.title: Worked example: SL(2,ℝ) ⊴ GL(2,ℝ)
steps.body: For A ∈ GL(2,ℝ), B ∈ SL(2,ℝ): det(ABA⁻¹) = det A · 1 · (det A)⁻¹ = 1, so ABA⁻¹ ∈ SL(2,ℝ). Hence SL(2,ℝ) is normal.

steps.title: Worked example: a non-normal subgroup
steps.body: H = {e, (1 2)} in S₃. Conjugate by (1 3): (1 3)(1 2)(1 3) = (2 3) ∉ H. So H is not normal (consistent with Unit 3, where (1 3)H ≠ H(1 3)).

steps.title: Worked example: V₄ ⊴ A₄
steps.body: V = {e, (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3)}. Conjugation preserves cycle type, and V contains all elements of A₄ of type (2,2), so gVg⁻¹ = V for all g ∈ A₄.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: gH = Hg does NOT mean gh = hg for each h; it is equality of sets. Normality is not transitive: K ⊴ H ⊴ G need not give K ⊴ G (e.g. a subgroup of order 2 in V₄ inside A₄).

activity.prompt: Normal in G or not?

quiz.q: A subgroup of index 2 is:
quiz.why: With only two cosets, the left and right cosets other than H are both G \ H, so gH = Hg.

quiz.q: (1 3)(1 2)(1 3) in S₃ equals:
quiz.why: Conjugating a transposition by (1 3) relabels 1 ↔ 3, turning (1 2) into (3 2) = (2 3).

quiz.q: In an abelian group every subgroup is:
quiz.why: ghg⁻¹ = hgg⁻¹ = h, so every conjugate lies in H.

quiz.q: gH = Hg means:
options: the sets gH and Hg are equal
quiz.why: Normality requires equality of cosets as sets; individual elements may be rearranged.

scenes.text: A clock does not care whether it is hour 3 or 15 or 27 — they are 'the same' modulo 12.
Gluing each coset of 12ℤ into one point gives ℤ/12ℤ ≅ ℤ₁₂, a quotient group.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: If N ⊴ G, the set G/N of cosets is a group under (aN)(bN) = abN. Normality is exactly what makes this well defined. Identity N, inverse (aN)⁻¹ = a⁻¹N, and |G/N| = |G|/|N|.

steps.title: Worked example: ℤ₁₈/⟨6⟩
steps.body: ⟨6⟩ = {0,6,12}, so |ℤ₁₈/⟨6⟩| = 18/3 = 6. The coset 4 + ⟨6⟩ has order 3 (since 3·4 = 12 ∈ ⟨6⟩ and 4, 8 ∉ ⟨6⟩). The quotient is cyclic, generated by 1 + ⟨6⟩, so ≅ ℤ₆.

steps.title: Worked example: (ℤ₄ × ℤ₄)/⟨(2,2)⟩
steps.body: |ℤ₄ × ℤ₄| = 16, the subgroup ⟨(2,2)⟩ = {(0,0),(2,2)} has order 2, so the quotient has order 8. The coset (1,0) + H has order 4. Element (1,1) + H: 2(1,1) = (2,2) ∈ H, order 2. This quotient is ≅ ℤ₄ × ℤ₂.

steps.title: G/Z theorem
steps.body: If G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is abelian. Consequence: G/Z(G) can never have prime order for non-abelian G; e.g. a non-abelian group of order pq cannot have |Z(G)| = p.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forming G/H when H is not normal — the coset product is then not well defined. Confusing the order of a coset aN with the order of a in G (it divides |a|).

activity.prompt: Find the order of the element 5 + ⟨4⟩ in the quotient group ℤ₂₄/⟨4⟩.

quiz.q: |ℤ₃₀/⟨5⟩| equals:
quiz.why: ⟨5⟩ has order 6 in ℤ₃₀, so the quotient has order 30/6 = 5.

quiz.q: Why must N be normal to form G/N?
options: so that (aN)(bN) = abN is well defined
quiz.why: Normality ensures that the product coset does not depend on which representatives a and b are chosen.

quiz.q: If G/Z(G) is cyclic, then:
quiz.why: Writing every element as gⁱz with z central shows any two elements commute.

quiz.q: Identity element of G/N is:
quiz.why: The coset eN = N satisfies (aN)N = aN, so N is the identity of the quotient.

scenes.text: The exponential map turns addition into multiplication: e^(x+y) = eˣeʸ.
A homomorphism is any such translation that respects the operations.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: φ : G → G' is a homomorphism if φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b). Then φ(e) = e', φ(a⁻¹) = φ(a)⁻¹, |φ(a)| divides |a|. Kernel ker φ = {a : φ(a) = e'} is a normal subgroup; φ is injective iff ker φ = {e}. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body: (1) det : GL(2,ℝ) → ℝ* has kernel SL(2,ℝ). (2) φ : ℤ → ℤₙ, φ(k) = k mod n, kernel nℤ. (3) sign : Sₙ → {±1}, kernel Aₙ. (4) exp : (ℝ, +) → (ℝ⁺, ×) is an isomorphism with inverse ln.

steps.title: Worked example: homomorphisms ℤ₁₂ → ℤ₃₀
steps.body: A homomorphism is fixed by φ(1) = a with 12a ≡ 0 (mod 30), i.e. |a| divides 12 and 30, so |a| divides gcd(12,30) = 6. The elements of ℤ₃₀ whose order divides 6 form the subgroup ⟨5⟩ of order 6. So there are 6 homomorphisms.

steps.title: Cayley's theorem
steps.body: Every group G is isomorphic to a group of permutations. Proof: for g ∈ G define T_g(x) = gx. Each T_g is a bijection of G, T_gT_h = T_gh, and g ↦ T_g is injective. So a group of order n embeds in Sₙ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming a map with φ(e) = e' is a homomorphism — you must check φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b). Two groups of the same order need not be isomorphic (ℤ₄ vs V₄): compare element orders.

scenes.text: The determinant forgets everything about a matrix except one number.
The first isomorphism theorem says: what survives (the image) is exactly the group modulo what is forgotten (the kernel).

steps.title: First isomorphism theorem
steps.body: If φ : G → G' is a homomorphism then G/ker φ ≅ φ(G), via ψ(g ker φ) = φ(g). Proof: ψ is well defined and injective since g ker φ = h ker φ ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ ker φ ⇔ φ(g) = φ(h); it is a homomorphism because φ is; it is onto φ(G) by construction.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: (1) ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ (reduction mod n). (2) GL(2,ℝ)/SL(2,ℝ) ≅ ℝ* (det is onto). (3) Sₙ/Aₙ ≅ ℤ₂. (4) ℝ/ℤ ≅ circle group S¹ via x ↦ e^(2πix).

steps.title: Second and third theorems
steps.body: Second: H ≤ G, N ⊴ G ⇒ HN ≤ G, H ∩ N ⊴ H and H/(H ∩ N) ≅ HN/N. Third: N ⊆ K both normal in G ⇒ (G/N)/(K/N) ≅ G/K.

steps.title: Worked example: second theorem in ℤ
steps.body: H = 6ℤ, N = 4ℤ. HN = H + N = gcd(6,4)ℤ = 2ℤ, H ∩ N = lcm(6,4)ℤ = 12ℤ. The theorem gives 6ℤ/12ℤ ≅ 2ℤ/4ℤ — both have order 2. ✔

steps.title: Worked example: third theorem
steps.body: (ℤ/12ℤ)/(4ℤ/12ℤ) ≅ ℤ/4ℤ ≅ ℤ₄. Check orders: 12/3 = 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting to prove that φ is onto when claiming G/ker φ ≅ G'. If not onto, the quotient is isomorphic only to the image.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Direct products, class equation and Sylow theorems
courses.summary: External direct products and when ℤₘ × ℤₙ is cyclic, the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, conjugacy classes and the class equation, Cauchy's theorem and the Sylow theorems with applications to groups of small order.
outcomes: Compute orders of elements in direct products using lcm
Decide when ℤₘ × ℤₙ ≅ ℤₘₙ
List all abelian groups of a given order up to isomorphism
Write the class equation and deduce that p-groups have non-trivial centre
Use Sylow theorems to show groups of certain orders are not simple

scenes.text: A lock has a 2-position dial and a 3-position dial turning together one click at a time.
After 6 clicks both return to start for the first time — ℤ₂ × ℤ₃ behaves like ℤ₆.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: G₁ × G₂ = {(g₁, g₂)} with componentwise operation. |G₁ × G₂| = |G₁||G₂|. The order of (g₁, g₂) is lcm(|g₁|, |g₂|).

steps.title: When is it cyclic?
steps.body: ℤₘ × ℤₙ ≅ ℤₘₙ iff gcd(m, n) = 1. Similarly U(st) ≅ U(s) × U(t) for coprime s, t.

steps.title: Worked example: element orders
steps.body: In ℤ₄ × ℤ₆, |(2, 3)| = lcm(2, 2) = 2; |(1, 1)| = lcm(4, 6) = 12 — the maximum, but |ℤ₄ × ℤ₆| = 24, so the group is not cyclic (gcd(4,6) = 2).

steps.title: Worked example: counting elements of order 2
steps.body: ℤ₂ × ℤ₄: elements of order dividing 2 are (a, b) with 2a = 0, 2b = 0: a ∈ {0,1}, b ∈ {0,2} → 4 elements, minus the identity → 3 elements of order 2.

steps.title: Fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups
steps.body: Every finite abelian group is a direct product of cyclic groups of prime-power order, uniquely up to order. The number of abelian groups of order pᵏ equals the number of partitions of k. Order 72 = 2³·3²: p(3)·p(2) = 3·2 = 6 groups.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ ≅ ℤ₄ — gcd(2,2) ≠ 1. Taking the product of orders instead of the lcm for an element's order.

lessons.title: Conjugacy classes and the class equation

scenes.text: In S₄, (1 2) and (3 4) look different but one is just a relabelling of the other.
Grouping elements by 'shape' gives conjugacy classes, and counting them gives the class equation.

steps.title: Conjugacy
steps.body: a ~ b if b = gag⁻¹ for some g. This is an equivalence relation; the class of a is cl(a). |cl(a)| = [G : C(a)], so class sizes divide |G|. In Sₙ, two permutations are conjugate iff they have the same cycle type.

steps.title: Class equation
steps.body: |G| = |Z(G)| + Σ [G : C(a)], the sum over one representative a of each non-central class (each term > 1 and divides |G|).

steps.title: Worked example: S₃
steps.body: Classes: {e}, three transpositions, two 3-cycles. Class equation 6 = 1 + 3 + 2. |Z(S₃)| = 1.

steps.title: Worked example: S₄
steps.body: Cycle types: e (1), transpositions C(4,2) = 6, double transpositions 3, 3-cycles 8, 4-cycles 6. Class equation 24 = 1 + 6 + 3 + 8 + 6.

steps.title: p-groups
steps.body: If |G| = pⁿ (n ≥ 1) then Z(G) ≠ {e}: every non-central term is a positive power of p, so |Z(G)| ≡ |G| ≡ 0 (mod p). Corollary: every group of order p² is abelian (ℤ_{p²} or ℤₚ × ℤₚ).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including central elements in the sum. Forgetting that class sizes must divide |G| — a class equation like 10 = 1 + 4 + 5 is impossible since 4 ∤ 10.

scenes.text: Lagrange limits what subgroups can exist; Sylow guarantees that some actually do.
For |G| = 12 = 2²·3, there must be subgroups of order 4 and 3.

steps.title: Cauchy's theorem
steps.body: If a prime p divides |G|, then G has an element of order p.

steps.title: Sylow theorems
steps.body: Let |G| = pᵏm with p ∤ m. (1) G has a subgroup of order pᵏ (a Sylow p-subgroup). (2) Any two Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate. (3) The number nₚ of Sylow p-subgroups satisfies nₚ ≡ 1 (mod p) and nₚ | m. nₚ = 1 iff the Sylow p-subgroup is normal.

steps.title: Worked example: groups of order 15 are cyclic
steps.body: n₃ | 5 and n₃ ≡ 1 (mod 3) ⇒ n₃ = 1. n₅ | 3 and n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5) ⇒ n₅ = 1. Both Sylow subgroups P (order 3) and Q (order 5) are normal, P ∩ Q = {e}, so G ≅ P × Q ≅ ℤ₃ × ℤ₅ ≅ ℤ₁₅.

steps.title: Worked example: no simple group of order 20
steps.body: 20 = 2²·5. n₅ | 4 and n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5) ⇒ n₅ = 1. So the Sylow 5-subgroup is normal and G is not simple.

steps.title: Worked example: order 12
steps.body: n₃ ∈ {1, 4}. If n₃ = 4, the four subgroups of order 3 give 4·2 = 8 elements of order 3, leaving 4 elements, which must form the unique Sylow 2-subgroup (normal). Either way a group of order 12 has a normal Sylow subgroup. A₄ is the case n₃ = 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using nₚ | |G| instead of nₚ | m. Forgetting that distinct subgroups of prime order p intersect trivially, which is what makes element counting work.

lessons.title: Lab: Classifying groups of small order

scenes.text: Up to order 8 there are only a handful of groups — learn them like animals in a zoo.
Knowing this table answers many 'show that' questions instantly.

steps.title: Table of groups up to order 8
steps.body: 1: trivial. 2, 3, 5, 7: ℤₚ. 4: ℤ₄, ℤ₂×ℤ₂. 6: ℤ₆, S₃. 8: ℤ₈, ℤ₄×ℤ₂, ℤ₂³, D₄, Q₈ (quaternions). Total for order 8: five groups, three abelian.

steps.title: Quaternion group Q₈
steps.body: Q₈ = {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} with i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1. It has one element of order 2 (−1) and six of order 4, while D₄ has five elements of order 2 — so Q₈ ≇ D₄.

steps.title: Groups of order 2p
steps.body: For an odd prime p, a group of order 2p is either ℤ₂ₚ or the dihedral group Dₚ. So groups of order 10 are ℤ₁₀ or D₅; of order 14, ℤ₁₄ or D₇.

steps.title: Decision procedure
steps.body: Given |G|: factor it; if prime → cyclic; if p² → abelian; if pq with p < q and p ∤ q − 1 → cyclic; otherwise use Sylow counting and element orders to decide.
